mcqs.question: Human to human transmission not seen in:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
73. Viral Meningitis and Myelitis: Polio, Coxsackie
mcqs.explanation:
(b) (Japanese...) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p488-89, Ananthanarayan 9/e p521
• Japanese encephalitis: Human infection is tangential dead end and it occurs when the infected mosquitoes reach high
density
• SARS and Bird’s flu will be transmitted from man to man by direct contact with infected respiratory secretions
• HIV-transmitted from human to human by parenteral route, vertical (infected mother) and sexual route
• Poliomyelitis transmitted through: Fe co-oral route (ingestion), Inhalation or through conjunctiva.

mcqs.question: According to Spaulding classification, laparoscope and arthroscopic instruments are under:
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: (a) (Critical item) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p42

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A previously healthy 30-year-old develops myocarditis. Which organism category is the most common infective cause overall?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Viruses, particularly Coxsackievirus and Herpesviruses, are the most common infective cause of myocarditis overall.
- (A) Bacterial myocarditis is a recognized but less common cause than viral myocarditis.
- (C) Trichinella spiralis is a recognized parasitic cause of myocarditis, but it is far less common than viral causes.
- (D) Fungal myocarditis is uncommon and generally seen in immunocompromised patients, not the leading overall cause.

• The most common food associated with botulism are home preserved foods such as home canned vegetables, smoked
or pickled fish, homemade cheese and similar low acid food.

mcqs.question: Best disinfectant for endoscopes is:
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control

options.text: High risk of anomalies, serious consideration for termination

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A female became pregnant after 1month of taking MMR vaccine; though was advised to avoid pregnancy. What advice the doctor should give to the patient?

66. Myxovirus Infections: Influenza, Parainfluenza, Mumps, RSV

(d) (wait and watch) Ref: Apurba Sastry's Essentials of Medical Microbiology/p473
Receipt of Rubella vaccine during pregnancy is not ordinarily a reason to consider termination of the pregnancy. Harrison
19th/p1299 (230e), Nelson’s paediatrics 20th/p1511
Vaccine should not be administered during pregnancy. If pregnancy occurs within 28 days of immunization, the patient
should be counselled on the theoretical risks to the foetus. Studies of over 200 women who had been inadvertently immunized with rubella vaccine during pregnancy showed that none of their offspring developed congenital rubella syndrome.
Therefore, interruption of pregnancy is probably not warranted ………… Nelson’s paediatrics 20th/p1511

options.text: A "ninja-star" nucleus appearance in myocyte nuclei
Myocyte nuclei with an "owl's-eye" inclusion body

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old man with a long history of heavy alcohol use presents with progressive dyspnea and biventricular heart failure. Echocardiography shows dilation of all four cardiac chambers with globally reduced contractility. Endomyocardial biopsy would most likely show which characteristic nuclear finding?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (A): Dilated cardiomyopathy (here, alcohol-related, one of its most common causes along with idiopathic and Titin gene mutation) classically shows a distinctive "ninja-star" nucleus appearance in myocyte nuclei on microscopy.
- (B) an "owl's-eye" nuclear inclusion is a classic descriptor for CMV inclusion bodies (a different, infectious context) or for Anitschkow cells in cross-section (a cytoplasmic/nuclear chromatin pattern, not a DCM finding).
- (C) "helter-skelter" myocyte disarray is the characteristic microscopic finding of HOCM, not DCM.
- (D) hemosiderin-laden macrophages are the "heart failure cells" seen in the lungs in left heart failure, not a myocyte nuclear finding in DCM.

options.text: Dilated cardiomyopathy, triggered by chronic alcohol use
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, triggered by a catecholamine surge from acute emotional stress
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, triggered by exertion
Restrictive cardiomyopathy, triggered by amyloid deposition

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 62-year-old woman develops sudden chest pain and ECG changes mimicking an acute MI shortly after learning of her husband's unexpected death. Coronary angiography is entirely normal, but echocardiography shows apical ballooning of the left ventricle with a hypercontractile base. What is the diagnosis and its trigger?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Takotsubo ("broken heart syndrome") is triggered by intense emotional (or physical) stress causing a catecholamine surge, producing transient apical LV ballooning while the base remains contractile, with normal coronary arteries — matching this vignette precisely.
- (A) DCM involves all four chambers chronically and is not triggered by an acute emotional event, nor does it typically present with normal coronaries mimicking an MI in this acute fashion.
- (C) HOCM is triggered by exertion (not emotional stress) and shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy, not apical ballooning.
- (D) Restrictive cardiomyopathy presents with diastolic heart failure, not acute apical ballooning mimicking MI.

options.text: DCM is a chronic structural disease involving all four chambers (genetic/toxic causes), while Takotsubo is an acute, usually reversible, catecholamine-driven event limited to the left ventricle
DCM is always reversible while Takotsubo causes permanent structural damage
DCM affects only the right ventricle while Takotsubo affects only the left atrium
There is no meaningful difference; they are two names for the same disease process

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: How do dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) and Takotsubo cardiomyopathy fundamentally differ, despite both causing ventricular dilation and heart failure symptoms?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (A): DCM is a chronic structural disease affecting all four chambers with genetic/toxic causes, whereas Takotsubo is an acute, usually fully reversible, catecholamine-driven event confined to the left ventricle (apical ballooning).
- (B) reverses the correct reversibility pattern — Takotsubo, not DCM, is the one that is usually reversible.
- (C) misdescribes both conditions' chamber involvement; DCM affects all four chambers, and Takotsubo affects the LV specifically (apex), not the left atrium.
- (D) incorrectly denies any meaningful distinction between two conditions with clearly different mechanisms, chronicity, and chamber involvement.

options.text: Inotropic agents, since they can worsen the dynamic outflow obstruction
Beta-blockers, which are the mainstay of supportive therapy
ACE inhibitors, which are used during recovery
Anticoagulants, which have no role in Takotsubo management

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In a patient with Takotsubo cardiomyopathy complicated by LV outflow tract obstruction and hypotension, which class of drug should generally be avoided?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (A): When LV outflow tract obstruction is present in Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, inotropic agents should generally be avoided, since increasing contractility can worsen the dynamic obstruction (similar reasoning to HOCM).
- (B) Beta-blockers are, in fact, part of supportive management during recovery, not a drug to avoid.
- (C) ACE inhibitors are also used during the recovery phase, not contraindicated.
- (D) is a distractor; anticoagulation may in fact be considered in some cases (e.g. apical thrombus risk from stunned myocardium), so it is not accurately described as having "no role."

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Patient has history of brain abscess. On examination, branching weak acid fast and Gram positive bacilli were seen.
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
55. Miscellaneous Bacterial Skin: Anthrax, Actinomycosis, Nocardiosis, Nonvenereal Treponematoses
mcqs.explanation:
(a) (Nocardia) Ref: ApurbaSastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p294
Nocardia is branching weak acid fast and Gram positive bacillus and is associated with brain abscess.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 19-year-old competitive athlete collapses suddenly during a match and cannot be resuscitated. Autopsy reveals asymmetric hypertrophy of the interventricular septum bulging into the LV outflow tract. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the gene most classically implicated in this condition. Which gene is this?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (D): This is the classic presentation of HOCM-related sudden cardiac death in a young athlete, caused by an autosomal dominant mutation in MYH7 (β-myosin heavy chain), a sarcomeric contractile protein gene.
- (A) Desmoplakin mutations are associated with ARVC, not HOCM.
- (B) Fibrillin-1 mutations cause Marfan syndrome, an unrelated connective tissue disorder.
- (C) Titin gene mutations are among the causes of dilated cardiomyopathy, not HOCM.

options.text: Standing suddenly from a seated position
Squatting (increases preload/afterload, reducing the dynamic outflow obstruction)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A young patient with HOCM has a harsh systolic ejection murmur. Which manoeuvre would be expected to DECREASE the intensity of this murmur, in contrast to its behaviour in aortic stenosis?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (D): Squatting increases venous return (preload) and afterload, which reduces the dynamic LV outflow obstruction in HOCM and therefore decreases the murmur — the opposite response compared to aortic stenosis, where squatting/increased afterload tends to increase the murmur.
- (A) Valsalva decreases preload, which worsens (increases) the HOCM murmur, not decreases it.
- (B) Standing also decreases preload, worsening (increasing) the HOCM murmur.
- (C) is a distractor not specifically described as decreasing the murmur in this context; the clearly described maneuver that decreases the HOCM murmur is squatting.

options.text: "Helter-skelter" myocyte disarray — disrupts normal conduction pathways, creating a substrate for re-entrant ventricular arrhythmias
Contraction band necrosis — indicates recent reperfusion injury
Aschoff body formation — pathognomonic for rheumatic carditis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Histologic examination of the hypertrophied interventricular septum in a patient with HOCM shows myocytes running in random, disorganised directions rather than neat parallel bundles. What is this finding called, and what is its clinical significance?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (A): This is the "helter-skelter" pattern of myocyte disarray characteristic of HOCM — the disorganised architecture disrupts normal conduction, creating a substrate for re-entrant ventricular arrhythmias, the mechanistic link to sudden cardiac death.
- (B) contraction band necrosis is a reperfusion-related acute finding with a different appearance (hypercontracted eosinophilic bands), unrelated to this chronic disarray pattern.
- (C) Aschoff bodies are the characteristic lesion of rheumatic carditis, an entirely different disease process.
- (D) fibrofatty replacement of the RV wall is the characteristic finding of ARVC, not HOCM.

options.text: Mutations in desmosomal proteins (e.g. plakophilin-2, desmoplakin), causing intercalated disc failure and myocyte detachment
Extracellular amyloid deposition stiffening the ventricular wall

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A young patient presents with palpitations and syncope. ECG shows an epsilon wave and T-wave inversion in leads V1–V3. Cardiac MRI shows the right ventricular free wall replaced by fibrofatty tissue with a thin, aneurysmal appearance. What is the molecular basis of this condition?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): This is the classic presentation of ARVC — caused by mutations in desmosomal proteins (plakophilin-2, desmoplakin, desmoglein, plakoglobin), which cause intercalated disc failure, myocyte detachment and death, and progressive fibrofatty replacement of the RV free wall.
- (A) MYH7 mutations cause HOCM, presenting with septal hypertrophy, not RV fibrofatty replacement.
- (C) Amyloid deposition causes restrictive cardiomyopathy, with diastolic dysfunction rather than this ECG/imaging picture.
- (D) Iron overload (hemochromatosis) classically causes dilated cardiomyopathy, not ARVC.

options.text: Desmoplakin mutation — Carvajal syndrome (a related but distinct AR desmosomal disease)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A child presents with a fully penetrant triad of cardiomyopathy resembling ARVC, woolly hair, and palmoplantar keratoderma. Genetic testing confirms an autosomal recessive mutation. Which gene and syndrome does this represent?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (D): This triad of ARVC + woolly hair + palmoplantar keratoderma, with autosomal recessive inheritance, is Naxos syndrome, caused specifically by a plakoglobin mutation.
- (A) MYH7 causes HOCM, not this cutaneous-cardiac triad.
- (B) Carvajal syndrome is a related but distinct desmoplakin-mutation AR disease (typically associated with dilated rather than arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy) — a close but incorrect distractor for this specific vignette, which matches the classic Naxos description.
- (C) Fibrillin-1 mutations cause Marfan syndrome, an unrelated connective tissue disorder with no cutaneous-cardiac triad of this type.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Surgical blade is sterilized by?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation:
(a) (Autoclave) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p41
• Steam is the preferred method for sterilizing critical medical and surgical instruments that are not damaged by heat,
steam, pressure, or moisture............ CDC Guideline, 2008
• Metal instruments and surgical blades are better sterilized by autoclave.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with restrictive cardiomyopathy is found to have extensive eosinophilic, extracellular deposits within the ventricular wall on biopsy, stiffening it and impairing diastolic filling while systolic function remains preserved until late in the disease. What is the most likely underlying cause?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Amyloidosis is the most common cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy, producing eosinophilic, extracellular deposits that stiffen the ventricular wall and impair diastolic filling while systolic function is preserved until late.
- (A) Hemochromatosis (iron overload) classically causes dilated cardiomyopathy (impaired contractility, systolic failure), NOT restrictive cardiomyopathy — a commonly flipped exam fact.
- (C) Titin gene mutations are associated with dilated cardiomyopathy, not restrictive cardiomyopathy.
- (D) Desmosomal protein mutations are associated with ARVC, not restrictive cardiomyopathy.

options.text: Metastasis (secondaries) from tumours elsewhere in the body

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Considering all cardiac tumours together (not just primary tumours), which is the most common cardiac malignancy overall?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Metastatic (secondary) tumours to the heart far outnumber all primary cardiac tumours combined, making metastasis the most common cardiac malignancy overall.
- (A) Angiosarcoma is the most common primary malignant cardiac tumour in adults, but this is a much smaller category than metastatic disease overall.
- (C) Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary malignant cardiac tumour in children, again a smaller category than metastatic disease.
- (D) "Myxosarcoma" is not a standard recognized entity in this classification scheme.

options.text: Myxoma; lepidic (stellate/globular) cells in a myxoid stroma

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with positional syncope that worsens when she lies down, along with fever, weight loss, and a raised ESR, initially raising suspicion for infective endocarditis. Echocardiography reveals a pedunculated, gelatinous mass attached by a stalk within the left atrium, prolapsing through the mitral valve. What is the most likely diagnosis, and its characteristic microscopic cell?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (C): This is the classic myxoma triad — obstructive (positional symptoms from the "ball valve" effect at the mitral orifice), embolic, and constitutional (fever, weight loss, raised ESR mimicking IE) — with characteristic lepidic cells in a myxoid stroma, and myxoma is the most common primary benign cardiac tumour in adults, classically in the left atrium.
- (A) Rhabdomyoma (spider cells) is the pediatric benign tumour, typically in the ventricles, not matching this adult presentation.
- (B) Papillary fibroelastoma arises directly on a valve leaflet (sea-anemone appearance), not as a pedunculated atrial mass with this constitutional symptom triad.
- (D) Angiosarcoma is an aggressive malignant tumour, typically right atrial, presenting with tamponade/metastasis — inconsistent with this relatively indolent, classic myxoma presentation.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: An infant is found to have multiple tumours within the ventricular myocardium causing outflow tract obstruction. Many of these lesions are expected to regress spontaneously over the following years. Which underlying genetic syndrome should be screened for?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (D): This is the classic presentation of cardiac rhabdomyoma — often multiple, in infants, causing outflow obstruction, with a tendency to regress spontaneously — and it is strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis, which should be screened for.
- (A) Carney complex is associated with myxoma, not rhabdomyoma.
- (B) Li-Fraumeni syndrome is a p53-related cancer predisposition syndrome, unrelated to cardiac rhabdomyoma.
- (C) Marfan syndrome is a connective tissue disorder unrelated to cardiac rhabdomyoma.

options.text: Carney complex — LAMB spectrum (Lentigines, Atrial myxoma, Mucocutaneous myxoma, Blue nevi)
Carney complex — NAME spectrum (Nevi, Atrial myxoma, Myxoid neurofibroma, Ephelids)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient has multiple lentigines, blue nevi, and an atrial myxoma. Genetic testing reveals a GNAS gene mutation. What syndrome does this represent, and which acronym captures this specific combination of features?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (A): The combination of lentigines, blue nevi, and atrial myxoma specifically matches the LAMB spectrum (Lentigines, Atrial myxoma, Mucocutaneous myxoma, Blue nevi) of Carney complex, driven by a GNAS mutation.
- (B) NAME spectrum (Nevi, Atrial myxoma, Myxoid neurofibroma, Ephelids/freckling) is the other Carney complex acronym, but does not specifically include "lentigines" and "blue nevi" as named features the way LAMB does.
- (C) Tuberous sclerosis is associated with rhabdomyoma, not myxoma, and its skin findings (ash-leaf spots) are different from those described.
- (D) Naxos syndrome involves ARVC, woolly hair, and keratoderma — an entirely different triad, unrelated to myxoma or GNAS mutation.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A pedunculated, papillary, frond-covered mass is found attached directly to a cardiac valve leaflet on echocardiography, described as resembling a "sea anemone." What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (C): Papillary fibroelastoma is the most common primary tumour of a cardiac valve, classically described as "sea-anemone-like" due to its papillary, frond-covered appearance sitting directly on a valve leaflet.
- (A) Myxoma is a pedunculated, gelatinous atrial mass, not a valve-leaflet tumour, and lacks the frond-covered "sea-anemone" appearance.
- (B) Rhabdomyoma is a ventricular myocardial tumour of infants, not a valve leaflet lesion.
- (D) Angiosarcoma is an aggressive, typically right atrial malignant tumour, not a frond-covered valve lesion.

options.text: Myxoma — children, left ventricle; Rhabdomyoma — adults, left atrium
Myxoma — adults, left atrium; Rhabdomyoma — children, left ventricle
Both occur predominantly in adults, but in different chambers
Both occur predominantly in children, but in different chambers

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Comparing myxoma and rhabdomyoma, which statement correctly pairs the tumour with its typical age group and cardiac chamber?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Myxoma is the most common benign primary cardiac tumour in adults, classically arising in the left atrium; rhabdomyoma is the most common benign primary cardiac tumour in children, classically arising in the left ventricle.
- (A) reverses the correct age-group and chamber pairings.
- (C) incorrectly claims both occur predominantly in adults, ignoring rhabdomyoma's pediatric predominance.
- (D) incorrectly claims both occur predominantly in children, ignoring myxoma's adult predominance.

(a) (Cetrimide + Chlorhexidine) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p39, Park 22/e p119
• Savlon contains— Cetrimide 3% (Cetavlon) + Chlorhexidine 0.3% (Hibitane)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Autopsy of a patient with long-standing right-sided heart failure reveals a liver with alternating dark, haemorrhagic centrilobular zones and pale, fatty periportal zones on cut section. What is this gross pattern called?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): This alternating pattern of dark, congested centrilobular zones and pale, fatty periportal zones, resembling a nutmeg seed on cut section, is called "nutmeg liver" — the classic hepatic finding of right-sided heart failure.
- (A) Cardiac cirrhosis is a later-stage complication (centrilobular fibrosis) that can develop from longstanding nutmeg liver congestion, not the acute alternating gross pattern itself.
- (C) "Chicken-wire fibrosis" describes a different histologic pattern (classically seen in alcoholic steatohepatitis), not this vignette's finding.
- (D) Bridging necrosis is a histologic pattern seen in severe hepatitis, unrelated to this congestive finding.

options.text: Perl's Prussian blue; heart failure cells

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with chronic left-sided heart failure undergoes lung biopsy, which shows alveolar macrophages containing golden-brown pigment. A special stain turns these macrophages vivid blue, confirming their identity. Which stain was used, and what are these cells called?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (C): Perl's Prussian blue stain highlights the iron (hemosiderin) within alveolar macrophages, turning them vivid blue and confirming they are the hemosiderin-laden "heart failure cells" characteristic of left-sided heart failure.
- (A) Masson's trichrome distinguishes muscle from collagen, not iron-laden macrophages; "contraction band cells" is not a standard entity.
- (B) Congo red detects amyloid, an unrelated substance to the hemosiderin described here.
- (D) PAS stains glycogen (e.g. in rhabdomyoma "spider cells"), not hemosiderin in lung macrophages.

mcqs.question: Rabies free country:

74. Viral Encephalitis and Encephalopathy: Rabies, HSV, Arboviral, Nipah, Prion
mcqs.explanation:
(d) (Australia) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p501-2, Park, 22/e p251

options.text: Direct bacterial infection of the alveoli
Raised pulmonary venous pressure causing RBCs to leak into the alveolar spaces, which are then phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages
Iron deposition directly from the systemic circulation into alveolar macrophages
Autoimmune destruction of alveolar epithelial cells

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the immediate pathophysiologic step that leads to hemosiderin-laden macrophage formation in the lungs of a patient with left ventricular failure?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): LV failure raises pulmonary venous pressure, causing RBCs to leak into the alveolar spaces (chronic passive congestion); alveolar macrophages then phagocytose these extravasated RBCs, breaking down haemoglobin into hemosiderin, producing "heart failure cells."
- (A) is incorrect — this is a non-infectious, hemodynamically driven process, not a bacterial infection.
- (C) incorrectly proposes direct systemic iron deposition rather than local breakdown of extravasated RBC haemoglobin.
- (D) incorrectly proposes an autoimmune mechanism, which is not the recognized pathophysiology here.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with chronic right-sided heart failure develops small, firm, rust-brown fibrotic nodules in the spleen, composed of organised haemorrhage encrusted with iron and calcium salts. What are these nodules called?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (C): Gamna–Gandy bodies are the small, firm, rust-brown fibrotic splenic nodules from organised foci of haemorrhage, encrusted with iron and calcium salts, classically seen in chronic congestive splenomegaly from right-sided heart failure.
- (A) Heart failure cells are hemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages in the lung (left HF), not splenic nodules.
- (B) MacCallum patches are a mural lesion of the left atrium in chronic RHD, an unrelated entity.
- (D) "Aschoff nodules" is not the standard term for this splenic finding; Aschoff bodies are a cardiac (myocardial) lesion of rheumatic carditis.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common overall cause of right-sided heart failure?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (D): Left-sided heart failure itself is the most common overall cause of right-sided heart failure, via the back-pressure transmitted through the pulmonary circulation.
- (A) Primary pulmonary hypertension is a recognized cause of right HF (cor pulmonale), but is much less common than left HF as the overall leading cause.
- (B) Tricuspid valve endocarditis can contribute to right heart dysfunction but is not the most common overall cause of right HF.
- (C) COPD-related cor pulmonale is a recognized cause of primary lung disease-driven right HF, but is not the single most common overall cause, which is left-sided heart failure.

options.text: It is transmitted by feco-oral route
Asymptomatic infections are common in children

Live attenuated vaccine produces herd immunity

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All of the following statements are true regarding poliovirus except:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
73. Viral Meningitis and Myelitis: Polio, Coxsackie
mcqs.explanation:
(c) (T here is single serotype causing infection) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p476
• There are three serotypes of Poliovirus: 1, 2, 3 and any of them can cause infection
• Polio is transmitted most commonly by feco-oral route followed by inhalation and conjunctival route
• Asymptomatic infections are common in children. The most vulnerable group for Polio is children of 6 months to 3
years.
• Herd immunity is produced by live attenuated vaccine: Because live vaccine progeny viruses can be excreted in feces
and spread to other house hold contacts.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: SARS is a type of:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation:
(c) (Coronavirus) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p521, Ananthanarayan 9/e p560
Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) was caused by a corona virus.
[UPDATE 2026] Two further highly pathogenic coronaviruses have emerged since SARS-CoV (2002-03): MERS-CoV (Saudi Arabia, 2012, with dromedary camels as the reservoir) and SARS-CoV-2, which emerged in Wuhan in December 2019 and caused the COVID-19 pandemic (declared a PHEIC in January 2020; PHEIC status ended in May 2023). SARS-CoV-2 is now an endemic seasonal respiratory pathogen.

options.text: Atherosclerosis; associated with subintimal foam cell accumulation
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis; associated with benign hypertension and diabetes mellitus
Monckeberg sclerosis; associated with old age, clinically silent
Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis; associated with malignant hypertension

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 68-year-old woman with a 20-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and mild hypertension dies of unrelated causes. Renal biopsy at autopsy shows arterioles with pink, glassy, homogeneous thickening of the wall. What is this finding, and its most likely associations?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Pink, glassy, homogeneous arteriolar wall thickening is the classic description of hyaline arteriolosclerosis, associated with benign hypertension and diabetes mellitus — matching this patient's risk factor profile exactly.
- (D) Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis shows an "onion-skin" concentric pattern from smooth muscle/fibroblast proliferation, seen in malignant hypertension, not this pink glassy appearance.
- (C) Monckeberg sclerosis involves dystrophic calcification specifically within the tunica media, a different histologic picture from hyaline thickening.
- (A) Atherosclerosis involves subintimal plaque formation with foam cells, a distinct process from diffuse arteriolar wall hyalinization.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Smallest unit of antigenicity is known as
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: An epitope (antigenic determinant) is the smallest unit of antigenicity, the part of an antigen that is recognized by the immune system. The epitope is the specific region of the antigen that binds to the antibody's paratope or T cell receptor.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The primary immune response is characterized by the production of
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The primary immune response is characterized by the production of IgM antibodies. IgM is the first immunoglobulin produced during an initial antigenic challenge. It appears early in infection and is a pentamer with high avidity. This is followed later by class switching to IgG.

Rectum and prostate are resistant to gonococci
Most patients present with symptoms of dysuria
Single dose of ciprofloxacin is effective in treatment

‘Acute urethritis is the most common clinical manifestation of gonorrhea in males and major symptoms are Urethral discharge and
dysuria, usually without urinary frequency or urgency’ ………Harrison 18/e p1222-23
About Other Options
• Fluoroquinolones offered the advantage of antichlamydial activity when administered for 7 days
• Third-generation cephalosporins have remained highly effective as single-dose therapy for gonorrhea
• Adult vagina is resistant to Gonococcus, so infection is less severe in female
• In males, it can involve rectum and prostate and epididymitis. (never involve testes).

options.text: Microscopic polyangiitis; renal involvement is the leading complication, with no cardiac risk
Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis; upper respiratory involvement only, no cardiac risk
Polyarteritis nodosa; hepatic involvement is the leading complication
Churg-Strauss syndrome (Eosinophilic GPA); cardiac involvement is a leading complication

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with a history of adult-onset asthma and marked peripheral eosinophilia develops new-onset heart failure and a p-ANCA positive vasculitis with granulomatous inflammation. What is the diagnosis, and which organ system involvement is a leading concern in this specific disease?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (D): The combination of asthma, marked eosinophilia, granulomatous p-ANCA vasculitis, and new cardiac involvement is classic for Churg-Strauss syndrome (Eosinophilic GPA); cardiac complications from eosinophil-mediated damage are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in this specific disease.
- (A) Microscopic polyangiitis is not associated with asthma/eosinophilia, and this vignette's eosinophilic and cardiac features do not fit that diagnosis.
- (B) GPA is not classically associated with asthma and marked eosinophilia; this vignette's features point specifically to the eosinophilic variant, not classic GPA.
- (C) PAN is not associated with asthma/eosinophilia, and hepatic involvement is not its leading described complication in this framework.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: An 80-year-old man undergoes lower limb radiography for an unrelated reason, incidentally revealing circumferential calcification of the medial layer of his femoral artery, without any luminal narrowing or history of vascular symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (A): Dystrophic calcification confined to the tunica media, typically an incidental finding in elderly patients without luminal narrowing or clinical symptoms, is the classic description of Monckeberg sclerosis.
- (D) Atherosclerosis involves subintimal (not medial) plaque formation and typically does cause luminal narrowing, unlike this incidental finding.
- (C) Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis shows an onion-skin pattern of smooth muscle/fibroblast proliferation, not medial calcification.
- (B) Hyaline arteriolosclerosis shows pink, glassy wall thickening, not calcification, and is linked to hypertension/diabetes rather than being an incidental finding.

options.text: Smooth muscle cell migration into the media
Platelet-derived growth factor release from an established thrombus

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A researcher studying the earliest event in atherosclerosis identifies a process that initiates the entire cascade leading to plaque formation. What is this initiating event?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Endothelial injury is the initiating trigger of atherosclerosis, setting off the entire downstream cascade of lipid accumulation, inflammation, and plaque formation.
- (C) Smooth muscle migration is a later event in plaque evolution, occurring after the initial endothelial injury and lipid accumulation.
- (A) Foam cell apoptosis contributes to the necrotic core of an advanced plaque, a late rather than initiating event.
- (D) Platelet-derived growth factor release occurs after thrombus formation, a downstream complication, not the initiating trigger.

options.text: Foam cells; Oil Red O stain

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Histologic examination of an early atherosclerotic lesion reveals lipid-laden macrophages within the subintimal space, positive on a lipid-specific stain. What are these cells called, and which special stain confirms their identity?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (C): Foam cells are lipid-laden macrophages found in the subintimal atheromatous plaque, and they stain positively with Oil Red O, a lipid-specific stain.
- (A) Anitschkow cells are the macrophage-derived cells of rheumatic Aschoff bodies, an unrelated cardiac lesion.
- (D) Touton giant cells are seen in fat necrosis and xanthomas, not the classic atherosclerotic plaque cell.
- (B) Reed-Sternberg cells are diagnostic of Hodgkin lymphoma; Congo red stains amyloid, neither relevant here.

76. Urinary Tract Infections and STIs: Enterobacteriaceae, Enterococcus, BK, Schistosoma

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with severe atherosclerosis develops a complication involving weakening and outward bulging of the arterial wall. Using the ACUTE mnemonic for atherosclerotic complications, which letter and complication does this represent?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (D): Weakening and outward bulging of the arterial wall describes an aneurysm, the "A" in the ACUTE mnemonic (Aneurysm, Calcification, Ulceration, Thrombosis, Embolism).
- (C) Calcification refers to mineral deposition within the plaque, not wall bulging.
- (B) Ulceration refers to breakdown of the plaque's fibrous cap surface, not aneurysmal dilation.
- (A) Thrombosis refers to clot formation on a disrupted plaque surface, a distinct complication from aneurysmal dilation.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: An autopsy study ranks the vessels most frequently affected by severe atherosclerosis. Which vessel is found to be the single most commonly involved, and which is the least commonly involved among the classically studied sites?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (D): In order of decreasing frequency, atherosclerosis most commonly involves the abdominal aorta, followed by coronary artery, popliteal artery, descending thoracic aorta, internal carotid artery, with the circle of Willis being the least commonly involved of these classic sites.
- (B) reverses the correct ranking — the abdominal aorta, not the coronary artery, is the most commonly affected site.
- (C) incorrectly identifies the circle of Willis as most common, when it is actually the least common of the listed sites.
- (A) misidentifies both the most and least common vessels from the correct ranking.

mcqs.question: V. cholerae is able to stay in GIT because of:

• V. cholerae is acid labile that is why high infective dose of 10 6 bacilli is required to cross the gastric juice barrier. (and
achlorohydria facilitates transmission)
• V. cholerae is bile resistant, hence can survive in the intestine. (bile resistant property helps to grow on TCBS
• V. cholerae is strongly aerobic but still grows slowly and scanty anaerobically.
Other reasons include:
• Factors that help to cross the protective mucus layer in small intestine are motility, chemotaxis, mucinase, and other
proteolytic enzymes.
• Other factors: Siderophore, neuraminidase, accessory colonizing factor
• Adhere to epithelium by TCP (Toxin Co-regulatory Pilus)
• Cholera Toxin: Principle virulence f actor binds to specific GM1 receptor on intestinal epithelium.

options.text: Subclavian artery; also called "pulseless disease" or aorto-arteritis
Popliteal artery; also called Buerger disease

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with weak, nearly impalpable pulses in both upper limbs, along with arm claudication. Imaging shows narrowing of the aortic arch branches with wall thickening. Which vessel is most commonly involved in this disease, and what is its other name?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): This is Takayasu arteritis, classically affecting young women (<50 years); the subclavian artery is the most commonly involved vessel, explaining the upper limb pulse weakness, and the disease is also known as "pulseless disease" or aorto-arteritis.
- (C) The coronary artery is, in fact, the least commonly involved vessel in Takayasu arteritis, not the most common.
- (A) The renal artery is the classic most commonly involved vessel in polyarteritis nodosa, a different disease.
- (D) The popliteal artery is not the characteristic vessel in Takayasu arteritis, and Buerger disease is an entirely separate entity associated with smoking.

options.text: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis; steroids started immediately to prevent sudden, irreversible blindness
Takayasu arteritis; steroids started early to prevent aortic dissection
Polyarteritis nodosa; steroids started to prevent renal failure
Kawasaki disease; steroids started to prevent coronary aneurysm

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 65-year-old woman presents with a new-onset, localized, throbbing headache. On further questioning, she reports jaw pain while chewing that resolves with rest. She is started on high-dose steroids immediately, before any biopsy is performed. What is the most likely diagnosis, and why was treatment started without waiting for biopsy confirmation?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (A): Localized throbbing headache (most common symptom) plus jaw claudication (most specific symptom) is classic for giant cell (temporal) arteritis, the most common vasculitis in adults over 50; steroids are started immediately on clinical suspicion because the most dangerous complication — sudden, irreversible blindness — can occur if treatment is delayed for biopsy confirmation.
- (B) Takayasu arteritis typically affects young women with limb claudication and pulse deficits, not the headache/jaw claudication picture described in an older patient.
- (C) Polyarteritis nodosa does not classically present with headache and jaw claudication; its urgency relates to renal and systemic involvement, not blindness.
- (D) Kawasaki disease occurs in children under 5, not a 65-year-old woman, and does not present with jaw claudication.

options.text: Prussian blue; highlights hemosiderin within the media
Congo red; highlights amyloid deposition in the intima
Verhoeff-Van Gieson stain; highlights fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina
Masson's trichrome; highlights collagen fragmentation in the adventitia

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Temporal artery biopsy in a patient with suspected giant cell arteritis shows giant cells, granulomatous inflammation, and fragmentation of a specific vessel wall layer. Which special stain best highlights this fragmented structure, and what is it?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (C): The Verhoeff-Van Gieson (VVG) stain highlights elastic fibers and is used to demonstrate the characteristic fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina (IEL) in giant cell arteritis.
- (D) Masson's trichrome distinguishes collagen from muscle, not the elastic lamina fragmentation characteristic of this disease.
- (B) Congo red detects amyloid, an unrelated substance to the elastic lamina finding in giant cell arteritis.
- (A) Prussian blue detects iron (hemosiderin), unrelated to elastic fiber fragmentation.

options.text: VZV causing progressive outer retinal necrosis

options.text: Renal artery; glomerulonephritis is NOT expected, since the disease affects renal arteries rather than glomerular capillaries
Renal artery; glomerulonephritis IS expected, since glomeruli are directly involved
Pulmonary artery; glomerulonephritis is not relevant since the kidney is spared
Coronary artery; glomerulonephritis is expected due to associated renal artery involvement

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with chronic hepatitis B infection develops fever, weight loss, abdominal pain, and hypertension. Renal angiography shows multiple small aneurysms along medium-sized renal arteries. Biopsy of an affected vessel shows fibrinoid necrosis. Which vessel is most classically involved in this disease, and is glomerulonephritis expected?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (A): This is polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), associated with HBsAg in about 30% of cases; the renal artery is the most commonly involved vessel, but because PAN affects medium-sized arteries rather than glomerular capillaries, glomerulonephritis does NOT occur (unlike ANCA-associated vasculitides).
- (B) incorrectly claims glomerulonephritis is expected; PAN specifically spares the glomeruli.
- (C) incorrectly identifies the pulmonary artery as the classic vessel; the pulmonary vasculature is actually characteristically spared in PAN, and the renal artery is the most commonly involved vessel.
- (D) incorrectly claims glomerulonephritis occurs via the coronary artery pathway, which is not the mechanism or vessel described in this classic vignette.

Neonate with hepatosplenomegaly, Giemsa stain of urine reveals owl’s eye appearance inclusions…..is suggestive of
neonatal CMV infection.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The most effective method of sterilization is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Autoclaving is the most effective method of sterilization. It uses moist heat at 121°C and 15 psi pressure for 15-20 minutes to kill all microorganisms, including endospores. Moist heat is more effective than dry heat because it penetrates cells more readily and denatures proteins.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which vessel bed is classically SPARED in polyarteritis nodosa, distinguishing it from many other systemic vasculitides?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Pulmonary vessels are classically spared in polyarteritis nodosa — PAN essentially never involves the lung, a useful distinguishing feature from ANCA-associated vasculitides that do involve the lung.
- (C) Renal vessels are, in fact, the most commonly involved vessel in PAN, not spared.
- (D) Mesenteric vessels are commonly involved in PAN, contributing to abdominal pain.
- (A) Coronary vessels can be involved in PAN (and are the classic vessel in Kawasaki disease), not a spared site.

options.text: Buerger disease is thromboangiitis obliterans associated with smoking; Berger disease is IgA nephropathy, a glomerular disease unrelated to vasculitis
Buerger disease is IgA nephropathy; Berger disease is thromboangiitis obliterans associated with smoking
Both refer to the same vasculitis affecting small kidney vessels
Both are variants of polyarteritis nodosa, differing only by vessel size involved

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A medical student confuses "Buerger disease" with "Berger disease" while studying for an exam. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (A): Buerger disease is thromboangiitis obliterans, a smoking-associated vasculitis of small/medium vessels; Berger disease is IgA nephropathy, a glomerular disease with no relationship to vasculitis — a classic same-sounding-name mix-up in exams.
- (B) reverses the two disease definitions.
- (C) incorrectly claims they are the same disease; they are entirely unrelated conditions.
- (D) incorrectly classifies both as PAN variants; neither is a subtype of polyarteritis nodosa.

options.text: ACUTE criteria; complication is aneurysm of the aorta
Jones criteria; complication is mitral stenosis
CREAM criteria for Kawasaki disease; complication is coronary artery involvement, potentially leading to MI
Duke criteria; complication is septic emboli

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old child presents with fever for 6 days, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, a diffuse rash, edema of the hands and feet, unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, and a strawberry tongue. Which diagnostic criteria framework is being applied, and what is the most feared complication if untreated?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (C): This child meets the CREAM criteria for Kawasaki disease (fever >5 days plus ≥4/5 of Conjunctivitis, Rash, Edema, Adenopathy, Mucosal changes/strawberry tongue); the most feared complication is coronary artery involvement, which can progress to myocardial infarction — Kawasaki disease is the most common cause of acquired heart disease in children.
- (B) Jones criteria are used to diagnose rheumatic fever, an unrelated condition with a different presentation.
- (D) Duke criteria are used to diagnose infective endocarditis, not Kawasaki disease.
- (A) "ACUTE" is the mnemonic for atherosclerotic complications, not a diagnostic criteria framework for any vasculitis.

options.text: Polyarteritis nodosa; granulomas are absent by definition
Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis; renal involvement is identical to PAN
Microscopic polyangiitis; unlike PAN, this disease DOES cause glomerulonephritis, making it functionally "the opposite of PAN"
Churg-Strauss syndrome; renal involvement is absent, similar to PAN

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient presents with palpable purpura and biopsy-proven small vessel vasculitis. Immunofluorescence shows no immune complex deposition (pauci-immune), and histology shows vessel wall inflammation WITHOUT granuloma formation. ANCA testing is positive with a perinuclear pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis, and how does its renal involvement compare to polyarteritis nodosa?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (C): The absence of granulomas (unlike GPA) plus a p-ANCA (MPO) pattern points to microscopic polyangiitis (also known as leucocytoclastic vasculitis); importantly, unlike PAN, microscopic polyangiitis does cause glomerulonephritis, making it functionally "the opposite of PAN" in terms of renal and small-vessel involvement.
- (B) GPA is characterized by granuloma formation, which is specifically absent in this vignette.
- (D) Churg-Strauss syndrome is associated with marked eosinophilia, not mentioned here, and also typically shows granulomas.
- (A) PAN does not typically test positive for ANCA and, by definition, spares the glomeruli (no glomerulonephritis) — the opposite of what's described in this vignette.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The following marker tells us about the viral load and degree of infectivity in Hepatitis B infected patient
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: HBeAg is an indicator of viral replication and infectivity in Hepatitis B patients. Its presence indicates high viral load and active replication.

options.text: Henoch-Schönlein purpura; the normal platelet count confirms the purpura is vasculitic (immune-complex mediated) rather than due to thrombocytopenia
Disseminated intravascular coagulation; platelet count is characteristically normal
Meningococcemia; platelet count is not relevant to this diagnosis
Immune thrombocytopenic purpura; platelet count is expected to be normal in this condition

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old child develops palpable purpura on the lower limbs, joint pain, abdominal pain, and hematuria one week after an upper respiratory infection. A complete blood count shows a normal platelet count. What is the most likely diagnosis, and why is the normal platelet count an important clue?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (A): This presentation (palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, hematuria following a URI, in a child) is classic for Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP), the most common vasculitis in children; the normal platelet count is an important clue because it confirms the purpura results from vascular inflammation and IgA immune complex deposition, not from platelet deficiency.
- (D) ITP is defined by low platelet count causing purpura; a normal platelet count argues against, not for, this diagnosis.
- (B) DIC characteristically causes thrombocytopenia (low platelets) due to consumption, not a normal count.
- (C) Meningococcemia can cause purpura, but platelet count (often low due to DIC) is highly relevant, and the overall vignette (post-URI, arthralgia, abdominal pain, hematuria in a child) fits HSP far better.

Baby has a risk of congenital Varicella infection
Give no treatment to mother and give antiviral treatment to baby

Infection of Varicella during pregnancy:
• If mother gets chickenpox > 5 days before delivery: T hen baby is mostly asymptomatic due to maternal antibody
• If mother gets chickenpox within 5 days of delivery: Mother would not have produced protective antibodies, hence:
disseminated infection in baby occurs with high-risk of pneumonia and encephalitis.
• In such cases, treatment with Varicella zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) is indicated within 96 hr.

options.text: X: amyloidosis; Y: thrombocytopenia; Z: HSP
X: HSP; Y: amyloidosis; Z: thrombocytopenia
X: thrombocytopenia; Y: HSP; Z: amyloidosis
X: HSP; Y: thrombocytopenia; Z: amyloidosis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A dermatologist evaluates purpuric lesions in three different patients: Patient X has raised, palpable purpura on the legs; Patient Y has flat, non-palpable purpura and a low platelet count; Patient Z has purpura that appeared after gentle pinching of the skin, along with periorbital ecchymoses ("raccoon eyes"). What is the most likely cause in each patient, respectively?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (D): Palpable purpura is characteristic of HSP (vasculitic, inflammation raises the lesion); non-palpable purpura with low platelets reflects thrombocytopenia; "pinch purpura" with raccoon eyes is characteristic of amyloidosis (fragile vessels from amyloid deposition).
- (C) and (A) and (B) each misassign at least one of the three purpura types to the wrong underlying cause.

options.text: Ischemic stroke from small vessel occlusion

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with known Behcet's disease presents with a severe headache, papilledema, and imaging findings of a thrombosed venous structure within the dura. What is the most common CNS manifestation of Behcet's disease being demonstrated here?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (C): Dural sinus thrombosis is the most common CNS manifestation of Behcet's disease, consistent with the imaging finding of a thrombosed dural venous structure and papilledema from resulting venous hypertension.
- (B) Ischemic stroke from small vessel occlusion is not the most common CNS manifestation of Behcet's disease.
- (A) Subarachnoid hemorrhage is not the characteristic CNS complication of Behcet's disease.
- (D) Demyelinating plaques are the hallmark of multiple sclerosis, an unrelated condition, not the classic Behcet's CNS finding.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A newborn is noted to have a bright red, raised skin lesion on the cheek, present since birth, which is expected to involute over the following years. Histology shows small, closely packed capillary-sized blood channels in the superficial dermis. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): A superficial, small-vessel vascular lesion in a newborn that tends to involute over time is classic for capillary hemangioma, also called "strawberry hemangioma," typically found in superficial sites (skin/mucosa) with small blood channels.
- (A) Cavernous hemangioma involves large blood channels in deep-seated tissues/organs, not this superficial small-vessel presentation.
- (C) Kaposi sarcoma is an HHV-8-associated tumour of adults (classically HIV-positive), not a congenital newborn skin lesion.
- (D) Glomus tumour is a painful, typically subungual lesion, not a superficial cheek lesion in a newborn.

mcqs.question: Most common cause of dysentery in adults is:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
45. Intestinal Protozoan Infections: Amoebiasis, Giardiasis, Coccidian, Balantidiasis
mcqs.explanation:
(d) (Entamoeba...) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Parasitology 1/e p31
• Entamoeba histolytica is one of the commonest cause of dysentery in man
• Other Agents dysentery include: Bacterial dysentery (e.g. Shigella and Campylobacter and Vibrio parahemolyticus),
Parasitic causes (schistosomiasis, Trichuris and Balantidium coli)
• In Cryptosporidium parvum, Giardia and Strongoloides infection: Diarrhea is the chief manifestation (not dysentery).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with multiple visceral hemangiomas, including a large hepatic lesion with large, dilated vascular channels on histology, is found on genetic testing to have a deletion on chromosome 3p. Which syndrome and vascular tumour type does this represent?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (A): Deep-seated hemangiomas with large, dilated blood channels (cavernous hemangioma) are associated with Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome, caused by a deletion on chromosome 3p.
- (C) Tuberous sclerosis is associated with cardiac rhabdomyoma, not cavernous hemangioma.
- (D) Sturge-Weber syndrome involves capillary (port-wine stain) malformations, not the large-channel cavernous hemangioma described, and is not linked to a 3p deletion.
- (B) Carney complex is associated with cardiac myxoma (via GNAS mutation), not cavernous hemangioma or a 3p deletion.

options.text: Glomus tumour, also called subungual tumour
Kaposi sarcoma, also called AIDS-related tumour
Pyogenic granuloma, also called granuloma gravidarum or pregnancy tumour

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A pregnant woman develops a rapidly growing, friable, bleeding gingival mass. Biopsy shows a lobular proliferation of capillary-sized blood vessels. What is the diagnosis, and by what other names is this lesion known?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (D): A rapidly growing, friable gingival mass in a pregnant patient with lobular capillary proliferation on histology is classic for pyogenic granuloma, also known as granuloma gravidarum or "pregnancy tumour."
- (C) Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and HIV, not pregnancy, and shows slit-like vessels with spindle cells, not a lobular capillary pattern.
- (A) Angiosarcoma is an aggressive malignant tumour, not the benign, pregnancy-associated lesion described here.
- (B) Glomus tumour is a painful subungual lesion, an entirely different site and presentation from this gingival mass.

options.text: Capillary hemangioma; associated with Turner syndrome
Glomus tumour; associated with Klinefelter syndrome
Cystic hygroma; a cavernous lymphangioma, associated with Turner syndrome
Cavernous hemangioma; associated with Down syndrome

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A newborn girl with a webbed neck and short stature is found to have a large, cystic, fluid-filled swelling in the posterior neck. Prenatal karyotype shows 45,XO. What is the name of this cystic vascular lesion, and what type of vascular malformation does it represent?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (C): A cystic neck mass in a newborn with the 45,XO karyotype (Turner syndrome) and webbed neck is classic for cystic hygroma, which represents a cavernous lymphangioma of the neck, associated with Turner syndrome.
- (A) Capillary hemangioma is a small-vessel skin/mucosal lesion, not the large cystic neck lymphatic malformation described, nor is it the classic Turner syndrome vascular finding.
- (D) Cavernous hemangioma is a blood vessel tumour (not lymphatic), and Down syndrome is not the karyotype described (45,XO indicates Turner syndrome).
- (B) Glomus tumour is a painful subungual lesion, unrelated to this presentation, and Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) does not match the 45,XO karyotype given.

options.text: Pyogenic granuloma; arises from capillary endothelium
Glomus tumour; arises from the glomus body (an arteriovenous structure)
Angiosarcoma; arises from malignant transformation of endothelial cells
Kaposi sarcoma; arises from HHV-8-infected endothelium

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient reports an exquisitely painful, small, reddish-blue nodule beneath a fingernail, rated 10/10 in intensity even with minimal contact. What is the diagnosis, and from what structure does this tumour arise?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): An exquisitely painful, small subungual nodule is the classic presentation of a glomus tumour, arising from the glomus body, a specialized arteriovenous structure involved in thermoregulation.
- (A) Pyogenic granuloma is typically found on gingiva or skin, is friable and bleeds, but is not classically described as the single most painful vascular lesion at a subungual site.
- (D) Kaposi sarcoma typically presents as cutaneous plaques/nodules on the lower limbs in HIV-positive patients, not a painful subungual nodule.
- (C) Angiosarcoma is an aggressive malignant tumour, typically presenting in the liver or skin of elderly patients, not this classic painful subungual presentation.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient who recently adopted a kitten develops multiple reddish-purple cutaneous papules. Biopsy shows vascular proliferation with clusters of small, curved, silver-staining organisms on special stain. What is the causative organism and the special stain used?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Bacillary angiomatosis, caused by Bartonella henselae (classically transmitted via cat scratch/contact), produces vascular proliferative skin lesions; the causative organism is demonstrated using the Warthin-Starry silver stain (WSSS).
- (A) Treponema pallidum (syphilis) can also be demonstrated with Warthin-Starry stain in some contexts, but it is not the organism causing bacillary angiomatosis or linked to the cat-exposure history in this vignette.
- (D) Congo red detects amyloid, not the causative organism of bacillary angiomatosis.
- (C) H. pylori is also demonstrable with a silver stain (a shared special-stain fact), but it causes gastric disease, not bacillary angiomatosis, and Giemsa is not the classic stain paired with this vignette's organism.

options.text: Kaposi sarcoma; caused by HHV-8; marker is LANA (Latency-Associated Nuclear Antigen)
Bacillary angiomatosis; caused by Bartonella henselae; marker is Warthin-Starry positivity
Hemangiopericytoma; caused by no known infectious agent; marker is CD34
Angiosarcoma; caused by vinyl chloride exposure; marker is CD31

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: An HIV-positive patient develops multiple violaceous plaques on the lower limbs. Biopsy shows spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces, and immunohistochemistry is positive for a marker representing a latency-associated viral protein. What is the diagnosis, the causative virus, and the IHC marker?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (A): Violaceous plaques with slit-like vascular spaces and spindle cells in an HIV-positive patient is classic Kaposi sarcoma, caused by HHV-8; the IHC marker LANA (Latency-Associated Nuclear Antigen) confirms HHV-8 infection of the tumour cells.
- (D) Angiosarcoma is linked to vinyl chloride, arsenic, or Thorotrast exposure, and is not the HIV-associated, HHV-8-driven tumour described here.
- (B) Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella henselae (detected by Warthin-Starry stain, not LANA), and though it can occur in HIV patients, the vignette's spindle cell/slit-vessel histology and LANA positivity specifically point to Kaposi sarcoma.
- (C) Hemangiopericytoma is not infection-associated and shows a "staghorn" vascular pattern, not the slit-like vessels and LANA positivity described.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old presents with progressive dysphagia, worse for liquids than solids. Barium swallow shows a 'bird beak' narrowing at the lower esophagus, and manometry shows elevated LES pressure with failure of relaxation. Which neurotransmitters are deficient at the site of the lesion?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) Acetylcholine is the excitatory neurotransmitter causing esophageal contraction; its loss would not explain failure of relaxation — rather, unopposed ACh activity contributes to the elevated LES tone.
- (B) Serotonin and dopamine are not the classic neurotransmitters implicated in achalasia pathophysiology.
- (C) Norepinephrine and epinephrine are not the classic inhibitory neurotransmitters lost in achalasia.
- (D) Achalasia results from loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons that normally release nitric oxide (NO) and VIP, causing failure of LES relaxation, elevated LES pressure on manometry, and a 'bird beak' appearance on barium swallow.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient from rural South America presents with megaesophagus and dysphagia. Serology confirms an infection with a protozoan parasite. Which organism and disease are responsible for this secondary form of achalasia?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) Trichinella spiralis causes muscle infection (trichinosis) from undercooked meat, not destruction of esophageal myenteric ganglia.
- (B) Entamoeba histolytica causes amoebic colitis/liver abscess with flask-shaped ulcers, not achalasia.
- (C) Trypanosoma cruzi causes Chagas disease, which destroys myenteric ganglion cells and can produce secondary achalasia (megaesophagus), classically in South America.
- (D) Toxoplasma gondii causes CNS/ocular/congenital infection, not esophageal ganglion destruction.

options.text: Development of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma as a complication of achalasia

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with long-standing achalasia, previously noted to have dysphagia worse for liquids than solids, now reports the opposite pattern — solids are now more difficult to swallow than liquids. What does this change most likely indicate?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) Resolution would improve symptoms overall, not selectively worsen solid dysphagia relative to liquids.
- (B) Boerhaave syndrome presents acutely with chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema after forceful vomiting, not a gradual change in dysphagia pattern.
- (C) A reversal from liquid-predominant to solid-predominant dysphagia in a patient with known achalasia suggests a new obstructing lesion — classically esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, a recognized long-term complication of achalasia.
- (D) Barrett's esophagus arises from chronic GERD-driven metaplasia and predisposes to adenocarcinoma, not squamous cell carcinoma, and achalasia's cancer risk is specifically for SCC.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with a history of heavy alcohol use develops severe, forceful vomiting followed by chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema, and a crunching sound heard over the precordium on auscultation. Endoscopy confirms a full-thickness esophageal rupture located above the gastroesophageal junction. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) Mallory-Weiss syndrome causes a superficial mucosal/submucosal tear (not full-thickness) below the GEJ, without the systemic findings of subcutaneous emphysema and Hamman's crunch.
- (B) Esophageal variceal rupture classically causes painless hematemesis, not the painful presentation with subcutaneous emphysema described here.
- (C) Plummer-Vinson syndrome is a chronic syndrome of iron deficiency anemia, esophageal webs, and dysphagia, unrelated to acute rupture after vomiting.
- (D) Boerhaave syndrome is a full-thickness esophageal rupture (classically above the GEJ, >2.5 cm) following forceful vomiting, presenting with Mackler's triad (chest pain, vomiting, subcutaneous emphysema) and Hamman's crunch.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All cause malabsorption except:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
46. Intestinal Helminthic Infections: Cestodes, Trematodes, Nematodes
mcqs.explanation:
(N one of the above) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Parasitology 1/e p325
• Giardiasis: Malabsorption syndrome and weight loss are complications both in adults and children.
• Ascaris lumbricoides: H eavy infection causes impairment of host nutrition leading to malabsorption of proteins,
carbohydrates and vitamins.
• Strongyloides stercoralis infection in children causes prolonged malabsorption of fat and protein in severe cases.
• Capillaria phillipinesis: Adult cause protein loosing enteropathy and severe malabsorption.

options.text: Patient A: Boerhaave syndrome; Patient B: Mallory-Weiss syndrome
Both patients have Mallory-Weiss syndrome, differing only in severity
Patient A: Mallory-Weiss syndrome; Patient B: Boerhaave syndrome
Both patients have Boerhaave syndrome, differing only in severity

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Two patients present after episodes of forceful retching. Patient A has a superficial mucosal tear below the gastroesophageal junction; Patient B has a full-thickness rupture above the gastroesophageal junction. What are the respective diagnoses?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) This reverses the classic depth/location distinction between the two syndromes.
- (B) Depth of injury (superficial vs. full-thickness) is a qualitative, defining difference between these two syndromes, not merely a difference in severity of the same process.
- (C) Mallory-Weiss syndrome is a superficial (mucosal/submucosal) tear below the GEJ, while Boerhaave syndrome is a full-thickness rupture above the GEJ — both triggered by forceful retching/vomiting, but distinct in depth and location.
- (D) Same reasoning — the two syndromes are pathologically distinct entities defined by depth and location, not two points on a severity spectrum of one disease.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with known cirrhosis develops sudden, large-volume hematemesis without any preceding chest pain. What is the most likely underlying cause?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) Mallory-Weiss tear classically produces painful hematemesis after retching, not the painless bleeding pattern described.
- (B) Boerhaave syndrome produces painful hematemesis along with chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema, not painless bleeding.
- (C) Esophageal varices classically present with painless hematemesis, in contrast to the painful hematemesis of Mallory-Weiss tear or Boerhaave syndrome.
- (D) Cushing ulcer is a stress ulcer from raised intracranial tension, not the classic painless hematemesis presentation of a cirrhotic patient.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 25 year boy presented with deep injury and abrasions of left shoulder, thigh and leg with immunisation status unknown. What is to be given now?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: (d) (dT+Ig) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1st/p263.

options.text: Barrett's esophagus; risk factor for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma
Barrett's esophagus; risk factor for esophageal adenocarcinoma
Eosinophilic esophagitis; risk factor for esophageal lymphoma
Reflux esophagitis; no significant malignant potential

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with chronic GERD undergoes endoscopy, which shows velvety red mucosa in the distal esophagus. Biopsy reveals columnar epithelium with goblet cells that stain positive with Alcian blue. What is the diagnosis, and what malignancy is this condition a risk factor for?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) Barrett's esophagus predisposes to adenocarcinoma, not squamous cell carcinoma — the risk factors for SCC (alcohol, smoking, HPV, etc.) are a distinct set.
- (B) Barrett's esophagus is intestinal metaplasia of the esophageal squamous epithelium (driven by chronic GERD), showing goblet cells with acidic mucin (Alcian blue positive) and velvety red endoscopic appearance; it is a risk factor for esophageal adenocarcinoma.
- (C) Eosinophilic esophagitis is a distinct allergic/immune-mediated condition without the goblet-cell intestinal metaplasia described, and is not classically linked to lymphoma risk.
- (D) Reflux esophagitis alone (without metaplasia) does not show goblet cells on biopsy, and Barrett's metaplasia does carry significant malignant potential.

options.text: Signet ring cells, confirming diffuse gastric carcinoma
Keratin pearls, confirming squamous cell carcinoma
Azzopardi effect, confirming small cell carcinoma

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Biopsy of a centrally-located esophageal mass in a heavy smoker and alcohol user shows whorls of keratinized cells forming concentric laminated structures. What is this histologic finding, and what tumor does it confirm?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) Signet ring cells (from loss of E-cadherin) are characteristic of diffuse gastric carcinoma, not esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
- (B) Keratin pearls — whorled, laminated keratinized cell nests — are the diagnostic histologic hallmark of squamous cell carcinoma, strongly associated with alcohol and smoking.
- (C) The Azzopardi effect is a crush artifact seen in small cell (neuroendocrine) carcinoma, unrelated to squamous histology.
- (D) Foam cells (PAS-positive macrophages) are seen in Whipple's disease, an unrelated small bowel infection.

options.text: Negative test — absence of bacterial urease activity
Positive test — H. pylori urease has hydrolyzed urea to ammonia, raising the pH
Positive test — indicates active Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
Indeterminate result requiring biopsy confirmation regardless of color

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A rapid urease test is performed on a gastric biopsy specimen, and the indicator solution turns from yellow-orange to pink/magenta within minutes. What does this color change indicate?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) A color change to pink/magenta specifically indicates a positive test, not a negative one — a negative test would remain yellow-orange.
- (B) H. pylori produces urease, which hydrolyzes urea to ammonia and CO2, raising the local pH; the pH indicator in the test medium shifts from yellow-orange to pink/magenta, signaling a positive test for H. pylori.
- (C) The urease test detects H. pylori infection, not gastrin-secreting tumors of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
- (D) A clear color change (yellow-orange to pink/magenta) is diagnostic of a positive result; it is not classified as indeterminate.

options.text: Antrum, same as with all other risk factors for gastric adenocarcinoma
Cardia, because pernicious anemia specifically damages the gastroesophageal junction
Pylorus, because gastrin-secreting cells are concentrated there
Fundus, because parietal cells (the autoimmune target in pernicious anemia) are concentrated there; most other risk factors instead favor the antrum

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old with long-standing pernicious anemia develops gastric adenocarcinoma. In which part of the stomach is this tumor most likely located, given the underlying mechanism, and how does this differ from most other risk factors for gastric adenocarcinoma?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) The antrum is the typical location for most other risk factors, but pernicious anemia specifically shifts the location to the fundus due to parietal cell distribution.
- (B) Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune process targeting parietal cells in the body/fundus, not a process localized to the gastroesophageal junction.
- (C) Gastrin-secreting G cells are concentrated in the antrum, but pernicious anemia's mechanism relates to parietal cell destruction (fundus), not gastrin cell distribution.
- (D) While gastric adenocarcinoma is most commonly located in the antrum overall (from most risk factors), pernicious-anemia-associated gastric adenocarcinoma classically arises in the fundus, since parietal cells — the target of the autoimmune attack — are concentrated in that region.

options.text: Virchow's node (supraclavicular); Sister Mary Joseph nodule (periumbilical)
Sister Mary Joseph nodule (supraclavicular); Virchow's node (periumbilical)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with gastric adenocarcinoma is found on physical exam to have a firm, enlarged left supraclavicular lymph node. What is this finding called, and what is the corresponding eponym for metastasis to the periumbilical region in the same patient?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) Irish node refers to axillary lymph node metastasis, and Krukenberg tumor refers to ovarian metastasis — neither matches the supraclavicular/periumbilical sites described.
- (B) Metastasis to the left supraclavicular lymph node in gastric (or other abdominal) cancer is called Virchow's node, while periumbilical metastasis is called a Sister Mary Joseph nodule.
- (C) This reverses the correct eponym-site pairing — Virchow's node is supraclavicular, Sister Mary Joseph nodule is periumbilical.
- (D) Blumer's shelf refers to rectal (Pouch of Douglas) metastasis, and Irish node refers to axillary metastasis — neither matches the sites described.

mcqs.question: Not a cause of epidemic encephalitis:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation:
(a) (b) (Herpes simplex virus, Rabies) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p488-89,
Ananthanarayan 9/e p469,518
• Herpes simplex encephalitis though RARE, is the MOST COMMON cause of acute sporadic viral encephalitis in most
part of the world.
• Rabies encephalitis is directly related dog bite, it is never epidemic.
• Nipah virus (belongs to paramyxovirus) had caused an outbreak of neurological and respiratory disease in pig farms
in Malaysia(1999), resulting in 257 human infections.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Regarding Clostridium perfringens gas gangrene, false is:

Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation:
(c) (Most...) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p258, 59, Ananthanarayan 9/e p254

Also remember
