mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Infarcts of the heart, kidney, and spleen are typically white/pale, while infarcts of the ovary, lung, and small intestine are typically red/hemorrhagic. What is the key anatomic feature distinguishing these two groups?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (A): White/pale infarcts occur with arterial occlusion in solid organs with end-arterial circulation and no dual supply (heart, spleen, kidney), and dense tissue preventing RBC diffusion. Red/hemorrhagic infarcts occur with venous occlusion (e.g. ovary), in loose-textured tissues allowing RBC diffusion (lung), or organs with dual blood supply (lung, small intestine).
- B, C, D are wrong: size, necrosis type (both types show ischemic coagulative necrosis per this content), and location are not the distinguishing features described.

options.text: A white/pale infarct, because reperfusion prevents any hemorrhage
A red/hemorrhagic infarct, because blood flow is re-established to a site of previous arterial occlusion and necrosis
No morphologic change occurs with reperfusion
A septic infarct, because angioplasty introduces bacterial contamination

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient undergoes successful coronary angioplasty to relieve an occluded coronary artery, restoring blood flow to a previously infarcted area. What type of infarct morphology can result from this reperfusion, and why?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Red/hemorrhagic infarcts can occur when blood flow is re-established to a site of previous arterial occlusion and necrosis, such as following coronary angioplasty of an obstructed coronary artery — the damaged, previously ischemic vessels allow blood to leak into the necrotic zone.
- A is wrong: reperfusion is specifically a cause of red, not white, infarcts.
- C is wrong: reperfusion does produce a recognized morphologic change (hemorrhagic conversion), not no change.
- D is wrong: septic infarction requires bacterial seeding of the infarct, not simply the angioplasty procedure itself.

options.text: Central nervous system; may become cystic (a "cystic infarct")

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In contrast to nearly every other organ, which organ shows liquefactive rather than coagulative necrosis when infarcted, and what can the necrotic focus become?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): In contrast to other organs, CNS infarction shows liquefactive necrosis; the necrotic focus may become cystic and filled with fluid, referred to as a cystic infarct.
- A, C, D are wrong: these organs follow the more typical coagulative necrosis pattern of infarction, not the CNS-specific liquefactive exception.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Septic shock is specifically defined as shock due to severe sepsis with hypotension that has which characteristic?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Septic shock is defined as shock due to severe sepsis with hypotension, which cannot be corrected by infusing fluids; it results from vasodilation and peripheral blood pooling and is associated with dysfunction of multiple organs distant from the infection site.
- A is wrong: septic shock does not resolve spontaneously without intervention — it is a serious, potentially fatal condition.
- C is wrong: septic shock is most commonly caused by gram-positive bacteria (and gram-negative bacteria, fungi, rarely protozoa/Rickettsiae), not primarily viral infection.
- D is wrong: septic shock is specifically associated with dysfunction of multiple organs distant from the infection site.

Microbiology 1/e p581-82
The skin and mucous membranes have 2 types normal flora:
• Resident flora: Consists of relatively fixed types of microorganisms regularly found in a given area at a given age; if
disturbed, it promptly reestablishes itself and cannot be removed permanently.
• Transient flora: Consists of nonpathogenic or potentially pathogenic microorganisms that inhabit the skin or mucous
membranes for hours, days, or weeks; it is derived from the environment, does not produce disease, and does not
establish itself permanently on the surface.
○ Transient flora is of little significance so long as the normal resident flora remains intact.
○ If the resident flora is disturbed, transient microorganisms may colonize, proliferate, and produce disease.
○ Members of transient flora: Microorganisms other than coagulase-negative Staphylococci, Corynebacterium
spp., Micrococcus spp., Bacillus spp. Candida spp., Trichomonas vaginalis, Neisseria meningitides, CMV, HSV,
Malassezia, Enterococcus, Bacteroides, M. smegmatis, Fusobacterium.

mcqs.question: ==Which enzyme is described as an exception to the general rule that it is inducible rather than constitutive, since it is constitutively expressed in the endothelium and CNS?==
mcqs.explanation:
- COX-2 is generally inducible (in contrast to the mostly constitutive/housekeeping COX-1), but a notable exception is that COX-2 is constitutively present in the endothelium and CNS.
- COX-1 (A) is the one that is mostly constitutive throughout, not the exception being described.
- 5-lipoxygenase (C) and phospholipase A2 (D) are enzymes in the arachidonic acid pathway, but the specific constitutive/inducible exception described applies to COX-2.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the "Six Rs" of the acute inflammatory response?
mcqs.explanation:
- "Rejection" is not one of the Six Rs; the actual six are: Recognition, Reaction of blood vessels, Reaction/recruitment of leukocytes, Removal of the causative agent, Regulation, and Resolution and repair.
- A, B, and D are all genuine components of the Six Rs framework.
- The distractor "rejection by antibody neutralization alone" also misrepresents how the injurious agent is actually removed (phagocytosis and multiple mechanisms, not antibody alone).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A local defect or excavation of the surface of an organ or tissue, commonly seen in the stomach, duodenum, or lower extremity skin, is termed:
mcqs.explanation:
- An ulcer is defined as a local defect or excavation of the surface of an organ or tissue, with common sites including the mucosa of the mouth/stomach/duodenum/intestines/genitourinary tract, and the skin/subcutaneous tissue of the lower extremities (e.g. varicose ulcers).
- An abscess (A) is a localized collection of pus, a fundamentally different lesion from a surface excavation.
- A granuloma (B) is an organized aggregate of activated macrophages, unrelated to a surface defect.
- A fistula (D) is an abnormal communication between two epithelial-lined surfaces, a distinct entity from a simple surface ulcer.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The transfer of genetic material through a bacteriophage is called
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Transduction is the transfer of genetic material from one bacterium to another via a bacteriophage (virus). This process can be generalized (transferring any bacterial DNA) or specialized (transferring specific genes). It plays a significant role in bacterial evolution and antibiotic resistance spread.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The phenomenon of transfer of naked DNA from one bacteria to another is called
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Transformation involves the uptake of naked DNA from the environment by competent bacteria. This process was first demonstrated by Frederick Griffith with Streptococcus pneumoniae. It is a crucial mechanism for horizontal gene transfer in bacteria.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The fertility factor (F factor) is associated with
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The F factor is involved in conjugation, a process where genetic material is transferred through direct cell-to-cell contact via sex pili. The F factor allows donor cells (F+) to transfer DNA to recipient cells (F-), promoting genetic exchange and evolution.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Rabies virus in human multiplies in
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
74. Viral Encephalitis and Encephalopathy: Rabies, HSV, Arboviral, Nipah, Prion
mcqs.explanation: Rabies virus can multiply in muscle, nerve endings, and connective tissue. The virus enters through a bite wound, replicates in muscle cells, then enters peripheral nerves and travels to the central nervous system.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The process of transfer of DNA from one bacterium to another through cell-to-cell contact is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Conjugation requires direct cell-to-cell contact for DNA transfer, mediated by the F pilus. This process is responsible for the spread of antibiotic resistance genes and virulence factors among bacterial populations.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The drug resistance plasmid is called
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: R-plasmid (resistance plasmid) carries genes for antibiotic resistance. These plasmids can transfer resistance to multiple antibiotics, often through conjugation, contributing to the emergence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacteria.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Bacterial endospores are resistant to
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Bacterial endospores are highly resistant to heat, radiation, chemicals, and desiccation due to their unique structure. The core contains dipicolinic acid and calcium, and the cortex and spore coat provide protection. This resistance makes sterilization protocols like autoclaving (121°C, 15 psi) necessary for complete elimination.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an enveloped virus?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
04. General Virology and Overview of Viral Infections
mcqs.explanation: Herpesviruses are enveloped viruses, meaning they possess a lipid bilayer derived from the host cell membrane. Enveloped viruses are more susceptible to lipid solvents, detergents, and environmental degradation compared to non-enveloped viruses.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a dimorphic fungus?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
06. General Mycology and Overview of Fungal Infections
mcqs.explanation: Sporothrix schenckii is a dimorphic fungus. It grows as a mold (with conidia) in the environment at 25°C, and as a yeast (with cigar-shaped cells) in tissue at 37°C. It causes sporotrichosis, often acquired through traumatic inoculation of contaminated material.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The asexual spores of fungi are called
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
06. General Mycology and Overview of Fungal Infections
mcqs.explanation: Conidia are asexual spores produced by fungi. They are formed exogenously on specialized hyphae called conidiophores. Conidia are the primary means of fungal reproduction and dissemination in the environment. Zygospores, ascospores, and basidiospores are sexual spores produced by zygomycetes, ascomycetes, and basidiomycetes, respectively.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a fungal infection of the skin?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
06. General Mycology and Overview of Fungal Infections
mcqs.explanation: Tinea versicolor is a superficial fungal infection of the skin caused by Malassezia furfur. It presents as hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules on the trunk. The causative organism is a lipophilic yeast that is part of normal skin flora but can cause infection under favorable conditions.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All of the following are characteristics of a good immunogen EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Immunogens are typically foreign substances, not normally found on host cells. The immune system distinguishes self from non-self, and antigens found on host cells are generally not immunogenic due to immunological tolerance. A good immunogen must be foreign, have high molecular weight, exhibit structural complexity, and possess sufficient epitopes.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The example of a serological test based on heterophile antigen is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The Paul-Bunnell test is used to detect heterophile antibodies in infectious mononucleosis (caused by Epstein-Barr virus). Heterophile antibodies are antibodies that react with antigens from a different species (e.g., sheep RBCs). The test is based on the principle that these antibodies agglutinate sheep red blood cells, which is specific to EBV infection.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: IgG is the only immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta, providing passive immunity to the fetus and newborn. This transfer occurs via neonatal Fc receptors (FcRn) on syncytiotrophoblasts, allowing IgG to be transported from maternal to fetal circulation.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The immunoglobulin present in secretions is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: IgA is the predominant immunoglobulin in secretions such as saliva, tears, colostrum, breast milk, and mucosal surfaces of the gastrointestinal, respiratory, and genitourinary tracts. Secretory IgA exists as a dimer with a J chain and secretory component, providing protection against mucosal pathogens.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The secondary immune response is characterized by
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The secondary immune response is characterized by the production of IgG antibodies. Due to the presence of memory B cells, the secondary response is faster, more robust, and produces higher affinity antibodies than the primary response. This forms the basis of immunological memory and vaccine efficacy.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The hypersensitivity reaction mediated by IgE is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Type I hypersensitivity is mediated by IgE antibodies. Mast cells and basophils coated with IgE release histamine and other mediators upon antigen cross-linking. This leads to immediate allergic reactions such as anaphylaxis, asthma, and hay fever.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Number of proteins in the complement system is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The complement system is traditionally described as consisting of nine main proteins (C1 to C9). However, the complement system actually includes approximately 30 proteins, including regulatory proteins. The cascade involves the classical, alternative, and lectin pathways converging at C3 to form membrane attack complex (MAC).

mcqs.question: Which sample is recommended for polio isolation?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
73. Viral Meningitis and Myelitis: Polio, Coxsackie
mcqs.explanation:
(a) (S tool) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p477, Park 22/e p188, 23/e p203-9
• Stool culture: Recommended for AFP surveillance and lab confirmation
• Isolation in stool: Does not correlate with disease as shedding occurs in subclinical cases also.
• Cultures of CSF, serum or throat swab are positive less frequently, but indicative of disease.

Microbiology 1/e p479, Park 23/e p203-9, 22/e p188
• VAPP occurs to recipients of OPV as well as to their contacts.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The classical complement pathway is activated by
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The classical complement pathway is primarily activated by antigen-antibody complexes. C1q binds to the Fc portion of IgG or IgM antibodies, triggering the cascade. This pathway is antibody-dependent and forms an important link between humoral immunity and the complement system.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: CD4 cells recognize antigen in association with
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: CD4 cells (helper T cells) recognize antigens presented by MHC class II molecules on the surface of antigen-presenting cells (APCs). This interaction is crucial for T cell activation and the initiation of both humoral and cell-mediated immune responses.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a major site for lymphocyte proliferation in the body?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Lymph nodes are a major site for lymphocyte proliferation and activation in the body. They filter lymph and provide a microenvironment where antigen-presenting cells and lymphocytes interact, initiating specific immune responses. Secondary lymphoid organs like lymph nodes support adaptive immune responses.

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
56. Viral Exanthems and Cutaneous Infections: Herpes, Pox, Parvovirus, Measles, Rubella, Coxsackie
mcqs.explanation: The Paul Bunnell test is used to diagnose infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus. The test detects heterophile antibodies that agglutinate sheep red blood cells.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is an example of RNA oncogenic virus?

04. General Virology and Overview of Viral Infections
mcqs.explanation:
(a) (Retroviruses) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p413, Ananthanarayan 9/e p565
• Oncogenic RNA viruses-HTLV1 (Retroviruses) and HCV.

chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control

(c) (Gloves) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p610
Hand hygiene is the most important as hands will be in contact first. So gloves will be the most effective method among
the options given here.

• Examples of primary cell lines: Rhesus Kidney cell line, Human amniotic cell line, Chick embryo fibroblast

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a primary lymphoid organ?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ where T lymphocytes mature. Primary lymphoid organs provide the environment for lymphocyte development and selection. They include the thymus (T cells) and bone marrow (B cells). Lymph nodes, spleen, and MALT are secondary lymphoid organs where mature lymphocytes respond to antigens.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Tuberculin test is an example of the following type of hypersensitivity reaction.
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The tuberculin test is an example of a type IV hypersensitivity reaction, which is a delayed-type hypersensitivity. It involves T cell-mediated immune responses, rather than antibody-mediated reactions, and takes 48-72 hours to develop.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Type I hypersensitivity reaction is mediated by
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: IgE antibodies mediate anaphylactic reactions by triggering mast cells and basophils to release histamine and other inflammatory mediators. IgE binds to high-affinity FcεRI receptors on mast cells, causing degranulation upon subsequent antigen exposure.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Type I hypersensitivity reaction is mediated by
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Type I hypersensitivity reactions are mediated by IgE antibodies. Mast cells and basophils release histamine and other mediators after antigen cross-links bound IgE, leading to immediate allergic reactions.

options.text: Genetically unrelated member of same species.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Allograft is taken from
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: An allograft is a graft taken from a genetically unrelated member of the same species. Allografts have different MHC molecules, triggering an immune response that can lead to rejection without immunosuppression. This is the most common type of transplant in clinical practice.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A graft taken from an individual and placed on another individual of the same genetic Constitution is called
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: An isograft (or syngeneic graft) is taken from an individual and placed on another individual with the same genetic makeup, such as identical twins. Isografts are not rejected because the donor and recipient are genetically identical, eliminating the immune barrier.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The synonym for hospital-acquired infection is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Hospital-acquired infections are also called nosocomial infections. The term "nosocomial" comes from the Greek words "nosos" (disease) and "komeion" (to care for). These infections develop 48 hours after hospital admission or within 3 days of discharge. They can be caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites and are often associated with medical procedures or antibiotic use.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The temperature and pressure used in an autoclave are
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Autoclaving uses 121°C and 15 lbs pressure (1 atm) for 15-20 minutes. This standard condition ensures the complete destruction of all microorganisms, including bacterial endospores. Lower temperatures or shorter times may not achieve sterilization.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Q fever is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii, an obligate intracellular bacterium. It is a zoonotic disease and is unique among rickettsiae because it is transmitted via aerosols, not arthropod vectors. C. burnetii is highly resistant to environmental conditions and can be a bioterrorism agent (Category B).

options.text: Derived from two separate germ layers that fused during development
Derived from a single clone (myoepithelial or ductal reserve cell) showing divergent differentiation into epithelial and myoepithelial components
A teratoma arising from totipotent cells within the salivary gland
A collision tumor of two independent neoplasms

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A parotid gland mass on histology shows epithelial cells forming ducts within a myxoid stroma resembling cartilage ("pseudocartilage"). Which best describes the origin of this mixed tumor?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Pleomorphic adenoma (mixed tumor of salivary gland) arises from a single germ layer / single clone, showing divergent differentiation into epithelial and myoepithelial elements — this defines a "mixed tumor," distinct from a teratoma.
- (A) incorrectly invokes two germ layers; mixed tumors arise from one germ layer.
- (C) confuses mixed tumor with teratoma, which specifically arises from totipotent germ cells and can show tissue from multiple germ layers.
- (D) describes an unrelated, much rarer phenomenon and is not the mechanism here.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An elderly man presented with fever and cough. Sputum examina tion revealed gram-negative organisms that were grown on Buffered charcoal yeast extract agar. The organism involved is:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
62. Bacterial Atypical Interstitial Pneumonia: Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella
mcqs.explanation:
(b) (Legionella) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p365-66, Harrison 19/e p1014-20
Fever, chest pain and dry cough is suggestive of atypical pneumonia.
Among the agents of atypical pneumonia, Legionella grows on charcoal yeast medium.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Human body louse is responsible for transmission of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Epidemic typhus is transmitted by the human body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis). It is caused by Rickettsia prowazekii. The louse becomes infected when feeding on a rickettsemic patient and transmits the bacteria through feces rubbed into the skin. Epidemic typhus occurs in conditions of overcrowding, poverty, and war.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Vector for Borrelia recurrentis is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Borrelia recurrentis is transmitted by the human body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis). It causes epidemic relapsing fever, characterized by recurrent episodes of fever separated by afebrile periods. This occurs due to antigenic variation of the bacterial surface proteins, allowing the organism to evade the immune response.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Causative agent of 'Weil's Disease' is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Weil's disease is caused by Leptospira species, particularly Leptospira interrogans serovar icterohaemorrhagiae. Weil's disease is the severe, icteric form of leptospirosis characterized by jaundice, renal failure, and hemorrhage. It is transmitted through contact with water contaminated with the urine of infected animals (especially rats).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Weil's disease is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Leptospira interrogans serovar icterohaemorrhagiae causes Weil's disease. This is the severe, icteric form of leptospirosis characterized by jaundice, renal failure, and hemorrhage. It is transmitted through contact with water contaminated with the urine of infected rats.

Reduces risk of infection to laboratory personnel

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Castaneda's method of blood culture is advantageous because it
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Castaneda's method contains solid and liquid media in one bottle, reduces chances of contamination, and reduces the risk of infection to lab personnel. It is a biphasic culture system used for the isolation of Brucella and Leptospira species, allowing for both liquid and solid phase growth in a single container.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Undulant fever is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Brucella melitensis is known to cause undulant fever. Brucellosis is a zoonotic disease transmitted from animals (sheep, goats, cattle) to humans through ingestion of unpasteurized milk or direct contact with infected animals. The fever is characterized by a rising and falling pattern (undulating fever).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following zoonotic diseases has no arthropod vector?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Brucellosis is transmitted through direct contact with infected animals or consumption of contaminated animal products and does not involve an arthropod vector. It is a zoonotic disease caused by Brucella species and is transmitted through ingestion, inhalation, or skin contact.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: 'Milk Ring test' is performed on whole milk for the detection of the following infection in cattle
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: The Milk ring test is used to detect Brucellosis in cattle. It is a simple screening test based on the agglutination of Brucella antibodies in milk. A positive test indicates the presence of Brucella antibodies, which helps in screening for brucellosis in dairy herds.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The nonsporing anaerobe associated with Vincent's angina is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Fusobacterium fusiforme is associated with Vincent's angina, a necrotizing ulcerative gingivostomatitis. The infection is a synergistic bacterial infection involving Borrelia vincentii and Fusobacterium fusiforme (fusospirochetal infection). It is also known as trench mouth and is common in immunocompromised individuals or those with poor oral hygiene.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All of the following statements about Genus Brucella are true EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Brucella species are not strict parasites of humans; they can infect various animals (cattle, goats, sheep, pigs) and humans are accidental hosts. Brucella is a nonmotile, fastidious, Gram-negative coccobacillus that causes brucellosis (undulant fever). Transmission to humans occurs through ingestion, inhalation, or skin contact.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Relapsing fever is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Borrelia recurrentis is the causative agent of relapsing fever. It is transmitted by lice (epidemic) or ticks (endemic). The disease is characterized by recurrent episodes of fever due to antigenic variation of the surface proteins, allowing the organism to evade the host immune response.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Reverse transcriptase enzyme is involved in the replication process of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Retroviruses, including HIV, use the enzyme reverse transcriptase to replicate their RNA genome into DNA. This enzyme is encoded by the viral genome and is essential for the viral life cycle, allowing the virus to integrate into the host genome and establish a persistent infection. The enzyme is a target for antiretroviral therapy (e.g., nucleoside and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which antibody is elevated in primary immune response?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation:
(b) (IgM) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology/p114, Ananthanarayan 9/e p146
• IgM: Elevated in primary immune response
• IgG: Elevated in secondary immune response

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following viral haemorrhagic fevers are seen in India?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Chikungunya, Dengue type 1-4, and Kyasanur forest disease are all viral haemorrhagic fevers seen in India. These diseases are endemic in various regions of India and are transmitted by arthropod vectors (mosquitoes and ticks). Kyasanur forest disease is particularly prevalent in Karnataka.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The arboviral infection that does not exist in India is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Yellow fever is an arboviral infection that is not present in India. Yellow fever is endemic in tropical areas of South America and Africa, where it is transmitted by Aedes and Haemagogus mosquitoes. Travelers to endemic areas require vaccination. India currently requires proof of yellow fever vaccination for travelers arriving from endemic countries.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Cerebral malaria is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Plasmodium falciparum is responsible for causing cerebral malaria, a severe and potentially fatal complication. P. falciparum is the most virulent malaria parasite, causing sequestration of infected erythrocytes in cerebral microvasculature, leading to altered consciousness and potentially death.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: For infection of mosquito, the blood of human carrier must contain at least
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: The blood of a human carrier must contain at least 10 gametocytes per microliter for effective transmission to a mosquito. The threshold for infectivity of gametocytes is approximately 10-20 per µL. Gametocytes are the sexual stage of the parasite responsible for transmission to mosquitoes, and their density determines the efficiency of transmission.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A female patient from a tribal area of Jharkhand reports with fever for last 3 days. Peripheral blood is collected and stained with Giemsa and diagnosis of malaria is made. The smear is shown in the Figure. What is the likely cause? (PG Entrance 2020)
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Plasmodium falciparum typically presents with multiple ring forms within the same red blood cell and is known for its high parasitemia levels. The rings appear delicate and thin, and the red blood cells are not enlarged, which are typical features of P. falciparum infection. Also, P. falciparum has appliqué (accolé) forms with rings at the edge of RBCs, and Maurer's dots may be present.

mcqs.question: Long history was given. Then the question was which has maximum risk of transmission by needle prick?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
48. Viruses Causing Hepatitis: Hepatitis Viruses, Yellow Fever
mcqs.explanation:
(c) (Hepatitis B) Ref: ApurbaSastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p 532
Following needle prick injury the risk of transmission of Hepatitis B is 30%, Hepatitis C is 3% and HIV is 0.3%.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following hepatitis viruses is a DNA virus?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
48. Viruses Causing Hepatitis: Hepatitis Viruses, Yellow Fever
mcqs.explanation:
(b) (Hepatitis B virus) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p527, Ananthanarayan 9/e p543
• Among Hepatitis viruses only Hepatitis B virus is a DNA virus.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Marker for diagnosing acute hepatitis B in 2–5 weeks:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
48. Viruses Causing Hepatitis: Hepatitis Viruses, Yellow Fever
mcqs.explanation:
(a) (IgM Anti HBc) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p534-35
Refer chapter review for explanation.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Relapse of malaria is not seen in infection with
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Relapses are not seen with Plasmodium falciparum, which does not have a dormant liver stage (hypnozoites). While P. falciparum can cause recrudescence due to persistent blood-stage parasites, it does not cause true relapse. P. vivax and P. ovale have hypnozoites and cause relapse, while P. malariae causes recrudescence (not relapse) due to low levels of persistent blood-stage parasites.

options.text: RAS becomes permanently trapped in its inactive GDP-bound state
RAS becomes permanently trapped in its active GTP-bound state, causing continuous proliferative signaling
RAS loses its farnesyl membrane anchor and becomes nonfunctional
RAS is degraded rapidly, reducing downstream signaling

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old man with pancreatic adenocarcinoma has molecular testing showing a point mutation in one of the RAS genes. What is the functional consequence of this mutation on RAS protein activity?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Point mutation converts RAS proto-oncogene to an oncogene by trapping RAS in its active, GTP-bound form (impairing GTPase-mediated hydrolysis back to GDP), resulting in continuous, unregulated proliferative signaling via the RAF/ERK and PI3K/AKT pathways.
- (A) describes the opposite (inactive) state, which would reduce rather than increase signaling.
- (C) describes loss of membrane anchoring, an unrelated mechanism not characteristic of RAS oncogenic mutations.
- (D) describes degradation, which would also reduce rather than increase oncogenic signaling — the opposite of the actual mechanism.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Kala-azar is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) is caused by Leishmania donovani. It is the most severe form of leishmaniasis, affecting the viscera (spleen, liver, bone marrow). The disease is characterized by fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The vector for Kala-azar is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Kala-azar is transmitted by the bite of infected female sandflies of the genus Phlebotomus (in the Old World) or Lutzomyia (in the New World). The sandfly injects promastigotes into the host, which are phagocytosed and transform into amastigotes within macrophages, causing the disease.

options.text: Homogeneous stainable regions (HSR); associated with a favorable prognosis
Double minutes; associated with poor prognosis
Ring chromosomes; of no prognostic significance
Barr bodies; indicate the tumor's sex chromosome complement

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A neuroblastoma specimen shows amplification of the N-MYC gene, seen as small extrachromosomal structures on karyotype. What are these structures called, and what is their clinical significance?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Gene amplification can appear as extrachromosomal "double minutes," and N-MYC amplification in neuroblastoma (whether as double minutes or as an integrated homogeneous stainable region) is associated with poor prognosis.
- (A) misassigns the correct term (homogeneous stainable regions, HSR, are the chromosomally integrated pattern, not the extrachromosomal one) and incorrectly states a favorable prognosis.
- (C) misidentifies the structure entirely; ring chromosomes are an unrelated cytogenetic finding.
- (D) is unrelated; Barr bodies reflect X-inactivation, not gene amplification.

options.text: There is nonproductive cough with wheeze
Blood eosinophil count is more than 300/cmm

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All of the findings below hold true for Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia EXCEPT that
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: In Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia, microfilariae are usually not seen in peripheral blood smears, as the condition is characterized by high eosinophil counts and a response to DEC (Diethylcarbamazine). TPE is a form of occult filariasis where the microfilariae are trapped in the pulmonary capillaries and do not appear in the peripheral blood.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Germ tube test is used for identification of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: The germ tube test is specifically used for the identification of Candida albicans. A positive germ tube test is indicative of C. albicans (and closely related C. dubliniensis). This test is rapid, simple, and highly specific for C. albicans, making it a valuable tool in the clinical laboratory.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Grafts between two genetically non identical members of same species are called
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Grafts between two genetically non-identical members of the same species are called allografts. Allografts are the most common type of transplant and require careful HLA matching and immunosuppressive therapy to prevent rejection.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: In renal transplant recipients which is likely organism causing reactivation disease within 4 months after surgery (PG Entrance 2020)
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a common cause of reactivation disease in renal transplant recipients, especially within the first few months after surgery. Immunosuppression increases the risk of CMV reactivation, which can cause pneumonitis, hepatitis, and colitis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a live attenuated vaccine?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin) is a live attenuated vaccine derived from Mycobacterium bovis. It is used for the prevention of tuberculosis, particularly in children. The attenuated strain retains immunogenicity but loses virulence, making it safe for immunization.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An HIV positive patient with a CD4 count of 300/mm³ presents with mucosal lesions in the mouth as shown in the figure. On microscopy budding yeasts and pseudohyphae are seen. What is the likely diagnosis (PG Entrance 2020)
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Candidiasis, caused by Candida species, often presents as white patches on the mucosal surfaces in immunocompromised patients, such as those with HIV. The presence of budding yeasts and pseudohyphae on microscopy further supports this diagnosis. Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) is a common opportunistic infection in HIV/AIDS patients, especially when CD4 counts drop below 350-400 cells/µL.

options.text: Both preformed toxin and infection with Cl. botulinum

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) caused by Cl. Botulinum is

options.text: Tumor development would still occur, since the order of exposure does not matter
Tumor development would not occur, because promoters only stimulate proliferation in cells that have already been initiated
The second agent would itself become a direct-acting initiator
The cell would undergo immediate apoptosis regardless of exposure order

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In the multistep hypothesis of chemical carcinogenesis, a cell is first exposed to a carcinogenic initiator, producing a permanent, nonlethal DNA mutation. A second, noncarcinogenic agent is subsequently applied, causing the initiated cell to proliferate. If the order of exposure is reversed (the second agent given before the initiator), what would be the expected outcome?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Promoters are noncarcinogenic agents that cannot directly damage DNA; tumors develop only if the promoter is applied after the initiator, since promoters act only on cells that have already sustained the initiator's permanent DNA damage.
- (A) is incorrect — order of exposure is critical to the multistep hypothesis; reversing it prevents tumor development.
- (C) incorrectly reclassifies a promoter as an initiator; this contradicts their defining, distinct properties.
- (D) is an unsupported and incorrect claim not part of the multistep hypothesis.

options.text: PSA is highly specific for prostate cancer and is never elevated in benign conditions

PSA elevation always indicates metastatic prostate cancer

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 62-year-old man presents with an elevated serum PSA. Biopsy is being considered. Which statement about PSA as a tumor marker is most accurate?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): PSA is organ-specific (prostate) but not cancer-specific — it can be elevated in benign prostatic hyperplasia as well as prostate cancer, giving it low sensitivity and low specificity for malignancy specifically.
- (A) overstates PSA's specificity, contradicting its well-known limitation of being elevated in benign disease too.
- (C) incorrectly implies that any PSA elevation signifies metastasis; PSA elevation is nonspecific and does not by itself indicate metastatic disease.
- (D) misattributes PSA to testicular tumors; that role belongs to markers like AFP and hCG, not PSA.

options.text: Cushing syndrome, due to ectopic ACTH secretion

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with small-cell (oat cell) carcinoma of the lung develops hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine. Which paraneoplastic syndrome and mechanism best explain this?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Small-cell (oat cell) carcinoma of the lung is the most common cause of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), producing dilutional hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine.
- (A) Cushing syndrome from ectopic ACTH is also associated with small-cell lung carcinoma but presents with a distinct clinical picture (hypercortisolism), not hyponatremia.
- (C) Carcinoid syndrome (serotonin, bradykinin) is associated with bronchial carcinoid, not small-cell carcinoma, and does not present primarily with hyponatremia.
- (D) Hypercalcemia of malignancy via PTHrP is classically associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, not small-cell carcinoma, and presents with elevated (not decreased) calcium/sodium disturbance pattern described here.

mcqs.question: At autopsy of a patient who died 8 days after an MI, histology at the margin of the infarct shows numerous new capillaries, fibroblasts, and scant collagen. What is this finding called, and what colour would it show on Masson's trichrome stain?

- Correct (C): By day 7–10, the infarct margin shows fibrovascular granulation tissue (new vessels, fibroblasts, scant collagen); on Masson's trichrome, low collagen content means it appears pink/pale rather than blue.
- (A) describes the later (>2 month), collagen-rich, strongly blue-staining mature scar — not the day-8 finding.
- (B) contraction band necrosis is a reperfusion-related acute finding, unrelated to this later healing-phase histology.
- (D) coagulative necrosis with a "brick-red" TPTC-type description does not apply to routine histologic staining at this healing stage.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient is at the highest risk of myocardial free-wall rupture during which post-MI time window, and why?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (D): The heart is structurally weakest around days 3–7 post-MI — maximal neutrophilic digestion of dead tissue has occurred, but granulation tissue has not yet deposited enough collagen to restore tensile strength, making this the peak window for free-wall/septal/papillary muscle rupture.
- (A) and (C) describe very early time points, before the neutrophilic digestion that weakens the wall has become maximal.
- (B) describes the fully healed, collagen-rich scar stage, when rupture risk has fallen sharply, not risen.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient who suffered an MI ten days ago now re-presents with recurrent chest pain concerning for reinfarction. Troponin was already elevated and slowly declining from the initial event. Which finding would best confirm a new reinfarction?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Because troponin remains elevated for 7–10 days after the initial infarct, a single elevated value cannot distinguish ongoing recovery from reinfarction — serial monitoring for a re-rise of more than 20% from the previous value is the recognized way to detect fresh myocardial damage.
- (A) an unchanged level argues against, rather than for, a new event.
- (C) a single LDH1 value lacks the serial comparison needed and LDH1 is not the marker specifically used for reinfarction detection.
- (D) urinary myoglobin detection is not the recognized method for diagnosing reinfarction.

options.text: Mitral valve, because it is the most commonly affected valve in the general population

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with a history of intravenous drug use presents with fever and a new murmur. Echocardiography reveals a large, bulky vegetation. Which valve is most likely involved, and why?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (C): In IV drug abusers, right-sided valves (tricuspid > pulmonary) are most commonly affected, because the intravenous entry route delivers organisms directly to the right heart first, before they pass through the pulmonary circulation.
- (A) describes the general population pattern (mitral, with aortic also involved), not the IV drug use pattern specifically asked about here.
- (B) invents a direct-damage mechanism to the aortic valve, which is not the recognized mechanism for IV drug-associated IE.
- (D) incorrectly claims the pulmonary valve is the single most vulnerable valve; tricuspid is more commonly affected than pulmonary even in this population.

Sputum and specimens from non-sterile sites need prior treatment for digestion (to liquefy the thick pus cells and
homogenization) and decontamination (to inhibit the normal flora) and concentration (to increase the yield).
• Petroff’s method (4% NaOH): Most commonly followed

options.text: Secondary right-sided heart failure, producing combined biventricular failure
Reversal of the left heart failure without further intervention

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with longstanding, untreated left-sided heart failure develops progressive pulmonary hypertension. Over time, this leads to which downstream complication?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (A): Untreated left HF can progress to acute pulmonary oedema and, over time, pulmonary hypertension and secondary right-sided heart failure — illustrating how untreated left HF is the classic route into combined biventricular failure.
- (B) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a distinct genetic condition, not a downstream consequence of left heart failure.
- (C) is incorrect — untreated left heart failure does not spontaneously reverse; it tends to progress and cause further complications.
- (D) Cardiac tamponade is an acute pericardial complication (e.g. from free-wall rupture or effusion), not the characteristic chronic downstream consequence of untreated left HF described here.

options.text: Increased blood flow to the upper limb, causing limb hypertrophy
Decreased blood flow to the upper limb, producing weak/absent pulses ("pulseless disease")
Increased blood flow to the lower limb via collateral shunting
Complete sparing of limb perfusion, with symptoms confined to the CNS only

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In Takayasu arteritis, intimal thickening of the subclavian artery leads to which downstream clinical consequence, and through what mechanism?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (B): Intimal thickening narrows the subclavian artery lumen, decreasing blood flow specifically to the upper limb (the vessel's typical distribution), producing the weak or absent pulses that give "pulseless disease" its name.
- (A) incorrectly claims increased flow, the opposite of what intimal thickening/luminal narrowing produces.
- (D) incorrectly claims complete sparing of limb perfusion; the upper limb is specifically and characteristically affected.
- (C) incorrectly redirects the mechanism to the lower limb; the subclavian artery supplies the upper limb.

options.text: Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans); treatment is smoking cessation
Giant cell arteritis; treatment is corticosteroids

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old heavy smoker presents with intermittent claudication of the lower limb progressing to pain at rest, along with digital ischemia. Angiography shows segmental occlusion of small and medium arteries and veins. Biopsy shows inflammation involving the artery, vein, and adjacent nerve together, with lymphatics spared. What is the diagnosis and the single most important treatment?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (C): This is Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans), strongly associated with smoking; it characteristically involves artery, vein, and nerve together while sparing lymphatics, producing claudication progressing to rest pain as nerves become involved. Smoking cessation is the single most important intervention.
- (B) Polyarteritis nodosa does not characteristically involve veins and nerves together with sparing of lymphatics, and its treatment is not smoking cessation.
- (A) Takayasu arteritis affects large vessels (aorta and its major branches), not the small/medium artery-vein-nerve triad described, and is treated with steroids, not smoking cessation.
- (D) Giant cell arteritis affects the temporal artery in older patients with headache/jaw claudication, an entirely different presentation and treatment approach.

options.text: Child A has Kawasaki disease and requires only supportive care with no specific treatment
Child A has scarlet fever, Child B has Kawasaki disease; only Child A needs antibiotics
Both children have the same diagnosis, differing only in severity

Child A has Kawasaki disease (systemic vasculitis with conjunctivitis/lymphadenopathy/edema), Child B has scarlet fever (post-streptococcal, with sandpaper rash); Child A requires IVIG plus aspirin to prevent coronary artery complications

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A pediatrician evaluates two children, both presenting with a "strawberry tongue." Child A also has bilateral conjunctivitis, cervical lymphadenopathy, and extremity edema. Child B has a sore throat, fever, and a diffuse sandpaper-like rash following a recent streptococcal infection. What is the key distinguishing feature between the two diagnoses, and what treatment does Child A require that Child B does not?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (D): Child A's presentation (conjunctivitis, lymphadenopathy, edema alongside strawberry tongue) fits Kawasaki disease, requiring IVIG plus aspirin specifically to reduce the risk of coronary artery aneurysm/MI; Child B's presentation (sore throat, sandpaper rash, recent strep infection) fits scarlet fever, treated with antibiotics for the underlying streptococcal infection — both children share strawberry tongue as a classic overlapping sign, but the rest of the picture and treatment differ.
- (B) swaps the two diagnoses incorrectly.
- (C) incorrectly claims they are the same diagnosis; they are distinct entities with different treatments.
- (A) understates Kawasaki disease's specific treatment need (IVIG + aspirin), which is essential to prevent coronary complications, not merely supportive care.

options.text: PR3; diagnosis is Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (Wegener's granulomatosis)
dsDNA; diagnosis is systemic lupus erythematosus

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with chronic sinusitis, nasal septal perforation, hemoptysis with cavitary lung lesions on CT, and rapidly progressive renal failure is found to have a cytoplasmic pattern of antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody on immunofluorescence. Which specific antigen does this antibody target, and what is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (A): The classic triad of upper respiratory (nasal septal perforation), lung (cavitary lesions), and kidney (RPGN) involvement, with a cytoplasmic (c-ANCA) staining pattern, defines Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA, formerly Wegener's granulomatosis); c-ANCA specifically targets PR3 (proteinase-3).
- (D) MPO is targeted by p-ANCA (perinuclear pattern), not the c-ANCA pattern described in this vignette, and is associated with microscopic polyangiitis rather than this triad.
- (B) Churg-Strauss syndrome is associated with p-ANCA/MPO and marked eosinophilia, not the c-ANCA/PR3 pattern and triad described here.
- (C) Anti-dsDNA antibodies are associated with SLE, an unrelated antibody and disease entirely.

options.text: Induction: Corticosteroids alone, with no other agents required

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient newly diagnosed with Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA) is started on induction therapy. Which drug is used for induction, and which drug follows it for maintenance?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (D): GPA treatment classically begins with Rituximab for induction, followed by Cyclophosphamide.
- (C) reverses the correct order of the two agents.
- (B) understates the treatment regimen, which requires more than corticosteroids alone for adequate disease control.
- (A) proposes an incorrect drug pairing not classically used as the primary induction-then-maintenance sequence for GPA in this framework.

options.text: Systemic lupus erythematosus; HLA-DR2; Pathergy test

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A young adult presents with recurrent painful oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. HLA typing reveals a specific allele association, and a skin prick test produces an exaggerated inflammatory response at the puncture site. What is the diagnosis, the associated HLA allele, and the diagnostic test demonstrated?
mcqs.explanation:
- Correct (D): The triad of recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis is classic for Behcet's disease, a small vessel vasculitis associated with HLA-B51; the exaggerated skin response to a needle prick described is the pathergy test, used to support the diagnosis.
- (C) Reactive arthritis is associated with HLA-B27 and a different clinical triad (arthritis, urethritis, conjunctivitis), and uses no pathergy test.
- (A) Sjogren syndrome involves dry eyes/mouth (tested by Schirmer test), not the oral/genital ulcer and uveitis triad described.
- (B) SLE is associated with different HLA alleles and does not use the pathergy test as a diagnostic tool.

options.text: Plummer-Vinson syndrome; increased risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma
Barrett's esophagus; increased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma
Zenker's diverticulum; increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the pharynx
Achalasia; increased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A middle-aged woman presents with dysphagia, iron deficiency anemia, atrophic glossitis, and esophageal webs on barium study. Which condition does she have, and what malignancy risk does it confer?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) Plummer-Vinson syndrome (also called Paterson-Brown-Kelly syndrome, or 'sideropenic dysphagia') presents with iron deficiency anemia, esophageal webs, dysphagia, and atrophic glossitis in middle-aged women, and predisposes to esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
- (B) Barrett's esophagus is a distinct entity from GERD-driven columnar metaplasia and does not present with this triad of anemia, webs, and glossitis.
- (C) Zenker's diverticulum is a pharyngoesophageal outpouching, distinct from this syndrome; while both are in the differential for dysphagia, the described triad is classic for Plummer-Vinson syndrome.
- (D) Achalasia is a motility disorder with bird-beak narrowing on barium study and predisposes to SCC, but does not classically present with esophageal webs, iron deficiency anemia, and atrophic glossitis as its defining triad.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A gastric biopsy is stained to detect a curved, spiral-shaped organism. The pathologist notes this stain is considered the single best method for visualizing this organism. Which stain is being used?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) H&E can sometimes show the organism but is not considered the best/most reliable stain for H. pylori detection.
- (B) Congo red stains amyloid, not H. pylori.
- (C) Modified Giemsa stain is considered the best special stain for detecting H. pylori on gastric biopsy (Warthin-Starry silver stain is also used).
- (D) Ziehl-Neelsen stains acid-fast organisms like Mycobacteria, not H. pylori.

options.text: Cushing ulcer (burns) and Curling ulcer (raised intracranial tension)
Both are called Curling ulcers, differing only by anatomic location
Both are called Cushing ulcers, differing only by depth
Curling ulcer (burns) and Cushing ulcer (raised intracranial tension)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with severe burns covering 40% of body surface area develops a superficial duodenal ulcer during their ICU stay. A separate patient with a large intracranial hemorrhage develops a deep, penetrating ulcer in the gastric cardia. What are these two stress ulcers called, respectively?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) This reverses the correct cause-eponym pairing — Curling is linked to burns, Cushing to raised intracranial tension.
- (B) The two ulcers differ in cause, site, and depth — they are not variants of the same named entity distinguished only by location.
- (C) Similarly, the two ulcers are distinct entities with different underlying causes, not depth-based variants of a single eponym.
- (D) Curling ulcer is a superficial duodenal stress ulcer caused by burns. Cushing ulcer is a deep, penetrating ('pushing') ulcer of the gastric cardia caused by raised intracranial tension (mnemonic: 'Cushing is pushing').

options.text: Decreased intrinsic factor, causing pernicious anemia
Increased TNF-α, causing amyloidosis-related nephrotic syndrome

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Endoscopy in a middle-aged man reveals giant, cerebriform gastric rugae. Biopsy shows marked foveolar cell hyperplasia. He also has significant peripheral edema and low serum albumin. What growth factor drives this condition, and what mechanism explains his edema?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) Menetrier's disease is driven by increased TGF-α, causing foveolar cell hyperplasia with giant cerebriform rugae; excessive gastric protein/mucus loss produces protein-losing enteropathy, leading to hypoalbuminemia and edema. It is more common in men.
- (B) Zollinger-Ellison syndrome results from gastrin-secreting tumors causing hyperacidity and ulcers, not giant cerebriform rugae with hypoalbuminemia from protein loss.
- (C) Decreased intrinsic factor causes pernicious anemia (B12 deficiency), not the gross/microscopic gastric findings or edema described here.
- (D) TNF-α is not the classic driver of Menetrier's disease, and amyloidosis-related nephrotic syndrome is an unrelated cause of edema/hypoalbuminemia.

options.text: Parietal cells; deficiency of intrinsic factor (Castle's factor)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient develops megaloblastic anemia due to autoimmune destruction of a specific gastric cell type, which also stains pink on routine H&E. Which cell type is destroyed, and what molecule's deficiency causes the anemia?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) Chief cells (blue on H&E) secrete pepsinogen, which has no role in B12 absorption or megaloblastic anemia.
- (B) Foveolar cells secrete mucin for mucosal protection, unrelated to B12 absorption.
- (C) G cells secrete gastrin, which stimulates acid secretion but has no direct role in B12 absorption via intrinsic factor.
- (D) Parietal cells (pink on H&E) secrete both HCl and intrinsic factor. Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells causes loss of intrinsic factor, impairing B12 absorption and causing megaloblastic (pernicious) anemia.

mcqs.question: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is caused by:

options.text: Hyperplastic polyp; generally no malignant potential
Sessile serrated adenoma; significant malignant potential

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Colonoscopic biopsy of a colonic polyp shows glandular architecture with serrations confined to the upper (luminal) portion of the crypts, with normal architecture at the crypt base. What type of polyp is this, and does it carry malignant potential?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) Hyperplastic polyps show serrations confined to the upper portion of the crypts (with a normal crypt base) and generally lack significant malignant potential, distinguishing them from sessile serrated adenomas.
- (B) Sessile serrated adenomas show serrations extending the full length of the crypt with boot-shaped crypt bases, and do carry malignant potential — a different pattern from the upper-crypt-only serrations described.
- (C) Tubular adenomas are a distinct neoplastic polyp category (not defined by serration pattern) with malignant potential via the adenoma-carcinoma sequence.
- (D) Peutz-Jeghers polyps are hamartomatous, defined by an arborizing smooth muscle pattern, not by crypt serration location.

mcqs.subject: Pathology

mcqs.explanation:

- (B) Tubular adenoma carries the lowest malignant risk of the three subtypes, not the highest.
- (C) Tubulovillous adenoma has intermediate risk (mixed architecture), not the highest.
- (D) The three subtypes have differing, not equal, malignant potential, with villous carrying the greatest risk.

- (A) PBC affects intrahepatic ducts only and does not classically show the beading/stricture pattern of both intra- and extrahepatic ducts described here — PSC is the better fit.

- (C) PBC does not involve extrahepatic bile ducts; the case described (both intra- and extrahepatic involvement with onion-skin fibrosis) is classic for PSC, not PBC.
- (D) PSC affects both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts (unlike PBC, which is limited to intrahepatic ducts), and shows the classic 'onion-skin' concentric periductal fibrosis on histology.

mcqs.question: A young adult develops mild scleral icterus during a viral febrile illness, which resolves spontaneously. He is otherwise asymptomatic and has normal liver enzymes. Which unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia syndrome is most consistent, and what inheritance pattern does it follow?
mcqs.explanation:
- (A) Crigler-Najjar type 1 causes severe, often fatal hyperbilirubinemia in infancy, not the mild, self-limited presentation described in this otherwise well young adult.
- (B) Crigler-Najjar type 2 causes more significant, persistent hyperbilirubinemia typically requiring treatment (phenobarbitone), and while it is autosomal dominant, the clinical picture does not match this mild, self-limited episode.
- (C) Gilbert syndrome results from a very mild UGT deficiency, is typically asymptomatic, and is precipitated by stress, fever, or illness; like most unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia syndromes, it is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern (the exception being Crigler-Najjar type 2, which is autosomal dominant).
- (D) Gilbert syndrome is the correct diagnosis, but it follows an autosomal recessive pattern, not autosomal dominant — Crigler-Najjar type 2 is the AD exception among these syndromes.

- Malakoplakia arises from a defect in phagocytosis; the calcified intracytoplasmic inclusions are Michaelis-Guttmann bodies, and the macrophages containing them are called Von Hansemann cells. It classically mimics bladder cancer grossly.

- (D) Renal TB shows caseous necrosis and granulomas, not calcified inclusion bodies within macrophages.

Persistent Infections are chara cterized as those in which the virus is not cleared but remains in specific cells of infected
individuals.
Responsible for 20% of human cancers. It is of 3 overlapping varieties.
1. Latent infection: Defined as a state of infection in which the virus is not replicating i.e. no demonstrable infectious virus
between episodes of recurrent disease. For example, Refer chapter review.
2. Chronic infection: Characterized by the continued presence of infectious virus following the primary infection. For
example, HBV, HCV
3. Slow infection: Characterized by a prolonged incubation period followed by progressive disease. Without any acute
period of viral multiplication. For example, Slow viruses.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following best describes what the Gleason grading system evaluates in prostate adenocarcinoma?
mcqs.explanation:
- The Gleason system grades prostate adenocarcinoma based on glandular architectural pattern (patterns 1 through 5), not nuclear features, mitotic count, or IHC markers.
- (D) Nuclear pleomorphism/mitotic count is the basis of many other grading systems (e.g., Nottingham for breast, leiomyosarcoma mitotic criteria), but not Gleason grading.
- (B) Perineural invasion is a separate reported feature, not the basis of the Gleason pattern itself.
- (C) IHC markers are not the basis of Gleason architectural grading.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A prostate biopsy shows a single glandular pattern throughout — a fused, cribriform pattern corresponding to Gleason pattern 4, with no other pattern identified. What is the Gleason score?
mcqs.explanation:
- When only a single Gleason pattern is present, the score is that pattern doubled: pattern 4 alone → 4 + 4 = 8.
- (D) and (B) both incorrectly introduce a pattern 3 component that was not described.
- (A) incorrectly introduces a pattern 5 component that was not described.

options.text: 4 (primary, most common) + 5 (highest-grade minor component takes priority over pattern 2) = 9

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A prostate biopsy shows adenocarcinoma predominantly in a cribriform pattern (Gleason pattern 4), a lesser crowded-but-separate-glands pattern (Gleason pattern 2), and a minor 5% component of single-cell infiltration (Gleason pattern 5). How is the Gleason score correctly calculated?
mcqs.explanation:
- The Gleason score uses the primary (most common) pattern plus the secondary pattern; when a minor higher-grade (tertiary) component is present, that higher-grade pattern is used as the secondary component instead of the true second-most-common pattern. Here: primary = 4, and pattern 5 (though only a minor 5% component) takes priority over pattern 2 as the secondary component, giving 4+5=9.
- (B) Uses the true second-most-common pattern (2) instead of correctly substituting the higher-grade minor component (5).
- (D) Incorrectly assigns pattern 2 as primary; pattern 4 is the most common (primary) pattern in this case.
- (C) Incorrectly assigns pattern 5 as primary; pattern 5 is only a minor (5%) component, not the primary pattern.

mcqs.explanation:
- The "staghorn" megakaryocyte, with its branching antler-like nuclear morphology, is classically associated with Essential Thrombocythemia (ET).
- (A) Pawn ball megakaryocytes (with separated, rounded nuclear lobes) are associated with MDS, not ET.
- (C) Dwarf megakaryocytes (small, hypolobated) are associated with CML, not ET.
- (B) Cloud-like megakaryocytes (with fine, cloud-shaped nuclear lobulation) are associated with Primary Myelofibrosis, not ET.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with a normal platelet count but a bleeding tendency undergoes platelet aggregation studies. Which of the following statements about platelet functional disorders is correct?
mcqs.explanation:
- In platelet functional (qualitative) disorders, the platelet count is typically normal — the abnormality lies in platelet function, not platelet number.
- (B) A decreased platelet count would suggest a quantitative disorder (e.g., ITP), not a purely functional defect.
- (C) Giant platelets are specific to Bernard-Soulier syndrome, not a universal feature of all functional disorders (e.g., Wiskott-Aldrich shows small platelets).
- (D) Functional platelet disorders can be either inherited (e.g., Bernard-Soulier, Glanzmann) or acquired, not exclusively one or the other.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which platelet disorder is classically associated with SMALL platelets, distinguishing it from Bernard-Soulier syndrome's giant platelets?
mcqs.explanation:
- Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS) is classically associated with small platelets, in contrast to the giant platelets seen in Bernard-Soulier syndrome.
- (B) Glanzmann Thrombasthenia typically shows normal-sized platelets, not small platelets.
- (A) Gray Platelet Syndrome is defined by its alpha granule deficiency (gray appearance), not specifically by small platelet size.
- (D) Hermansky-Pudlak Syndrome is defined by dense granule deficiency and albinism, not specifically by small platelet size.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Viable Mycobacterium tuberculosis organisms can persist in a dormant state within an old, calcified, fibrotic granuloma for years to decades. This phenomenon is the pathologic basis of:
mcqs.explanation:
- Latent TB infection is defined by the persistence of viable but dormant bacilli within a healed (fibrocalcific) granuloma, capable of reactivating if host immunity later declines.
- A (miliary TB) describes active, widespread hematogenous dissemination — the opposite of a dormant, contained state.
- C (cavitary TB) describes active progressive pulmonary disease with liquefaction and cavity formation, not dormancy.
- D (tuberculous meningitis) is a specific site of active disseminated disease, unrelated to the concept of latency.

• ‘Microscopy, often combined with serologic testing, remains the standard diagnostic approach in many hospitals and clinics
worldwide for the diagnosis of amebiasis.’
• Stool Microscopy— done to demonstrate:
○ Trophozoites: Indicates active infection
○ Quadrinucleated cysts: Indicates carrier state
• Microscopy is poorly sensitive (25–60% with single sample) but the sensitivity increases to 85–95% when three stool
samples are examined. It cannot differentiate between E. histolytica and other Entamoeba histolytica subspecies such as
E. dispar and E. moshkovskii.
• ELISA detecting 170 kDa of lectin antigen in stool shows > 95% sensitivity and specificity. It can also differentiate
pathogenic E. histolytica (lectin antigen positive) and nonpathogenic E.dispar ((lectin antigen negative).
• Polyxenic culture: 50–70% sensitivity and 100% specificity (gold standard). Serves as a research tool but not available
for clinical use.
• PCR assay for DNA in stool samples is currently the most sensitive and specific method for identifying E. histolytica
infection and has become a valuable epidemiologic and research tool.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: In a postoperative ward, 4 out of 10 patients developed wound discharge, which on culture was found to be positive for coagulase positive gram positive cocci. chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation:
(c) (The orga...) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p219, Ananthanarayan 9/e p205, 8/e p197
• Coagulase positive gram positive cocci: Indicates Staphylococcus aureus
• Resistant to Methicillin: Indicates MRSA (Methicillin resistant S taphylococcus aureus)
• Health care personnel of the hospital found to be nasal carrier for the same agent: Indicates that the infection has spread
to the patient from health care personnel of the hospital
• “The MC way of spread of infection in hospital: Through the hospital staff (not from other patient from the hospital)”
• Mechanism of Resistance of MRSA: Due to chromosomally mediated Mec A gene which codes for altered PBP 2a (Penicillin
Binding protein or receptor 2a) which has less affinity for β lactam drugs.
About Other Options
• The major route of spread causing the outbreak is through the hands of hospital staff
• The resistance to Methicillin is chromosomally mediated
• Since MRSA coded altered PBP 2a (Penicillin Binding protein 2a) has less affinity for β lactam drugs, so MRSA
strains are resistant to all β lactam drugs. Even combination of β lactam and β lactamase inhibitor will not work.

HPV vaccines under trial
• Recently developed HPV vaccines dramatically reduce rates of infection and disease produced by the HPV types in
the vaccines.
• These products are directed against virus types that cause anogenital tract disease and are derived from expression of

• HPV types 6 and 11 cause 90% of anogenital warts
• HPV types 16 and 18 are responsible for 70% of cervical cancers.
[UPDATE 2026] A nonavalent HPV vaccine (Gardasil-9) is now available, and India's indigenous quadrivalent vaccine CERVAVAC was launched in 2023. WHO now endorses a single-dose schedule for girls aged 9-20 years. HPV vaccination for 14-year-old girls was added to India's UIP in February 2026.
