mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The concept of "spontaneous generation" was disproved by
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Louis Pasteur's famous swan-neck flask experiment conclusively disproved the theory of spontaneous generation by demonstrating that microbial growth only occurred when the flask was open to air, proving that microorganisms come from pre-existing microorganisms.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following bacteria is acid-fast?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is acid-fast due to the presence of mycolic acid in its cell wall. Mycolic acid forms a waxy lipid layer that resists staining with conventional methods but retains carbolfuchsin dye even after acid-alcohol decolorization. This property is the basis for Ziehl-Neelsen staining.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the smallest bacteria?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Mycoplasma species are the smallest known bacteria, measuring only 0.2–0.3 µm in diameter. They lack a cell wall, making them resistant to penicillin and beta-lactam antibiotics. They are also the simplest self-replicating organisms and can pass through bacterial filters.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The transfer of genetic material through a bacteriophage is called
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Transduction is the transfer of genetic material from one bacterium to another via a bacteriophage (virus). This process can be generalized (transferring any bacterial DNA) or specialized (transferring specific genes). It plays a significant role in bacterial evolution and antibiotic resistance spread.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The shape of Vibrio cholerae is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Vibrio cholerae is a Gram-negative, comma-shaped bacterium. It is highly motile with a single polar flagellum. Its curved shape is characteristic of the genus Vibrio, distinguishing it from other enteric pathogens.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The phenomenon of transfer of naked DNA from one bacteria to another is called
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Transformation involves the uptake of naked DNA from the environment by competent bacteria. This process was first demonstrated by Frederick Griffith with Streptococcus pneumoniae. It is a crucial mechanism for horizontal gene transfer in bacteria.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The fertility factor (F factor) is associated with
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The F factor is involved in conjugation, a process where genetic material is transferred through direct cell-to-cell contact via sex pili. The F factor allows donor cells (F+) to transfer DNA to recipient cells (F-), promoting genetic exchange and evolution.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a gram-negative bacterium?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Escherichia coli is a Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium. It has a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide (LPS), which is characteristic of Gram-negative bacteria. Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Clostridium tetani are Gram-positive organisms.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The smallest virus is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
04. General Virology and Overview of Viral Infections
mcqs.explanation: Parvoviruses are the smallest viruses known, measuring approximately 18-26 nm in diameter. They have a single-stranded DNA genome and lack an envelope. The human parvovirus B19 causes fifth disease (erythema infectiosum) in children.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The largest virus is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
04. General Virology and Overview of Viral Infections
mcqs.explanation: Poxviruses are the largest viruses, measuring up to 400 nm in diameter. They have complex morphology, a large double-stranded DNA genome, and can be visualized under a light microscope. The smallpox virus (Variola) is a member of this group.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The genetic material of a virus can be
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
04. General Virology and Overview of Viral Infections
mcqs.explanation: Viruses contain either DNA or RNA as their genetic material, but never both. The nucleic acid can be single-stranded or double-stranded, linear or circular, and segmented or non-segmented. This classification is the basis of the Baltimore classification of viruses.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The protein coat of a virus is called
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
04. General Virology and Overview of Viral Infections
mcqs.explanation: The capsid is the protein coat of a virus, protecting the nucleic acid genome and facilitating viral attachment. It is composed of capsomeres, which are repeating protein subunits. The capsid and the nucleic acid together form the nucleocapsid.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The cultivation of viruses can be done in
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
04. General Virology and Overview of Viral Infections
mcqs.explanation: Viruses can be cultivated in cell culture (primary, continuous, or diploid cell lines), embryonated hen's eggs (chorioallantoic membrane, amniotic cavity, allantoic cavity, or yolk sac), and laboratory animals. Cell culture is the most commonly used method for virus isolation and propagation.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The fungal cell wall is composed of
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
06. General Mycology and Overview of Fungal Infections
mcqs.explanation: The fungal cell wall is primarily composed of chitin, a polysaccharide of β(1→4)-linked N-acetylglucosamine. Chitin provides structural integrity to the fungal cell. This is a key difference from bacteria, which have peptidoglycan cell walls.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Dimorphic fungi exist as
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
06. General Mycology and Overview of Fungal Infections
mcqs.explanation: Dimorphic fungi exist as yeast at 37°C (host body temperature) and as mold at 25°C (environmental temperature). This temperature-dependent morphological transition is a key virulence factor for many pathogenic fungi, including Histoplasma capsulatum, Sporothrix schenckii, and Blastomyces dermatitidis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a dimorphic fungus?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
06. General Mycology and Overview of Fungal Infections
mcqs.explanation: Sporothrix schenckii is a dimorphic fungus. It grows as a mold (with conidia) in the environment at 25°C, and as a yeast (with cigar-shaped cells) in tissue at 37°C. It causes sporotrichosis, often acquired through traumatic inoculation of contaminated material.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The asexual spores of fungi are called
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
06. General Mycology and Overview of Fungal Infections
mcqs.explanation: Conidia are asexual spores produced by fungi. They are formed exogenously on specialized hyphae called conidiophores. Conidia are the primary means of fungal reproduction and dissemination in the environment. Zygospores, ascospores, and basidiospores are sexual spores produced by zygomycetes, ascomycetes, and basidiomycetes, respectively.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a fungal infection of the skin?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
06. General Mycology and Overview of Fungal Infections
mcqs.explanation: Tinea versicolor is a superficial fungal infection of the skin caused by Malassezia furfur. It presents as hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules on the trunk. The causative organism is a lipophilic yeast that is part of normal skin flora but can cause infection under favorable conditions.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All of the following are characteristics of a good immunogen EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Immunogens are typically foreign substances, not normally found on host cells. The immune system distinguishes self from non-self, and antigens found on host cells are generally not immunogenic due to immunological tolerance. A good immunogen must be foreign, have high molecular weight, exhibit structural complexity, and possess sufficient epitopes.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: To eradicate measles, the % of infant to be vaccinated:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
56. Viral Exanthems and Cutaneous Infections: Herpes, Pox, Parvovirus, Measles, Rubella, Coxsackie
mcqs.explanation:
(d) (95%) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p467-470, PSM Park 23/e p147, 22/e p141
• To eradicate measles, 96% of infant to be vaccinated.
• Epidemic of measles occurs if proportion of susceptible children > 40%.
• If measles is introduced in a virgin community, it infects > 90% of children.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Lens antigens of the eye are
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Lens antigens are sequestered from the immune system during embryonic development, preventing immune tolerance. These sequestered antigens are hidden in immunologically privileged sites and are not normally recognized as self, potentially leading to autoimmune reactions if released.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Super antigens are produced by which of the following.
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Superantigens are produced by bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes. These proteins stimulate a massive, non-specific T cell activation by binding to both MHC class II and T cell receptors. This leads to a cytokine storm and severe symptoms.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The example of a serological test based on heterophile antigen is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The Paul-Bunnell test is used to detect heterophile antibodies in infectious mononucleosis (caused by Epstein-Barr virus). Heterophile antibodies are antibodies that react with antigens from a different species (e.g., sheep RBCs). The test is based on the principle that these antibodies agglutinate sheep red blood cells, which is specific to EBV infection.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: IgG is the only immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta, providing passive immunity to the fetus and newborn. This transfer occurs via neonatal Fc receptors (FcRn) on syncytiotrophoblasts, allowing IgG to be transported from maternal to fetal circulation.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The immunoglobulin present in secretions is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: IgA is the predominant immunoglobulin in secretions such as saliva, tears, colostrum, breast milk, and mucosal surfaces of the gastrointestinal, respiratory, and genitourinary tracts. Secretory IgA exists as a dimer with a J chain and secretory component, providing protection against mucosal pathogens.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Smallest unit of antigenicity is known as
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: An epitope (antigenic determinant) is the smallest unit of antigenicity, the part of an antigen that is recognized by the immune system. The epitope is the specific region of the antigen that binds to the antibody's paratope or T cell receptor.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The secondary immune response is characterized by
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The secondary immune response is characterized by the production of IgG antibodies. Due to the presence of memory B cells, the secondary response is faster, more robust, and produces higher affinity antibodies than the primary response. This forms the basis of immunological memory and vaccine efficacy.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The antigen-binding site of an antibody is located on
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The antigen-binding site is located on the Fab (Fragment antigen binding) fragment of the antibody. The Fab fragment consists of the variable regions (VH and VL) and the first constant domains (CH1 and CL). The paratope, the specific site that binds the epitope, is formed by the hypervariable regions (CDRs) within the VH and VL domains.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The hypersensitivity reaction mediated by IgE is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Type I hypersensitivity is mediated by IgE antibodies. Mast cells and basophils coated with IgE release histamine and other mediators upon antigen cross-linking. This leads to immediate allergic reactions such as anaphylaxis, asthma, and hay fever.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The tuberculin test is an example of
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The tuberculin test (Mantoux test) is a delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV) reaction. It involves T cells rather than antibodies. Upon intradermal injection of tuberculin, sensitized T cells release cytokines, leading to induration and erythema after 48-72 hours. This test is used to detect exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most abundant immunoglobulin?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: IgG is the most abundant immunoglobulin in serum, constituting approximately 70-80% of total serum immunoglobulins. It plays a crucial role in opsonization, complement activation, and passive immunity. IgG is also the only antibody capable of crossing the placenta, providing fetal immunity.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Number of proteins in the complement system is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The complement system is traditionally described as consisting of nine main proteins (C1 to C9). However, the complement system actually includes approximately 30 proteins, including regulatory proteins. The cascade involves the classical, alternative, and lectin pathways converging at C3 to form membrane attack complex (MAC).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The classical complement pathway is activated by
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The classical complement pathway is primarily activated by antigen-antibody complexes. C1q binds to the Fc portion of IgG or IgM antibodies, triggering the cascade. This pathway is antibody-dependent and forms an important link between humoral immunity and the complement system.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: C1 inhibitor deficiency can cause
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Deficiency of C1 inhibitor leads to hereditary angioneurotic oedema (HAE). This condition is characterized by recurrent episodes of edema in the skin, gastrointestinal tract, and airways due to uncontrolled activation of the complement and contact systems. C1 inhibitor normally prevents excessive complement activation.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All of the following immunological effects are mediated by complements EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Type I hypersensitivity reactions are mediated by IgE antibodies and mast cell degranulation, and do not involve the complement system. Complement is involved in opsonization (phagocytosis), inflammation, and agglutination, but is not part of the IgE-mediated allergic response.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Hereditary angioneurotic oedema is caused by
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Hereditary angioneurotic oedema is caused by a deficiency of C1 inhibitor, which normally regulates the complement and contact systems. Without C1 inhibitor, excessive C1 activation leads to increased vascular permeability and edema. This condition is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: CD4 cells recognize antigen in association with
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: CD4 cells (helper T cells) recognize antigens presented by MHC class II molecules on the surface of antigen-presenting cells (APCs). This interaction is crucial for T cell activation and the initiation of both humoral and cell-mediated immune responses.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a major site for lymphocyte proliferation in the body?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Lymph nodes are a major site for lymphocyte proliferation and activation in the body. They filter lymph and provide a microenvironment where antigen-presenting cells and lymphocytes interact, initiating specific immune responses. Secondary lymphoid organs like lymph nodes support adaptive immune responses.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Interleukin-1 is produced by
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
15. Immune Responses: Cell Mediated and Antibody Mediated
mcqs.explanation: Interleukin-1 (IL-1) is primarily produced by activated macrophages. It is a pro-inflammatory cytokine that plays a central role in the inflammatory response, acting as a pyrogen (fever-inducer) and co-stimulator for T cell activation. IL-1 is also produced by other cells, including monocytes and dendritic cells.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Negative phase is observed in
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
15. Immune Responses: Cell Mediated and Antibody Mediated
mcqs.explanation: The negative phase is a temporary decrease in antibody levels following antigen exposure, observed in the primary humoral response. This occurs because circulating antibodies bind to the newly introduced antigen, depleting the free antibody pool before the secondary response begins.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Most widely accepted theory of antibody production is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
15. Immune Responses: Cell Mediated and Antibody Mediated
mcqs.explanation: The clonal selection theory is the most widely accepted explanation for antibody production. It states that each B cell produces a specific antibody and proliferates upon encountering its specific antigen. This theory explains immunological memory, tolerance, and the specificity of the immune response.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: CMI participates in
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
15. Immune Responses: Cell Mediated and Antibody Mediated
mcqs.explanation: Cell-mediated immunity (CMI) participates in allograft rejection, graft-versus-host reaction, and delayed hypersensitivity. CMI is mediated by T lymphocytes and macrophages and is crucial for defense against intracellular pathogens, tumor cells, and transplant rejection.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Most widely accepted theory of antibody production is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
15. Immune Responses: Cell Mediated and Antibody Mediated
mcqs.explanation: The clonal selection theory explains how specific antibodies are produced by the proliferation of B cells upon encountering their specific antigen. This theory is the foundation of modern immunology and explains the specificity and diversity of the immune response.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Most widely accepted theory of antibody production is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
15. Immune Responses: Cell Mediated and Antibody Mediated
mcqs.explanation: The clonal selection theory describes the process of specific antibody production, where B cells bearing specific receptors proliferate upon antigen recognition, generating clones of antibody-secreting cells. This theory is the basis for understanding the immune system's ability to respond to a vast array of antigens.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Toxoids are
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
15. Immune Responses: Cell Mediated and Antibody Mediated
mcqs.explanation: Toxoids are modified toxins that are antigenic but no longer toxic. They are produced by treating toxins with heat or formaldehyde to inactivate their toxic properties while retaining immunogenicity. Toxoids are used in vaccines to induce immunity against diphtheria and tetanus.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Cell mediated immunity does not play a role in
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
15. Immune Responses: Cell Mediated and Antibody Mediated
mcqs.explanation: Anaphylaxis is a Type I hypersensitivity reaction mediated by IgE and mast cell degranulation, which involves humoral immunity rather than cell-mediated immunity. CMI is involved in contact dermatitis, graft rejection, and tumor immunity, which are primarily T cell-mediated responses.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Anaphylaxis is hypersensitivity of type
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Anaphylaxis is a severe, immediate allergic reaction classified as type I hypersensitivity. It is mediated by IgE antibodies that trigger mast cells and basophils to release histamine and other mediators, causing vasodilation, bronchoconstriction, and cardiovascular collapse.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Tuberculin test is an example of the following type of hypersensitivity reaction.
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The tuberculin test is an example of a type IV hypersensitivity reaction, which is a delayed-type hypersensitivity. It involves T cell-mediated immune responses, rather than antibody-mediated reactions, and takes 48-72 hours to develop.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Type I hypersensitivity reaction is mediated by
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: IgE antibodies mediate anaphylactic reactions by triggering mast cells and basophils to release histamine and other inflammatory mediators. IgE binds to high-affinity FcεRI receptors on mast cells, causing degranulation upon subsequent antigen exposure.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Type I hypersensitivity reaction is mediated by
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Type I hypersensitivity reactions are mediated by IgE antibodies. Mast cells and basophils release histamine and other mediators after antigen cross-links bound IgE, leading to immediate allergic reactions.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Contact dermatitis is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Contact dermatitis is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction (delayed-type hypersensitivity). It is caused by T cell-mediated immune response to chemicals, haptens, or contact allergens. The reaction typically develops 24-72 hours after exposure and is characterized by erythema, edema, and vesicle formation.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: In a splenectomized patient there is increase of infection by all the organisms except:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation:
25. An s. (d) (Staph. aureus) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p235, 170, Ananthanarayan 9/e p18, 200
• Capsulated organism can resist killing by preventing phagocytosis.
• Spleen has an important role in removing these capsulated organisms where opsonization takes place.
• Certain complements (opsonins) can attach to these organisms and once delivered to spleen, their uptake is facilitated
by complement receptors like CR1, 2. etc. present on splenic phagocyte surface (Process known as Opsonization).
• Hence, in a splenectomized patient there is increase risk of infection by capsulated organisms.
• Among the options, all are capsulated except S. aureus.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: In Myasthenia gravis, auto antibodies are produced against
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: In Myasthenia gravis, autoantibodies target and block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, impairing muscle contraction. This leads to muscle weakness and fatigability, which improves with anticholinesterase drugs like edrophonium or neostigmine.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The diagnosis of Myasthenic crisis is done by using
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Edrophonium, a short-acting acetylcholine esterase inhibitor, is used in the Tensilon test to diagnose myasthenia gravis. It temporarily improves muscle strength by increasing acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, differentiating myasthenic crisis from cholinergic crisis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a systemic autoimmune disease?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is a systemic autoimmune disease that affects multiple organ systems, including the skin, kidneys, joints, and CNS. It is characterized by the production of autoantibodies against nuclear antigens (ANA, anti-dsDNA), leading to immune complex deposition and tissue injury.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Lymphogranuloma venereum is treated by
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Lymphogranuloma venereum, caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis (serotypes L1-L3), is treated with antibiotics such as sulphonamides, tetracyclines, and macrolides. C. trachomatis is an obligate intracellular pathogen, requiring antibiotics that can penetrate cells.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: DiGeorge syndrome is primarily due to
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome is primarily due to a T cell defect resulting from a deletion on chromosome 22q11.2. The thymus is hypoplastic, impairing T cell maturation. B cells are present but function may be affected due to the absence of T cell help. This leads to increased susceptibility to viral, fungal, and intracellular bacterial infections.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: C1 inhibitor deficiency can cause
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: C1 inhibitor deficiency leads to hereditary angioedema, a condition characterized by recurrent episodes of swelling in various parts of the body, particularly the face, throat, and abdomen. This condition results from uncontrolled complement activation, leading to increased vascular permeability.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Grafts between identical twins is an example of
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: A graft between genetically identical individuals, such as identical twins, is called an isograft or syngeneic graft. Isografts are the only grafts that are not rejected because the donor and recipient have identical MHC molecules, preventing immune recognition.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The major cause of transfusion associated hepatitis is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a major cause of transfusion-associated hepatitis. Despite screening, there remains a risk of transmission through blood transfusion, particularly in areas with high HBV prevalence. This has led to the implementation of universal screening protocols and nucleic acid testing.

options.text: A graft from an identical twin.
A graft from another area of the same individual's body.
A graft from one of same species.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An allograft implies
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: An allograft is a transplant of tissue from one individual to another of the same species but with a different genotype. Allografts require immunosuppression to prevent rejection because the recipient's immune system recognizes the donor tissue as foreign.

options.text: Testing all samples for anti-HIV antibodies.
Use of protective barriers by health care workers.
Testing all samples for anti-HIV antibodies; HBsAg & anti-HCV antibodies.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Universal precautions means
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Universal precautions involve using protective barriers (like gloves, masks, and gowns) to prevent the spread of infections. This applies to all patients regardless of their infection status, recognizing that many infectious diseases are asymptomatic.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: HLA typing and cross matching is required in which type of Grafts?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: HLA typing and cross-matching are crucial for allografts to ensure compatibility and reduce the risk of graft rejection. HLA molecules (MHC) must be matched as closely as possible to prevent T cell-mediated rejection. This is particularly important in kidney, heart, and bone marrow transplants.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Graft versus host reaction is mediated by
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) is mediated by donor T cells attacking the recipient's tissues. This occurs when immunocompetent cells in the graft recognize the recipient's tissues as foreign. GVHD is a major complication of bone marrow transplants.

mcqs.question: Lymphogranuloma venereum is treated by
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Lymphogranuloma venereum, caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis (serotypes L1-L3), is treated with antibiotics such as sulphonamides, tetracyclines, and macrolides. C. trachomatis is an obligate intracellular pathogen, requiring antibiotics that can penetrate cells.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Allograft is taken from
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: An allograft is a graft taken from a genetically unrelated member of the same species. Allografts have different MHC molecules, triggering an immune response that can lead to rejection without immunosuppression. This is the most common type of transplant in clinical practice.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Legionella pneumophila spreads by:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases

mcqs.explanation:

• Aspiration is now known to be the predominant mode of transmission
• Aerosolization of Legionella by devices filled with tap water, including whirlpools, nebulizers, and humidifiers, cooling
tower, air-conditioners, has been implicated.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A graft taken from an individual and placed on another individual of the same genetic Constitution is called
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: An isograft (or syngeneic graft) is taken from an individual and placed on another individual with the same genetic makeup, such as identical twins. Isografts are not rejected because the donor and recipient are genetically identical, eliminating the immune barrier.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Grafts between two genetically non identical members of same species are called
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Grafts between two genetically non-identical members of the same species are called allografts. Allografts are the most common type of transplant and require careful HLA matching and immunosuppressive therapy to prevent rejection.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: In renal transplant recipients which is likely organism causing reactivation disease within 4 months after surgery (PG Entrance 2020)
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a common cause of reactivation disease in renal transplant recipients, especially within the first few months after surgery. Immunosuppression increases the risk of CMV reactivation, which can cause pneumonitis, hepatitis, and colitis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a live attenuated vaccine?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin) is a live attenuated vaccine derived from Mycobacterium bovis. It is used for the prevention of tuberculosis, particularly in children. The attenuated strain retains immunogenicity but loses virulence, making it safe for immunization.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The first vaccine developed was for
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The first vaccine developed was for smallpox by Edward Jenner in 1796. Jenner observed that milkmaids who contracted cowpox did not develop smallpox. He used cowpox material (Vaccinia) to immunize against smallpox (Variola), marking the beginning of modern immunology and vaccination.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The polio vaccine developed by Jonas Salk is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The Salk vaccine is an inactivated (killed) polio vaccine (IPV). It contains inactivated poliovirus strains of all three serotypes. IPV is administered intramuscularly and induces humoral immunity, protecting against paralysis, but does not induce mucosal immunity like the oral vaccine.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The polio vaccine developed by Albert Sabin is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The Sabin vaccine is a live attenuated polio vaccine (OPV). It contains attenuated poliovirus strains that replicate in the gut, inducing both humoral and mucosal immunity. OPV is administered orally and induces intestinal IgA, preventing viral shedding and transmission.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The tetanus vaccine is an example of
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Tetanus vaccine is a toxoid vaccine. It contains inactivated tetanus toxin (toxoid) that retains immunogenicity but is non-toxic. The vaccine induces neutralizing antibodies that protect against tetanus toxin, which is produced by Clostridium tetani. Toxoid vaccines are also used for diphtheria.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The most common hospital-acquired infection is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are the most common type of hospital-acquired infection, accounting for approximately 30-40% of all nosocomial infections. They are primarily associated with indwelling urinary catheter use, making them preventable through proper catheter care and aseptic technique.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The most common hospital acquired infection is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are the most common type of hospital-acquired infection, often associated with catheter use. Catheter-associated UTIs are a significant cause of morbidity and healthcare costs, emphasizing the importance of infection control measures.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The synonym for hospital-acquired infection is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Hospital-acquired infections are also called nosocomial infections. The term "nosocomial" comes from the Greek words "nosos" (disease) and "komeion" (to care for). These infections develop 48 hours after hospital admission or within 3 days of discharge. They can be caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites and are often associated with medical procedures or antibiotic use.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Universal precautions include
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Universal precautions include the use of gloves, hand washing, and use of masks, gowns, and protective eyewear when exposure to blood or body fluids is anticipated. These precautions apply to all patients, regardless of their infection status, to prevent the transmission of bloodborne pathogens like HIV, HBV, and HCV.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Best criteria for tuberculosis diagnosis by WHO:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation:
(a) (Sputum...) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p276, Park 23/e p182, 22/e p170
• Sputum examination of symptomatic patients by Zn stain: It is case finding tool for tuberculosis under RNTCP.
[UPDATE 2026] RNTCP was renamed the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP) in January 2020, with the goal of eliminating TB in India by 2025. Under NTEP, upfront nucleic acid amplification testing (CBNAAT/GeneXpert, or the Indian Truenat) has largely replaced sputum smear microscopy as the initial diagnostic test.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The most important measure to prevent hospital-acquired infections is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Hand hygiene is the single most important measure to prevent hospital-acquired infections. Regular hand washing with soap and water or using alcohol-based hand rubs significantly reduces the transmission of pathogens from healthcare workers to patients and between patients. Hand hygiene is the cornerstone of infection control practices in healthcare settings.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The most effective method of sterilization is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Autoclaving is the most effective method of sterilization. It uses moist heat at 121°C and 15 psi pressure for 15-20 minutes to kill all microorganisms, including endospores. Moist heat is more effective than dry heat because it penetrates cells more readily and denatures proteins.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The temperature and pressure used in an autoclave are
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Autoclaving uses 121°C and 15 lbs pressure (1 atm) for 15-20 minutes. This standard condition ensures the complete destruction of all microorganisms, including bacterial endospores. Lower temperatures or shorter times may not achieve sterilization.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The principle of hot air oven sterilization is
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: The hot air oven uses dry heat for sterilization. It operates at 160-180°C for 1-2 hours and is used for heat-stable materials like glassware and metal instruments. Dry heat is less effective than moist heat because it kills microorganisms through oxidation and protein denaturation, requiring higher temperatures and longer times.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a chemical sterilizing agent?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Ethylene oxide, glutaraldehyde, and formaldehyde are all chemical sterilizing agents. Ethylene oxide is a gaseous sterilant used for heat-sensitive items. Glutaraldehyde and formaldehyde are liquid sterilants used for medical equipment and tissue fixation.

tags: Enteric Fever (Salmonella Typhi and Salmonella Paratyphi)
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Kauffman-White scheme of classification is the basis of serotyping of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
30. Enteric Fever: Salmonella Typhi and Paratyphi
mcqs.explanation: The Kauffman-White classification is used for the serotyping of Salmonella species based on their surface antigens (O and H antigens). This scheme categorizes Salmonella into over 2,500 serotypes, which is essential for epidemiological tracking and outbreak investigations.

tags: Enteric Fever (Salmonella Typhi and Salmonella Paratyphi)
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Wilson and Blair medium is selective for
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
30. Enteric Fever: Salmonella Typhi and Paratyphi
mcqs.explanation: Wilson and Blair medium (bismuth sulfite agar) is used for the selective isolation of Salmonella species, particularly S. Typhi from clinical specimens. S. Typhi produces black colonies with a metallic sheen due to hydrogen sulfide production, making it a valuable differential medium.

tags: Enteric Fever (Salmonella Typhi and Salmonella Paratyphi)
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: In partially treated cases of enteric fever, the most appropriate sample for isolation of salmonellae is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
30. Enteric Fever: Salmonella Typhi and Paratyphi
mcqs.explanation: Bone marrow culture is considered the most reliable sample for isolating Salmonella in partially treated cases of enteric fever. Bone marrow cultures remain positive even after antibiotic therapy has been initiated and have a higher sensitivity than blood cultures, particularly in patients who have already received antibiotics.

tags: Enteric Fever (Salmonella Typhi and Salmonella Paratyphi)
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following serotypes of Salmonella is/are anaerogenic?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
30. Enteric Fever: Salmonella Typhi and Paratyphi
mcqs.explanation: S. typhi is anaerogenic, meaning it does not produce gas from carbohydrates. This is a key biochemical characteristic used to differentiate S. typhi from other salmonellae. Unlike S. typhi, S. paratyphi A and B produce gas during sugar fermentation.

tags: Enteric Fever (Salmonella Typhi and Salmonella Paratyphi)
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Example of anaerobic bacteria is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
30. Enteric Fever: Salmonella Typhi and Paratyphi
mcqs.explanation: Salmonella typhi is an anaerogenic bacterium (note: "anaerobic" here refers to gas production, not oxygen requirement). In bacteriology, "anaerogenic" specifically means not producing gas during carbohydrate fermentation, which is a key distinction in the identification of Salmonella species.

tags: Enteric Fever (Salmonella Typhi and Salmonella Paratyphi)
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Enteric fever is best diagnosed in first week by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
30. Enteric Fever: Salmonella Typhi and Paratyphi
mcqs.explanation: Blood culture is the most effective method for diagnosing enteric fever in the first week of illness. It has the highest sensitivity during the early bacteremic phase and is considered the gold standard for diagnosis. Widal test becomes positive only in the second week of illness.

tags: Enteric Fever (Salmonella Typhi and Salmonella Paratyphi)
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Wilson and Blair medium is an example of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
30. Enteric Fever: Salmonella Typhi and Paratyphi
mcqs.explanation: Wilson and Blair medium (bismuth sulfite agar) is a selective medium used to isolate Salmonella species. It inhibits the growth of other enteric bacteria while allowing Salmonella to grow, producing characteristic black colonies due to hydrogen sulfide production.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The vector for Q fever is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Q fever is transmitted through aerosols rather than arthropod vectors. The primary mode of transmission is inhalation of contaminated dust or aerosols from infected animals (cattle, sheep, goats). Coxiella burnetii, the causative agent, is highly infectious and can survive in the environment for long periods.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Q fever is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii, an obligate intracellular bacterium. It is a zoonotic disease and is unique among rickettsiae because it is transmitted via aerosols, not arthropod vectors. C. burnetii is highly resistant to environmental conditions and can be a bioterrorism agent (Category B).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Vector for scrub typhus is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Scrub typhus is transmitted by mites (chiggers), specifically the larval stage of trombiculid mites (Leptotrombidium species). It is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi and is endemic in the "tsutsugamushi triangle" in Southeast Asia, India, and Australia.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Rickettsia mooseri causing endemic typhus is transmitted by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Rickettsia mooseri (also known as Rickettsia typhi) causes endemic (murine) typhus and is transmitted by the rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis). The reservoir is rats, and humans are accidental hosts. The disease is milder than epidemic typhus and is found worldwide.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Scrub typhus is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Scrub typhus is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi (formerly Rickettsia tsutsugamushi). It is transmitted by trombiculid mites and is endemic in Asia, Australia, and the Pacific islands. It presents with eschar, lymphadenopathy, and maculopapular rash.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Causative microorganism for scrub typhus is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: The causative agent of scrub typhus is Orientia tsutsugamushi (formerly Rickettsia tsutsugamushi). It is distinct from other Rickettsiae in its cell wall structure and genetic makeup, and is transmitted by mites (chiggers). The disease is characterized by eschar formation, lymphadenopathy, and fever.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Causative organism of cat scratch disease is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Cat scratch disease is caused by Bartonella henselae, a fastidious, Gram-negative bacillus. It is transmitted through cat scratches or bites, especially from kittens. The disease is characterized by regional lymphadenopathy, fever, and a papule at the inoculation site.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Heterophile antibody detection in Typhus fever is carried out using antigen derived from
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: The Weil-Felix test uses Proteus species antigens (OX19, OX2, OXK) to detect heterophile antibodies in typhus fever. This is due to cross-reacting antigens shared between Rickettsia and Proteus. Although the test is nonspecific and has low sensitivity, it remains a useful diagnostic tool in resource-limited settings.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Epidemic typhus is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Epidemic typhus is caused by Rickettsia prowazekii. It is transmitted by the human body louse and is a severe, potentially fatal disease characterized by high fever, headache, and a maculopapular rash (sparing the face, palms, and soles). Brill-Zinsser disease is a recrudescent form.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The vector transmitting Epidemic typhus is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: The human body louse transmits epidemic typhus. Unlike many other vector-borne diseases, the louse becomes infected with R. prowazekii and transmits it through its feces, which are scratched into the skin. The louse dies shortly after infection, making the disease highly dependent on human-to-human transmission.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Causative agent of 'Weil's Disease' is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Weil's disease is caused by Leptospira species, particularly Leptospira interrogans serovar icterohaemorrhagiae. Weil's disease is the severe, icteric form of leptospirosis characterized by jaundice, renal failure, and hemorrhage. It is transmitted through contact with water contaminated with the urine of infected animals (especially rats).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Weil's disease is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Leptospira interrogans serovar icterohaemorrhagiae causes Weil's disease. This is the severe, icteric form of leptospirosis characterized by jaundice, renal failure, and hemorrhage. It is transmitted through contact with water contaminated with the urine of infected rats.

options.text: For demonstrating leptospires in blood, the sample should be collected in the first week of the illness.
Serological tests are mandatory for clinical management.
It is necessary to demonstrate the organism in the urine of rats.
A negative culture rules out the disease.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about laboratory diagnosis of leptospirosis is true?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: To demonstrate leptospires in the blood, samples should be collected during the first week of illness, when the organism is present in the bloodstream. After the first week, leptospires are cleared from the blood and can be found in the urine. Culture is difficult and slow, making serological tests essential for diagnosis.

options.text: Contains solid and liquid media in one bottle
Reduces risk of infection to laboratory personnel

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Castaneda's method of blood culture is advantageous because it
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Castaneda's method contains solid and liquid media in one bottle, reduces chances of contamination, and reduces the risk of infection to lab personnel. It is a biphasic culture system used for the isolation of Brucella and Leptospira species, allowing for both liquid and solid phase growth in a single container.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Undulant fever is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Brucella melitensis is known to cause undulant fever. Brucellosis is a zoonotic disease transmitted from animals (sheep, goats, cattle) to humans through ingestion of unpasteurized milk or direct contact with infected animals. The fever is characterized by a rising and falling pattern (undulating fever).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following zoonotic diseases has no arthropod vector?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Brucellosis is transmitted through direct contact with infected animals or consumption of contaminated animal products and does not involve an arthropod vector. It is a zoonotic disease caused by Brucella species and is transmitted through ingestion, inhalation, or skin contact.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Diagnosis of Brucellosis in animals is done using which of the following tests?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: The Milk ring test is commonly used for the detection of Brucellosis in cattle. It is a serological test that detects antibodies in milk. A positive test indicates the presence of Brucella antibodies, which helps in screening for brucellosis in dairy herds.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The nonsporing anaerobe associated with Vincent's angina is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Fusobacterium fusiforme is associated with Vincent's angina, a necrotizing ulcerative gingivostomatitis. The infection is a synergistic bacterial infection involving Borrelia vincentii and Fusobacterium fusiforme (fusospirochetal infection). It is also known as trench mouth and is common in immunocompromised individuals or those with poor oral hygiene.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All of the following statements about Genus Brucella are true EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Brucella species are not strict parasites of humans; they can infect various animals (cattle, goats, sheep, pigs) and humans are accidental hosts. Brucella is a nonmotile, fastidious, Gram-negative coccobacillus that causes brucellosis (undulant fever). Transmission to humans occurs through ingestion, inhalation, or skin contact.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Relapsing fever is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Borrelia recurrentis is the causative agent of relapsing fever. It is transmitted by lice (epidemic) or ticks (endemic). The disease is characterized by recurrent episodes of fever due to antigenic variation of the surface proteins, allowing the organism to evade the host immune response.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The organism transmitted via water contamination by the urine of an infected rat to man is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
32. Miscellaneous Bacterial Bloodstream: Brucellosis, Leptospirosis, Borreliosis
mcqs.explanation: Leptospira icterohaemorrhagiae is transmitted through water contaminated with the urine of infected rats. This bacterium is the causative agent of leptospirosis (Weil's disease), which is characterized by jaundice, renal failure, and hemorrhage. Outbreaks are common after flooding.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Universal safety precautions should be followed while treating
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Universal precautions are guidelines to prevent the transmission of diseases and should be applied to all patients to ensure safety for both patients and healthcare workers. Universal precautions are based on the principle that all blood and body fluids should be treated as potentially infectious, regardless of the patient's known or suspected infection status.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The number of which cells decrease drastically in AIDS?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: In AIDS, the number of CD4 cells (T-helper cells) decreases significantly, compromising the immune system. HIV selectively infects and destroys CD4+ T lymphocytes through a combination of direct cytopathic effects and apoptosis, leading to progressive immunodeficiency.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Obligate intracellular organism is:
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation:
(b) (Chlamydia) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p92
Refer chapter review

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Reverse transcriptase enzyme is involved in the replication process of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Retroviruses, including HIV, use the enzyme reverse transcriptase to replicate their RNA genome into DNA. This enzyme is encoded by the viral genome and is essential for the viral life cycle, allowing the virus to integrate into the host genome and establish a persistent infection. The enzyme is a target for antiretroviral therapy (e.g., nucleoside and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: HIV testing is mandatory in following situation
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: HIV testing is mandatory for blood donations to prevent transmission through transfusion. This is a critical public health measure to ensure the safety of the blood supply and prevent transfusion-related HIV transmission. Donor screening is mandatory under the National Blood Policy.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The commonly used screening test for HIV infection is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: The ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay) test is widely used as a screening test for HIV infection due to its high sensitivity. ELISA detects HIV-specific antibodies (and now also p24 antigen in fourth-generation tests) and is used as the initial screening test for HIV infection. Positive ELISA results must be confirmed by a Western Blot or other confirmatory test.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The vector for chikungunya virus is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: The Aedes mosquito, particularly Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, is the primary vector for the chikungunya virus. These mosquitoes also transmit dengue and Zika viruses, making them significant public health threats. Chikungunya is characterized by severe joint pain that can persist for months.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The arboviral infection that does not exist in India is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Yellow fever is an arboviral infection that is not present in India. Yellow fever is endemic in tropical areas of South America and Africa, where it is transmitted by Aedes and Haemagogus mosquitoes. Travelers to endemic areas require vaccination. India currently requires proof of yellow fever vaccination for travelers arriving from endemic countries.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: "Doubled up due to severe joint pain" is a classical clinical picture due to
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Severe joint pain causing patients to be "doubled up" is a characteristic symptom of chikungunya. The word "chikungunya" itself means "that which bends up" in the Makonde language of Tanzania, referring to the stooped posture of sufferers due to incapacitating joint pain. This symptom can persist for weeks to months.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The term "Break bone fever" was coined for infection of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Dengue fever is often referred to as 'break bone fever' due to the severe pain it causes in muscles and joints. The intense myalgia and arthralgia associated with dengue fever mimic the pain of broken bones, hence the term. This symptom is a hallmark of the disease.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: For infection of mosquito, the blood of human carrier must contain at least
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: The blood of a human carrier must contain at least 10 gametocytes per microliter for effective transmission to a mosquito. The threshold for infectivity of gametocytes is approximately 10-20 per µL. Gametocytes are the sexual stage of the parasite responsible for transmission to mosquitoes, and their density determines the efficiency of transmission.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: For malarial parasite man is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: In the life cycle of the malarial parasite, humans are the intermediate host where asexual reproduction (schizogony) occurs, while the mosquito is the definitive host where sexual reproduction (sporogony) takes place. Humans become the intermediate host because they harbor the asexual stages of the parasite.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Maurer's dots in red blood cells are seen in infection with
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Maurer's dots (clefts) are seen in red blood cells infected with Plasmodium falciparum. These are distinctive morphological features, appearing as cytoplasmic clefts or dots in the infected erythrocytes, distinguishing P. falciparum from other species. They are particularly visible in thin blood smears.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is seen in Plasmodium falciparum infection in man?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Plasmodium falciparum can cause cerebral malaria, blackwater fever, and severe anaemia. P. falciparum is the most severe form of malaria, causing a wide range of complications including severe anemia, cerebral malaria, acidosis, and multi-organ failure. Blackwater fever is a complication characterized by massive hemolysis and hemoglobinuria.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All of the following is 'TRUE' about P. falciparum infection EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Plasmodium falciparum does not have the longest incubation period among malarial parasites; this is characteristic of Plasmodium malariae (incubation period up to 40 days). P. falciparum has an incubation period of 7-14 days. P. falciparum is characterized by accolé forms, Maurer's dots, high parasitemia, and does not cause relapses (only recrudescence) because it lacks a dormant liver stage (hypnozoites).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Crescent-shaped gametocytes are found in
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Plasmodium falciparum produces crescent-shaped (banana-shaped) gametocytes. These are the sexual stage of the parasite, responsible for transmission to mosquitoes. P. falciparum gametocytes are distinctive and help in differentiating it from other Plasmodium species.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Recrudescence in malaria is seen with which malarial parasite?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Recrudescence, the recurrence of symptoms from persistent bloodstream parasites, is commonly associated with Plasmodium falciparum. This occurs when low numbers of parasites persist in the blood and multiply. It differs from relapse, which is due to reactivation of dormant liver-stage parasites (hypnozoites) in P. vivax and P. ovale.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Rotavirus is a common cause of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Rotavirus is a common cause of severe gastroenteritis, especially in young children. It is the leading cause of severe diarrhea in children worldwide.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Relapse in vivax malaria is due to
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Relapse in vivax malaria is due to the activation of dormant liver stage forms called hypnozoites. These are dormant forms of P. vivax (and P. ovale) that remain in the liver for weeks to years before reactivating. They are resistant to standard antimalarial treatment like chloroquine but are susceptible to primaquine.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Definitive host in Malaria infection is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: The definitive host, where sexual reproduction of the malarial parasite occurs, is the mosquito. In the mosquito, the sexual cycle (sporogony) takes place, producing sporozoites that are transmitted to humans during a blood meal. Humans are the intermediate host where asexual reproduction occurs.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The infective form of the malaria parasite transmitted by mosquito is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Sporozoites are the infective form of the malaria parasite that is transmitted to humans by mosquito bites. When an infected female Anopheles mosquito bites a human, it injects sporozoites along with its saliva into the bloodstream. The sporozoites then travel to the liver and infect hepatocytes.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The form of Plasmodium falciparum NOT seen in peripheral blood smear of patients is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Schizonts of Plasmodium falciparum are typically not seen in peripheral blood smears because they are sequestered in the tissues. P. falciparum schizonts sequester in deep vascular beds (e.g., brain, placenta) due to cytoadherence to endothelial receptors, making them absent from the peripheral circulation. This is a key difference from other Plasmodium species where schizonts are seen in peripheral blood.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Relapse of malaria is not seen in infection with
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Relapses are not seen with Plasmodium falciparum, which does not have a dormant liver stage (hypnozoites). While P. falciparum can cause recrudescence due to persistent blood-stage parasites, it does not cause true relapse. P. vivax and P. ovale have hypnozoites and cause relapse, while P. malariae causes recrudescence (not relapse) due to low levels of persistent blood-stage parasites.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Sandfly is the vector for
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Sandfly is the vector for Leishmaniasis. The female phlebotomine sandfly transmits the parasite (Leishmania species) during blood meals. Leishmaniasis includes visceral (Kala-azar), cutaneous, and mucocutaneous forms, depending on the species.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The vector for Kala-azar is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Kala-azar is transmitted by the bite of infected female sandflies of the genus Phlebotomus (in the Old World) or Lutzomyia (in the New World). The sandfly injects promastigotes into the host, which are phagocytosed and transform into amastigotes within macrophages, causing the disease.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Candida albicans is differentiated from other candida species by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Candida albicans can be differentiated from other Candida species by the germ tube test, chlamydospore formation, and sugar assimilation tests. The germ tube test is a rapid method where C. albicans forms germ tubes when incubated in serum at 37°C for 2-3 hours. Chlamydospore formation on corn meal agar is also characteristic of C. albicans. Sugar assimilation patterns further differentiate C. albicans from other Candida species (e.g., C. tropicalis, C. krusei, C. glabrata).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Leishman-Donovan bodies are seen in
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Leishman-Donovan bodies (amastigotes) are seen in Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis). These are the intracellular, nonflagellated forms of Leishmania donovani found within macrophages and other mononuclear cells. They appear as small oval bodies with a nucleus and kinetoplast.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following biopsy may lead to diagnosis of Wuchereria bancrofti infection?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Wuchereria bancrofti resides in the lymphatic system, and a lymph node biopsy can help diagnose the infection. Adults live in the lymphatic vessels, and their presence can lead to chronic lymphatic obstruction and elephantiasis. Biopsy may reveal adult worms and the surrounding inflammatory reaction.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: True about Rhinosporidium Seebri:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation:
(d) (Present in coastal India) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p562
• Rhinosporidium seeberi was thought to be a fungus but based on molecular studies it is now considered to be a
hydrophilic protistian parasite, hence called as pseudofungal organism.
• R.seeberi cannot be cultured in cell-free artificial media.
• Infection is acquired by coming in contact with fresh or stagnant water and hence it is believed as hydrophilic organism.
• Common in India (Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Andhra Pradesh) and Sri Lanka.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Tail tip contains two nuclei in microfilariae of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Microfilariae of Brugia malayi have two nuclei in the tail tip, distinguishing them from Wuchereria bancrofti, which has no nuclei in the tail tip. The presence of nuclear staining in the tail tip is a key morphological feature used in species identification of microfilariae.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Blindness caused by a parasite transmitted to humans by the black fly is the clinical manifestation of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Onchocerciasis, also known as river blindness, is caused by Onchocerca volvulus and is transmitted by the black fly (Simulium species). The microfilariae migrate to the skin and eyes, causing severe itching and progressive visual impairment, including blindness. The disease is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa, Yemen, and parts of Central and South America.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The filarial worm that can be seen in conjunctiva is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Loa loa, also known as the African eye worm, can be seen migrating across the conjunctiva. It is transmitted by deer flies (Chrysops) and causes loiasis. Patients may experience Calabar swellings (localized angioedema) as the adult worms migrate through subcutaneous tissues.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A sheathed microfilaria is a characteristic of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Microfilariae of Brugia malayi are sheathed, distinguishing them from other filarial worms like Onchocerca volvulus. Sheathed microfilariae have a transparent membrane covering the body, which can be identified in blood smears. The sheath is a key morphological characteristic used in species identification.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following worms reside/s in subcutaneous tissue?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Loa loa, Onchocerca volvulus, and Dracunculus medinensis all reside in subcutaneous tissue. These are tissue nematodes that cause subcutaneous infections. Loa loa causes loiasis, O. volvulus causes onchocerciasis, and D. medinensis causes dracunculiasis (guinea worm disease).
