Blood eosinophil count is more than 300/cmm

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All of the findings below hold true for Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia EXCEPT that
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: In Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia, microfilariae are usually not seen in peripheral blood smears, as the condition is characterized by high eosinophil counts and a response to DEC (Diethylcarbamazine). TPE is a form of occult filariasis where the microfilariae are trapped in the pulmonary capillaries and do not appear in the peripheral blood.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Germ tube test is used for identification of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: The germ tube test is specifically used for the identification of Candida albicans. A positive germ tube test is indicative of C. albicans (and closely related C. dubliniensis). This test is rapid, simple, and highly specific for C. albicans, making it a valuable tool in the clinical laboratory.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An HIV positive patient with a CD4 count of 300/mm³ presents with mucosal lesions in the mouth as shown in the figure. On microscopy budding yeasts and pseudohyphae are seen. What is the likely diagnosis (PG Entrance 2020)
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Candidiasis, caused by Candida species, often presents as white patches on the mucosal surfaces in immunocompromised patients, such as those with HIV. The presence of budding yeasts and pseudohyphae on microscopy further supports this diagnosis. Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) is a common opportunistic infection in HIV/AIDS patients, especially when CD4 counts drop below 350-400 cells/µL.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Lancefield's classification is used for
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
40. Food Poisoning: Staph, Bacillus, Clostridium botulinum
mcqs.explanation: Lancefield classification categorizes beta haemolytic streptococci based on the carbohydrate composition of bacterial antigens found on their cell walls. This system classifies streptococci into groups A through V.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following staphylococci produce coagulase?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
40. Food Poisoning: Staph, Bacillus, Clostridium botulinum
mcqs.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus produces coagulase, an enzyme that causes blood to clot. This is a key characteristic that distinguishes S. aureus from other staphylococci.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Cell component of Staphylococcus aureus used for co-agglutination test is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
40. Food Poisoning: Staph, Bacillus, Clostridium botulinum
mcqs.explanation: Protein A is a cell wall component of Staphylococcus aureus used in coagglutination tests. Protein A binds to the Fc portion of immunoglobulins, making it useful for detection of bacterial antigens.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following organisms is used to enhance the growth of Hemophilus influenzae on blood agar?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
40. Food Poisoning: Staph, Bacillus, Clostridium botulinum
mcqs.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus produces factors V (NAD) and X (hemin) that enhance the growth of Haemophilus influenzae on blood agar. This phenomenon is called satellitism and is used in the identification of H. influenzae.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Staphylococcus food poisoning usually manifests after hours of ingesting contaminated food
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
40. Food Poisoning: Staph, Bacillus, Clostridium botulinum
mcqs.explanation: Symptoms of staphylococcal food poisoning typically appear within 2-6 hours after consumption of contaminated food. This is due to the ingestion of preformed enterotoxins produced by S. aureus in the food.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Pigment production of staphylococcus species is enhanced on
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
40. Food Poisoning: Staph, Bacillus, Clostridium botulinum
mcqs.explanation: Milk agar enhances pigment production of Staphylococcus species. The presence of milk provides additional nutrients that promote the production of pigments, particularly in S. aureus.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) caused by Cl. Botulinum is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
40. Food Poisoning: Staph, Bacillus, Clostridium botulinum
mcqs.explanation: Foodborne botulism is caused by ingestion of preformed botulinum toxin. This toxin is produced by Clostridium botulinum when it grows in food and is highly toxic, causing flaccid paralysis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following characteristics is a feature of only Staphylococcus aureus?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
40. Food Poisoning: Staph, Bacillus, Clostridium botulinum
mcqs.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase positive, distinguishing it from other staphylococci. Coagulase production is a key characteristic that differentiates S. aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Ludlam's medium is used for isolation of Staph. aureus from
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
40. Food Poisoning: Staph, Bacillus, Clostridium botulinum
mcqs.explanation: Ludlam's medium is selective for isolating Staphylococcus aureus from pus samples. This medium contains antibiotics that inhibit other organisms, allowing S. aureus to grow.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A group of patients having nausea and vomiting within 2-6 hrs after consuming sweet-meats from a common source is most likely caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
40. Food Poisoning: Staph, Bacillus, Clostridium botulinum
mcqs.explanation: Staphylococcus food poisoning manifests quickly, usually within 2-6 hours. This is due to the ingestion of preformed enterotoxins produced by S. aureus in the contaminated food.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The toxin responsible for Toxic shock syndrome is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
40. Food Poisoning: Staph, Bacillus, Clostridium botulinum
mcqs.explanation: Enterotoxin F, also known as toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1), is responsible for toxic shock syndrome. This toxin acts as a superantigen, causing massive T cell activation and cytokine release.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The tube coagulase test detects
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
40. Food Poisoning: Staph, Bacillus, Clostridium botulinum
mcqs.explanation: The tube coagulase test detects free coagulase produced by Staphylococcus aureus. This is in contrast to the slide coagulase test, which detects bound coagulase.

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
40. Food Poisoning: Staph, Bacillus, Clostridium botulinum
mcqs.explanation: Symptoms typically appear within 2-6 hours after ingestion. This is due to the ingestion of preformed enterotoxins produced by S. aureus in the contaminated food.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
41. GI Infections: Enterobacteriaceae, Diarrheagenic E. coli, Shigella, NTS, Yersinia
mcqs.explanation: The Sereny test is used to detect Enteroinvasive Escherichia coli (EIEC). This test evaluates the invasive ability of the organism by instilling it into the guinea pig conjunctiva and observing for keratoconjunctivitis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Verotoxin in Escherichia coli is similar to
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
41. GI Infections: Enterobacteriaceae, Diarrheagenic E. coli, Shigella, NTS, Yersinia
mcqs.explanation: Verotoxin produced by Escherichia coli is similar to Shiga toxin produced by Shigella dysenteriae. Both toxins inhibit protein synthesis and cause hemorrhagic colitis.

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
41. GI Infections: Enterobacteriaceae, Diarrheagenic E. coli, Shigella, NTS, Yersinia
mcqs.explanation: Sorbitol MacConkey agar is used for the selective isolation of E. coli O157. This strain does not ferment sorbitol, unlike other E. coli strains, allowing it to be differentiated on this medium.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Sereny test is used for the detection of which type of diarrheagenic E. coli?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
41. GI Infections: Enterobacteriaceae, Diarrheagenic E. coli, Shigella, NTS, Yersinia
mcqs.explanation: The Sereny test is used to detect Enteroinvasive Escherichia coli (EIEC). This test evaluates the invasive ability of the organism by instilling it into the guinea pig conjunctiva and observing for keratoconjunctivitis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following complications can be associated with Shigella dysenteriae type I infection?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
41. GI Infections: Enterobacteriaceae, Diarrheagenic E. coli, Shigella, NTS, Yersinia
mcqs.explanation: Shigella dysenteriae type I infection can lead to arthritis, toxic neuritis, and hemolytic uremic syndrome. Shiga toxin produced by S. dysenteriae type I causes these complications.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Shigella are classified on the basis of fermentation of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
41. GI Infections: Enterobacteriaceae, Diarrheagenic E. coli, Shigella, NTS, Yersinia
mcqs.explanation: Shigella species are classified based on their ability to ferment mannitol. S. dysenteriae is mannitol-negative, while other species (S. flexneri, S. boydii, S. sonnei) are mannitol-positive.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The following organisms are usually motile EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
41. GI Infections: Enterobacteriaceae, Diarrheagenic E. coli, Shigella, NTS, Yersinia
mcqs.explanation: Shigella species are nonmotile, unlike Salmonella typhi, E. coli, and Proteus species which are motile. This is a key characteristic used in the identification of Shigella.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Psittacosis is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
62. Bacterial Atypical Interstitial Pneumonia: Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella
mcqs.explanation: Psittacosis is caused by Chlamydia psittaci. It is transmitted from birds to humans and causes respiratory infection.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Pus accumulating specifically within a hollow organ or the pleural cavity is given a specific name. What is it called?
mcqs.explanation:
- When pus accumulates in a hollow organ or the pleural cavity specifically, it is termed empyema (e.g. pleural empyema).
- Effusion (A) is a more general term for fluid accumulation in a serous cavity, not specific to purulent/infected collections.
- Transudate (C) refers to a non-inflammatory, protein-poor fluid — the opposite of the purulent exudate implied by pus.
- Granuloma (D) is an unrelated, organized aggregate of activated macrophages, not a fluid collection.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Ziehl-Neelsen staining is used for the demonstration of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Ziehl-Neelsen staining is used to demonstrate acid-fast bacilli, such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis. This staining method uses carbolfuchsin as the primary stain, followed by acid-alcohol decolorization, and then a counterstain.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Fecal pollution of water can be confirmed by the detection of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
41. GI Infections: Enterobacteriaceae, Diarrheagenic E. coli, Shigella, NTS, Yersinia
mcqs.explanation: The detection of thermotolerant E. coli confirms fecal pollution of water. E. coli is used as an indicator organism for fecal contamination because it is a normal inhabitant of the human gut.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which organism has the lowest infective dose?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
41. GI Infections: Enterobacteriaceae, Diarrheagenic E. coli, Shigella, NTS, Yersinia
mcqs.explanation: Shigella has a very low infective dose compared to Salmonella, Vibrio, and Campylobacter. As few as 10-100 organisms can cause infection, making it highly transmissible.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Traveler's diarrhea is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
41. GI Infections: Enterobacteriaceae, Diarrheagenic E. coli, Shigella, NTS, Yersinia
mcqs.explanation: Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) is a common cause of traveler's diarrhea. It produces heat-labile and heat-stable enterotoxins that cause watery diarrhea.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following Shigella does NOT ferment mannitol?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
41. GI Infections: Enterobacteriaceae, Diarrheagenic E. coli, Shigella, NTS, Yersinia
mcqs.explanation: Shigella dysenteriae does not ferment mannitol, unlike other Shigella species. This is a key characteristic used in the identification of S. dysenteriae.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following bacteria can serve as indicator organism for fecal pollution of water?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
41. GI Infections: Enterobacteriaceae, Diarrheagenic E. coli, Shigella, NTS, Yersinia
mcqs.explanation: Escherichia coli is commonly used as an indicator organism for fecal pollution of water. Its presence in water indicates fecal contamination and potential presence of enteric pathogens.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Glanders is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Glanders is caused by Burkholderia mallei. It is a zoonotic disease affecting horses, donkeys, and humans, causing respiratory and cutaneous infections.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The following Vibrio species has been implicated in marine wound infection
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Vibrio vulnificus is associated with marine wound infections. It can cause severe, rapidly progressing wound infections, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Characteristic appearance of stool in cholera is described as
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Cholera stools are characteristically described as rice water stools. They are watery, odorless, and contain mucus flakes, resembling rice water.

mcqs.question: Vibrio cholerae is usually infective when consumed in very high count because they
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Vibrio cholerae needs to be consumed in high numbers to overcome the acidic environment of the stomach and cause infection. The organism is killed by gastric acid, requiring a large inoculum to reach the intestine.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Rice water stool is characteristically caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Vibrio cholerae is the causative agent of cholera, which is characterized by the production of rice water stools. This is a hallmark of the disease.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: In stained films of mucous flakes from acute cholera cases, the arrangement of vibrios is described as
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: The arrangement of vibrios in stained films of mucous flakes from acute cholera cases is described as "fish in stream." This appearance is due to the organism's characteristic morphology and arrangement.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Halophilic vibrios can't grow in media lacking
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Halophilic vibrios require sodium chloride (NaCl) for growth. This is a defining characteristic of the genus Vibrio, as these organisms are halophilic.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT primarily recommended in a given case of cholera?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: While isolation may help prevent the spread of infection, the primary recommendations for cholera are rehydration and examination of stool. Antibiotics may also be used in certain cases.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Kanagawa phenomenon of human RBC's is exhibited by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: The Kanagawa phenomenon, which involves hemolysis of human red blood cells, is exhibited by Vibrio parahaemolyticus. This phenomenon is associated with the organism's pathogenicity.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 19 year old immunocompetent male patient presents with passage of rice water stools, vomiting and shows rapid progressive signs of dehydration. He is MOST likely suffering from
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: The symptoms described are characteristic of cholera. Rice water stools and rapid dehydration are classic features of the disease.

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The most common cause of bacterial meningitis in neonates is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
71. Bacterial Meningitis: Acute Pyogenic and Chronic
mcqs.explanation: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus) is the most common cause of meningitis in neonates. It is transmitted from the mother during childbirth.

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases

mcqs.explanation: Helicobacter pylori colonization is strongly associated with peptic ulcer disease. H. pylori infection is the most common cause of chronic gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
43. Miscellaneous Bacterial GI: Helicobacter, Campylobacter, C. difficile
mcqs.explanation: Pseudomembranous colitis is a severe form of antibiotic-associated diarrhea caused by Clostridium difficile. The organism produces toxins A and B, causing inflammation and pseudomembrane formation.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Antibiotic associated diarrhea is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
43. Miscellaneous Bacterial GI: Helicobacter, Campylobacter, C. difficile
mcqs.explanation: Clostridium difficile is the most common cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhea. It causes a spectrum of diseases ranging from mild diarrhea to pseudomembranous colitis.

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Viral diarrhoea is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Viral diarrhoea can be caused by Calicivirus, Norwalk virus, and Rotavirus. These viruses are all causes of viral gastroenteritis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Antibiotic associated diarrhea is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Antibiotic associated diarrhea is commonly caused by Clostridium difficile. It is the most common cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis.

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
45. Intestinal Protozoan Infections: Amoebiasis, Giardiasis, Coccidian, Balantidiasis

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
45. Intestinal Protozoan Infections: Amoebiasis, Giardiasis, Coccidian, Balantidiasis
mcqs.explanation: The mature cyst of Entamoeba histolytica has a maximum of four nuclei. This is a key morphological feature used in the identification of the organism.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM) is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
45. Intestinal Protozoan Infections: Amoebiasis, Giardiasis, Coccidian, Balantidiasis
mcqs.explanation: Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM) is caused by the free-living amoeba Naegleria fowleri. It is a rare but rapidly fatal infection acquired through inhalation of contaminated water during swimming.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Keratitis in healthy contact lens users is usually caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
45. Intestinal Protozoan Infections: Amoebiasis, Giardiasis, Coccidian, Balantidiasis
mcqs.explanation: Acanthamoeba culbertsoni is known to cause keratitis, especially in contact lens users. The infection is associated with poor contact lens hygiene.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Flask-shaped intestinal ulcers are caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
45. Intestinal Protozoan Infections: Amoebiasis, Giardiasis, Coccidian, Balantidiasis
mcqs.explanation: Entamoeba histolytica causes characteristic flask-shaped ulcers in the intestines. These ulcers are a hallmark of amoebic dysentery.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Enterotest is used to diagnose
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
45. Intestinal Protozoan Infections: Amoebiasis, Giardiasis, Coccidian, Balantidiasis
mcqs.explanation: The Enterotest is used to diagnose giardiasis by obtaining samples from the small intestine for examination. It involves swallowing a gelatin capsule with a nylon string that is retrieved after a few hours.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All of the following helminths enter human body by ingestion EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
46. Intestinal Helminthic Infections: Cestodes, Trematodes, Nematodes
mcqs.explanation: Necator americanus (hookworm) typically enters the human body through skin penetration, often through the feet when walking barefoot on contaminated soil. The other helminths listed enter the body through ingestion of their eggs.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: B12 deficiency anaemia is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
46. Intestinal Helminthic Infections: Cestodes, Trematodes, Nematodes
mcqs.explanation: Diphyllobothrium latum, also known as the fish tapeworm, can cause vitamin B12 deficiency leading to anemia. It is the only tapeworm that causes B12 deficiency.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Following is most safe vaccine for prevention of Rabies
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
74. Viral Encephalitis and Encephalopathy: Rabies, HSV, Arboviral, Nipah, Prion
mcqs.explanation: Human Diploid Cell Vaccine (HDCV) is considered the safest rabies vaccine. It is prepared from rabies virus grown in human diploid cells, which eliminates the risk of neurological complications associated with nerve tissue vaccines.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Intracytoplasmic and intra-nuclear inclusion body is seen in
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
74. Viral Encephalitis and Encephalopathy: Rabies, HSV, Arboviral, Nipah, Prion
mcqs.explanation: Rabies virus produces intracytoplasmic Negri bodies. Mumps and measles viruses produce both intracytoplasmic and intranuclear inclusions in infected cells.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the smallest cestode?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
46. Intestinal Helminthic Infections: Cestodes, Trematodes, Nematodes
mcqs.explanation: Hymenolepis nana, also known as the dwarf tapeworm, is the smallest cestode. It measures only a few centimeters in length and is the most common cestode in humans.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Hydatid fluid for Casoni's test is sterilized by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
46. Intestinal Helminthic Infections: Cestodes, Trematodes, Nematodes
mcqs.explanation: Hydatid fluid for Casoni's test is sterilized by filtration. This method is used to avoid denaturation of the antigen, which would occur with heat sterilization.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which is not a n important cause of neonatal sepsis?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
41. GI Infections: Enterobacteriaceae, Diarrheagenic E. coli, Shigella, NTS, Yersinia
mcqs.explanation:
(c) (Acinetobacter) Ref: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, 18/e Chapter 176
Among the options, Acinetobacter is the best answer.
The infectious agents associated with sepsis in pediatric patients:
• In the neonatal age group, group B streptococcus, Escherichia coli, Listeria monocytogenes, enteroviruses, and herpes
simplex virus are the pathogens most commonly associated with sepsis.
• In older children Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Staphylococcus aureus are more common.
• Toxic shock syndrome from group A streptococcus or S. aureus can also be seen in older children.
• Infections with gram-negative bacteria (e.g. Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Serratia)
and fungi (e.g. Candida, Aspergillus) most often occur in immunocompromised and hospitalized patients colonized
with these organisms.
• Pseudobacteremia may be associated with contaminated heparin flush solutions, intravenous solutions, albumin,
cryoprecipitate, and infusion equipment. Contaminants include waterborne organisms, such as Burkholderia cepacia,
Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Serratia.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Cysticercus cellulosae is the larval form of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
46. Intestinal Helminthic Infections: Cestodes, Trematodes, Nematodes
mcqs.explanation: Cysticercus cellulosae is the larval stage of Taenia solium, also known as the pork tapeworm. It causes cysticercosis in humans.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Casoni's test is used in the diagnosis of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
46. Intestinal Helminthic Infections: Cestodes, Trematodes, Nematodes
mcqs.explanation: Casoni's test is used to diagnose hydatid disease, caused by Echinococcus granulosus. It is a skin test that detects delayed-type hypersensitivity to hydatid antigens.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT a cestode?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
46. Intestinal Helminthic Infections: Cestodes, Trematodes, Nematodes
mcqs.explanation: Schistosoma is a trematode (fluke), not a cestode (tapeworm). Schistosoma causes schistosomiasis, a parasitic infection of the blood vessels.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Ribbon like helminth parasites are known as
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
46. Intestinal Helminthic Infections: Cestodes, Trematodes, Nematodes
mcqs.explanation: Tapeworms are ribbon-like helminth parasites. They are flat, segmented worms that belong to the class Cestoda.

tags: Infective Syndromes of Urinary Tract and Sexually Transmitte
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Bacterium is considered significant when the bacterial count per ml of urine is more than
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
76. Urinary Tract Infections and STIs: Enterobacteriaceae, Enterococcus, BK, Schistosoma
mcqs.explanation: Significant bacteriuria is typically defined as the presence of more than 100,000 (10⁵) organisms per milliliter of urine. This is the standard criterion for diagnosing a urinary tract infection.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a DNA virus?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a DNA virus, whereas HAV, HCV, and HEV are RNA viruses. HBV is a member of the Hepadnaviridae family.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following serological markers is/are positive in super carriers of Hepatitis B?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Super carriers of Hepatitis B have both HBsAg and HBeAg positive. These markers indicate high infectivity and active viral replication.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A patient comes with history of unresponsive fever and cough. On examination of sputum it is negative for mycobacterium. Chest X-ray shows pneumonia. BAL shows gram-positive branching filaments. Organism was partially AFB positive. Causative organism is:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
55. Miscellaneous Bacterial Skin: Anthrax, Actinomycosis, Nocardiosis, Nonvenereal Treponematoses
mcqs.explanation:
(b) (Nocardiosis) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p294-95, Ananthanarayan 9/e p393
• Gram-positive branching filaments – Actinomyces or Nocardia
• Partially AFB positive - Suggestive of Nocardia

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The following marker tells us about the viral load and degree of infectivity in Hepatitis B infected patient
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: HBeAg is an indicator of viral replication and infectivity in Hepatitis B patients. Its presence indicates high viral load and active replication.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Universal safety precautions should be followed while treating
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Universal safety precautions should be followed for all patients to prevent the spread of infections. This approach treats all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An individual with hepatomegaly, jaundice and elevated liver enzymes has the following laboratory results; HBs Ag positive, IgM anti-HAV positive, IgM anti-HBs positive, anti-HCV negative. These findings support the diagnosis of:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: The presence of IgM anti-HAV and IgM anti-HBs along with HBs Ag indicates an acute hepatitis infection. This is due to the presence of both acute hepatitis A and acute hepatitis B infections.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following does NOT infect CNS?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Hepatitis B virus does not typically infect the central nervous system, whereas HTLV-III (HIV), Herpes simplex I, and Herpes simplex II can infect the CNS.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A recent Hepatitis B infection is confirmed by the demonstration of serum
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: The presence of Anti-HBc IgM antibodies indicates a recent Hepatitis B infection. This marker appears during the acute phase of infection and usually persists for several months.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following microorganisms form the normal flora of the skin?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
50. Infective Syndromes: Skin, Soft Tissue, Musculoskeletal
mcqs.explanation: Coryneform bacilli (diphtheroids) are part of the normal flora of the skin. These are Gram-positive, pleomorphic rods that are commonly found on the skin surface and are generally non-pathogenic. They include species like Corynebacterium xerosis and Corynebacterium jeikeium, which can cause opportunistic infections in immunocompromised patients.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: "CAMP" test is used for identifying which group of streptococci?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation: The CAMP test is used to identify Group B Streptococci, such as Streptococcus agalactiae. The test is based on the synergistic hemolysis of CAMP factor produced by Group B streptococci with beta-hemolysin from Staphylococcus aureus. A positive test results in enhanced hemolysis in a "arrowhead" pattern on blood agar.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Streptococcal glomerulonephritis is more common after
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Streptococcal glomerulonephritis is more commonly associated with skin infections, such as impetigo, caused by Streptococcus pyogenes. The nephritogenic strains of Group A streptococci (especially M types 2, 49, 55, 57, 60) are more likely to cause post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis following skin infections (pyoderma) rather than pharyngitis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: CAMP test is exhibited by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus) exhibits a positive CAMP test. The CAMP factor produced by Group B streptococci enhances the hemolytic activity of beta-lysin from Staphylococcus aureus, creating a characteristic arrowhead-shaped zone of hemolysis on blood agar.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A positive CAMP test is useful in identification of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation: A positive CAMP test is used to identify Group B Beta hemolytic streptococci, such as Streptococcus agalactiae. The CAMP factor produced by S. agalactiae causes enhanced lysis of sheep erythrocytes when combined with the beta-hemolysin of S. aureus, resulting in a characteristic arrowhead-shaped zone of hemolysis.

tags: Gas Gangrene (Clostridium perfringens) and Infections due to
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The only clostridium species that produces serologically related alpha toxin with that of clostridium perfringens is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Clostridium septicum produces an alpha toxin that is serologically related to the alpha toxin of Clostridium perfringens. Both organisms are important causes of gas gangrene and produce phospholipase C (alpha toxin), which is a major virulence factor.

tags: Gas Gangrene (Clostridium perfringens) and Infections due to
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Capsulated species of clostridium is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Clostridium perfringens is known to have a capsule. This encapsulated species is an important pathogen causing gas gangrene, food poisoning, and necrotizing enteritis. The capsule contributes to its virulence and resistance to phagocytosis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Undifferentiated histiocytes containing lepra bacilli are called
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Foamy cells are undifferentiated histiocytes containing numerous lepra bacilli, typically seen in lepromatous leprosy. These cells are filled with lipid-laden bacilli, giving them a foamy appearance under the microscope. They are also known as Virchow cells.

tags: Gas Gangrene (Clostridium perfringens) and Infections due to
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Toxin responsible for target haemolysis in clostridium perfringens is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Alpha and theta toxins are responsible for the target haemolysis characteristic of Clostridium perfringens. Alpha toxin is a phospholipase C, while theta toxin is a pore-forming cytolysin (perfringolysin O). Together, they cause hemolysis in the presence of oxygen, which is a characteristic feature of C. perfringens infections.

tags: Gas Gangrene (Clostridium perfringens) and Infections due to
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Nagler reaction is useful for identification of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation: The Nagler reaction is used to identify Clostridium perfringens by detecting the presence of alpha toxin. This reaction demonstrates the lecithinase activity of C. perfringens, where colonies on egg yolk agar produce a zone of opacity due to phospholipase C activity.

tags: Gas Gangrene (Clostridium perfringens) and Infections due to
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Stormy clot fermentation is seen in
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Clostridium perfringens produces a characteristic stormy clot reaction in milk due to gas production and clot formation. This reaction is used in the identification of C. perfringens, where the organism produces acid and gas, causing the milk to clot and fragment violently.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
80. Organisms with Oncogenic Potential: HPV, KSHV, HTLV, HIV, EBV, HBV, HCV
mcqs.explanation: Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV). It is commonly seen in immunocompromised patients, particularly those with AIDS.

tags: Gas Gangrene (Clostridium perfringens) and Infections due to
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Alpha toxin of Cl perfringens can be detected by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation: The Nagler reaction is used to detect the alpha toxin of Clostridium perfringens. The test involves streaking the organism on egg yolk agar and observing for zones of opacity, which are indicative of lecithinase activity.

tags: Gas Gangrene (Clostridium perfringens) and Infections due to
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Toxigenicity of Clostridium perfringens is confirmed by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Nagler's reaction confirms the toxigenicity of Clostridium perfringens by demonstrating the presence of alpha toxin. The test is based on the detection of lecithinase activity, which is characteristic of C. perfringens and confirms its toxigenicity.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Most commonly involved site in diphtheria is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: The fauces, or throat area, is the most commonly affected site in diphtheria. The infection typically presents with a grayish-white pseudomembrane on the tonsils and pharynx. It is most commonly seen in young children.

tags: Gas Gangrene (Clostridium perfringens) and Infections due to
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following bacteria form spores?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Clostridium perfringens, being a member of the genus Clostridium, forms spores. Clostridia are Gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming bacilli. Spores are highly resistant to heat, drying, and disinfectants, allowing the organism to survive in the environment for long periods.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Lepromatous leprosy has following features EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Thickening of peripheral nerves is more commonly seen in tuberculoid leprosy, not lepromatous leprosy. Lepromatous leprosy is characterized by poor cell-mediated immunity, numerous acid-fast bacilli in lesions, and a negative lepromin test. Nerve damage occurs in all forms of leprosy, but it is more prominent in the tuberculoid form due to the granulomatous reaction.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Cigar bundle appearance is a morphological feature of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Mycobacterium leprae can exhibit a cigar bundle appearance due to its arrangement in tissues. The bacilli are arranged in parallel bundles, resembling cigars, particularly in lepromatous leprosy where there are numerous bacilli in macrophages.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Classification of leprosy into five groups on the basis of clinical, histopathological and immunological findings have been introduced by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Ridley and Jopling introduced the classification system for leprosy. This system classifies leprosy into five groups (TT, BT, BB, BL, LL) based on clinical, histopathological, and immunological findings. It is the most widely used classification system for leprosy.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Tuberculoid form of leprosy is seen in patients with
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Tuberculoid leprosy is associated with a strong cell mediated immune response. The patient mounts an effective T cell response against M. leprae, leading to granuloma formation, few bacilli, and localized disease. The Lepromin test is positive, indicating good CMI.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a category A bioterrorism agent? (PG Entrance 2020)
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
55. Miscellaneous Bacterial Skin: Anthrax, Actinomycosis, Nocardiosis, Nonvenereal Treponematoses
mcqs.explanation: Bacillus anthracis is classified as a category A bioterrorism agent due to its potential for widespread impact and high mortality. Category A agents are the highest priority bioterrorism agents, as they can be easily disseminated, cause high mortality, and require special public health preparedness.

options.text: A microorganism should be constantly associated with the lesions of the disease
It should be possible to isolate the bacterium in pure culture from the lesions

Administration of broad spectrum antimicrobial agent dependably eradicates the organisms and cures the diseases

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All are Koch’s postulates except:
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: (d) Administration of broad spectrum antimicrobial agent dependably eradicates the organisms and cures the diseases Refer text Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p4, Ananthanarayan 9/e p5

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Corynebacterium diphtheriae is also called:
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation:
(b) (Kleb-Loeffler’s...) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p5, Ananthanarayan 9/e p236
• Corynebacterium diphtheriae is also called Klebs-Loeffler bacillus

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Acid fast bacilli – stained by:
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation:
(a) (Ziehl–Neelsen) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p16, Ananthanarayan 9 /e p13
Refer chapter review of chapter 1.1

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Not used in grams staining:
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation:
(a) (Methylene blue) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p14-15, Ananthanarayan 9/e p13
• Gram stain has four steps (refer chapter review)
• Methylene blue is used a counter stain for acid fast stain

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Fried egg appearance of colonies is seen in
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
62. Bacterial Atypical Interstitial Pneumonia: Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella
mcqs.explanation: Mycoplasma colonies have a "fried egg" appearance on agar plates. This morphology is due to the growth of the organism into the agar, with a dense center and a lighter periphery.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: "Medusa Head" colonies are characteristic of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
55. Miscellaneous Bacterial Skin: Anthrax, Actinomycosis, Nocardiosis, Nonvenereal Treponematoses
mcqs.explanation: Bacillus anthracis colonies exhibit a characteristic "Medusa Head" appearance. This morphology is due to the presence of long chains of bacilli that grow on the agar surface, producing a characteristic wavy edge.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Man acquires psittacosis from
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
62. Bacterial Atypical Interstitial Pneumonia: Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella
mcqs.explanation: Psittacosis is commonly transmitted to humans from parrots and other birds. The disease is caused by Chlamydia psittaci and is characterized by flu-like symptoms.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The tests used for presumptive diagnosis of anthrax is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
55. Miscellaneous Bacterial Skin: Anthrax, Actinomycosis, Nocardiosis, Nonvenereal Treponematoses
mcqs.explanation: McFadyean's reaction is used for the presumptive diagnosis of anthrax. It is a staining method where methylene blue is used to demonstrate the characteristic pinkish-purple bacilli with square-ended ("box-car") appearance, which is suggestive of B. anthracis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which is a eukaryote:
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation:
(c) (fungus) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p9, Ananthanarayan 9 e/p427, 8/e p425
• Prokaryotes – include bacteria and blue green algae
• Eukaryotes – include fungi, algae (other than blue green), protozoa, helminths and slime moulds
• See the table from the text for detail.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: "String of pearls" reaction is given by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
55. Miscellaneous Bacterial Skin: Anthrax, Actinomycosis, Nocardiosis, Nonvenereal Treponematoses
mcqs.explanation: Bacillus anthracis gives the string of pearls reaction when grown on penicillin-containing media. The bacilli form spherical bodies (protoplasts) due to penicillin-induced cell wall damage, which gives a "string of pearls" appearance when viewed under the microscope.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following organisms is Gram negative?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
55. Miscellaneous Bacterial Skin: Anthrax, Actinomycosis, Nocardiosis, Nonvenereal Treponematoses
mcqs.explanation: Bordetella species are Gram-negative bacteria. Clostridium, Bacillus, and Actinomyces are Gram-positive bacteria. Bordetella pertussis, the causative agent of whooping cough, is a Gram-negative coccobacillus.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Malignant pustule is a characteristic of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
55. Miscellaneous Bacterial Skin: Anthrax, Actinomycosis, Nocardiosis, Nonvenereal Treponematoses
mcqs.explanation: Cutaneous anthrax is characterized by the development of a malignant pustule. It is the most common form of anthrax, where the lesion begins as a papule, develops into a vesicle, and then forms a characteristic black eschar (malignant pustule). The lesion is usually painless and accompanied by local edema.

tags: Viral Exanthems and Other Cutaneous Viral Infections
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Koplik's spots on the buccal mucosa is a characteristic feature of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
56. Viral Exanthems and Cutaneous Infections: Herpes, Pox, Parvovirus, Measles, Rubella, Coxsackie
mcqs.explanation: Koplik's spots are a characteristic feature of measles. These are small, white, granular spots on the buccal mucosa, often appearing before the rash develops. They are pathognomonic for measles.

mcqs.question: Population doubling time in coliform bacilli is:
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control

(b) (20 minutes) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p26, Ananthanarayan 9/e p22

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Obligate intracellular organism is:
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation:
(b) (Chlamydia) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p92
Refer chapter review

tags: Viral Exanthems and Other Cutaneous Viral Infections
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The recommended age for measles vaccine in India is

mcqs.explanation: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a rare, chronic complication of measles infection. It is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by persistent measles virus infection in the brain, occurring years after the initial infection. SSPE is characterized by cognitive decline, motor deterioration, and death.

mcqs.explanation: Reactivation of Herpes simplex virus typically causes herpes labialis, also known as cold sores. HSV-1 remains latent in the trigeminal ganglia and reactivates due to triggers like stress, fever, or UV light, causing recurrent vesicular lesions on the lips and perioral area.

mcqs.explanation: There are 8 known herpesviruses that infect humans, not 12. The human herpesviruses include HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, EBV, CMV, HHV-6, HHV-7, and HHV-8 (KSHV). These viruses are characterized by their ability to establish lifelong latency and reactivation.

mcqs.explanation: Glandular fever (infectious mononucleosis) is caused by Epstein-Barr virus. It is characterized by fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, and atypical lymphocytosis. The disease is transmitted through saliva and is commonly seen in adolescents and young adults.

mcqs.explanation: Poxviruses are the largest known viruses, measuring up to 400 nm in diameter. They have complex morphology, a large double-stranded DNA genome, and can be visualized under a light microscope. The smallpox virus (Variola) is a member of this group.

options.text: Most common mechanism is production of neutralizing enzymes
If resistance is plasmid mediated, it is always transferred vertically
Alteration of target seen in pneumococcal resistance

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Not true about bacterial drug resistance mechanism:
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation:
(b) (If resistance is plasmid mediated, it is always transferred vertically) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical
Microbiology 1/e p82, Ananthanarayan 9/e p63, 8/e p67, Harrison 18/e p1157
• If resistance is chromosomally mediated, it is usually transferred vertically from parent to daughter bacteria.
• If resistance is plasmid mediated, it is usually transferred by horizontal route mainly by conjugation.
About Other Options
• Clinically, enzymatic drug inactivation is the most common mechanism for acquired microbial resistance by bacteria
• Most common mechanism of bacterial drug resistance:
• Pneumococcal resistance: is mainly due to Alteration of target, i.e. Penicillin binding protein (PBP)
• Resistance to Vancomycin is due to complete removal of target D alanyl-D alanine present the bacterial cell wall is the
target site for Vancomycin, which binds there and inhibits it and thus inhibits the cell wall synthesis.
The four Major Mechanisms of Antibacterial Resistance: Refer chapter review.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology

chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation:
(d) (Conjugation) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p73, Ananthanarayan 9/e p60-61
• Resistance (R) factors are extrachromosomal plasmids responsible for spread of multiple drug resistance among
bacteria.
• They are circular double stranded DNA carry genes for variety of enzymes that can destroy antibiotics
• R factor consists of 2 components: Resistance transfer factor (RTF) and resistant determinant (r).
• The resistance transfer factor is responsible for conjugational transfer while each r determinant carries resistance for
one of the several antibiotics.

agent that will inhibit the visible growth of a microorganism.
• MIC is calculated by: (i) Agar dilution method, (ii) Broth dilution method and (iii) Epsilometer (E test)

mcqs.explanation: All of the listed nematodes (Brugia timori, Brugia malayi, and Wuchereria bancrofti) are located in the lymphatics. These are the major causes of lymphatic filariasis, leading to lymphedema, elephantiasis, and hydrocele.

mcqs.question: The smallest nematode infecting man is

Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
57. Parasitic Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Cutaneous Leishmaniasis, Cysticercosis, Tissue Nematodes, Larva Migrans
mcqs.explanation: Trichinella spiralis is the smallest nematode infecting humans. It causes trichinellosis, which is acquired by ingesting undercooked meat containing encysted larvae. The small size of the adult worms (female 3-4 mm, male 1-2 mm) makes them difficult to detect.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Intermediate host for Dracunculus medinensis is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
57. Parasitic Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Cutaneous Leishmaniasis, Cysticercosis, Tissue Nematodes, Larva Migrans
mcqs.explanation: Cyclops, a type of small crustacean, is the intermediate host for Dracunculus medinensis. The larvae develop in Cyclops and are transmitted to humans through drinking contaminated water.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All of the following helminths enter human body by ingestion EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
57. Parasitic Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Cutaneous Leishmaniasis, Cysticercosis, Tissue Nematodes, Larva Migrans
mcqs.explanation: Necator americanus (hookworm) enters the human body through skin penetration, often through the feet when walking barefoot on contaminated soil. The other helminths listed (Trichuris trichiura, Ascaris lumbricoides, and Enterobius vermicularis) enter the body through ingestion of their eggs.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following infection has been eradicated from India?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
57. Parasitic Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Cutaneous Leishmaniasis, Cysticercosis, Tissue Nematodes, Larva Migrans
mcqs.explanation: Dracunculus medinensis (Guinea worm) infection has been eradicated from India. India was certified guinea worm-free by WHO in 2000. The successful eradication was achieved through health education, safe water supply, and case containment measures.

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
57. Parasitic Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Cutaneous Leishmaniasis, Cysticercosis, Tissue Nematodes, Larva Migrans
mcqs.explanation: Cyclops serves as the intermediate host for Dracunculus medinensis. The larvae develop in Cyclops and are transmitted to humans through drinking contaminated water.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: Microsporum species infect hair and skin but not nails. This dermatophyte causes tinea capitis (scalp ringworm) and tinea corporis, but does not invade nails. This is in contrast to Trichophyton, which infects hair, skin, and nails, and Epidermophyton, which infects skin and nails only.

58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: Germ tube test is used to identify Candida albicans. A positive germ tube test is indicative of C. albicans (and closely related C. dubliniensis). This test is rapid, simple, and highly specific for C. albicans, making it a valuable tool in the clinical laboratory.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Tinea versicolor is caused due to
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: Tinea versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur. This is a superficial fungal infection of the skin characterized by hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules on the trunk. The organism is a lipophilic yeast that is part of normal skin flora and requires lipids for growth.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Madura foot is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: Madura foot, or mycetoma, can be caused by Nocardia species. Mycetoma is a chronic, granulomatous infection characterized by the formation of draining sinuses and grains. Nocardia causes actinomycetoma, which is a type of mycetoma.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Tinea nigra is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: Tinea nigra is a superficial fungal infection caused by Hortaea werneckii. The infection presents as brown or black macules on the palms and soles. It is commonly seen in tropical and subtropical regions.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Presence of nasal polyp is a feature of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: Rhinosporidiosis is characterized by the presence of nasal polyps. This chronic granulomatous infection is caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi and typically presents as friable, vascular polyps in the nasal cavity.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Tinea cruris is a dermatophyte infection of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: Tinea cruris, also known as jock itch, is a fungal infection of the groin area. It is caused by dermatophytes such as Trichophyton rubrum and Epidermophyton floccosum. The infection is more common in men and is characterized by erythematous, pruritic lesions in the groin and upper thighs.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The fungus which can NOT be cultivated in laboratory is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: Rhinosporidium seeberi cannot be cultivated in the laboratory. It requires histological examination for diagnosis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All of the following can cause systemic mycoses, EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: Madurella grisea is an agent of mycetoma, not a systemic mycosis. Systemic mycoses involve internal organs and are caused by fungi that can disseminate through the bloodstream. M. grisea causes localized subcutaneous infections.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All of the following can cause dermatophytes, EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: Tinea versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur, not by dermatophytes like Trichophyton, Epidermophyton, or Microsporum. Dermatophytes are keratinophilic fungi that infect the skin, hair, and nails, while Malassezia is a lipophilic yeast.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Tinea cruris is ringworm infection which involves
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: Tinea cruris is an infection of the groin area. It is a common dermatophyte infection in warm, humid conditions, characterized by erythematous, pruritic lesions in the groin and upper thighs.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Macroconidia of Trichophyton rubrum are
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: Macroconidia of Trichophyton rubrum are pencil-shaped. This morphological feature is used to identify T. rubrum, which is one of the most common dermatophytes causing infections of the skin, hair, and nails.

options.text: It is not cultivable on artificial media

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Rhinosporidium seeberi has been cultivated on
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: Rhinosporidium seeberi cannot be cultivated on artificial media. It is an obligate intracellular parasite that causes rhinosporidiosis, characterized by nasal polyps. Diagnosis is based on histological examination.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following dermatophyte infect hair, skin & nails?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: Trichophyton species can infect hair, skin, and nails. This dermatophyte is the most common cause of tinea infections, including tinea corporis, tinea pedis, and tinea unguium (onychomycosis).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following dermatophytes is geophilic?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: Microsporum gypseum is a geophilic dermatophyte. Geophilic dermatophytes are found in soil, in contrast to anthropophilic (human) and zoophilic (animal) dermatophytes. They can cause infections in humans and animals.

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases

58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: KOH mount is used to demonstrate dermatophytes in clinical specimens. The potassium hydroxide (KOH) solution digests keratin and cellular debris, clearing the sample and allowing visualization of fungal hyphae and spores. This is a rapid and simple method for diagnosing dermatophytosis.

(a) (C2, C4, C3...) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p142-3, Ananthanarayan 9/e p121
C2, C3, and C4 all are utilized in Classical pathway, hence their serum level will be low.
Classical pathway:
• Starts by Activation of C1 by antigen antibody complex
• Activated C1 in turn activates C4 to C4a (anaphylotoxin) and C4b
• C1 4b in turn activates C2 (in presence of Mg ion) to form C2a and C2b (kinin like, increases vascular permeability)
• C14b2a is known as C3 convertase which activates C3 to C3a (chemotactic and anaphylotoxin) and C3b
• C14b2a3b is known as C5 convertase which activates C5 to C5a (chemotactic and anaphylotoxin) and C5b
• Late components add to C5b – to form C56789 (membrane attack complex) which forms pores on cell membrane
causing cell lysis and also activates bystander cells to make them susceptible to lysis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The causative agent of pityriasis versicolor is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur. This is a superficial fungal infection characterized by hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules on the trunk. The organism is a lipophilic yeast that is part of normal skin flora.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A fungal infection initiated by thorn prick and characterized by a pustular lesion, with satellite lesions along lymphatics is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: Sporotrichosis, caused by Sporothrix schenckii, often presents with pustular lesions and satellite nodules along lymphatics following traumatic inoculation. This is a classic presentation of the fixed cutaneous or lymphocutaneous form of sporotrichosis, commonly acquired through puncture wounds from thorns or plant material.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The fungus which live exclusively on the dead layer of skin includes
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
58. Fungal Infections Skin and Soft Tissue: Superficial, Subcutaneous, Candidiasis, Penicillium
mcqs.explanation: These fungi live on the dead layer of skin. Pityrosporum orbiculare, Piedraia hortae, and Malassezia furfur are all superficial fungi that colonize the stratum corneum of the skin.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Toxin production in C. diphtheriae depends on
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: The production of diphtheria toxin by C. diphtheriae is due to the presence of a lysogenic bacteriophage carrying the toxin gene. This is an example of lysogenic conversion, where the bacterial genome is altered by the integration of phage DNA.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Metachromatic granules of C. diphtheriae are seen best by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Albert's stain is used to demonstrate the metachromatic granules in C. diphtheriae. These granules appear as dark blue or violet beads against a pale green background, providing a characteristic "barred" or "beaded" appearance.

mcqs.explanation:

mcqs.explanation:

Exogenous (foreign) antigens are first phagocytosed by APCs, then they are processed by APCs and presented on the
surface of APCs along with MHC II to be recognized by CD 4+ T Cells.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Laboratory diagnosis of Diphtheriae is made by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: The diagnosis of diphtheria includes isolating the bacteria and confirming its ability to produce toxin. This is done through culture and toxigenicity testing (Elek's test), which is essential for confirming the diagnosis and initiating appropriate treatment.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Diphtheria toxin production is caused by a bacteriophage
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: The gene for diphtheria toxin is carried by a bacteriophage (a virus that infects bacteria). This is an example of lysogenic conversion, where the bacterial genome is altered by the integration of phage DNA.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Diphtheria toxin is demonstrated by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Elek's test is used to demonstrate the presence of diphtheria toxin. This is a gel immunodiffusion test where the bacterial strain is streaked on a medium containing diphtheria antitoxin, and the production of toxin is indicated by the formation of a precipitin line.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which organism produces toxin that acts on organs and tissues distant from the site of colonization?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Corynebacterium diphtheriae produces a toxin that can affect distant organs and tissues. The diphtheria toxin is an A-B toxin that inhibits protein synthesis, leading to damage to the heart, nerves, and kidneys.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Elek's gel precipitation test is used to detect
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Elek's test detects the presence of diphtheria toxin. It is a gel immunodiffusion test that demonstrates the production of toxin by C. diphtheriae, which is confirmed by the formation of a precipitin line.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Toxoids are
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Toxoids are inactivated toxins that are antigenic but not toxic. They are used in vaccines to induce immunity against diphtheria and tetanus. The toxin is treated with formaldehyde or heat to destroy toxicity while retaining immunogenicity.

options.text: Prophylaxis with erythromycin and diphtheria antitoxin
Immunize with booster of diphtheria toxoid

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old boy presents with sore throat for the last two days. On examination he has a greyish white pseudomembrane around his tonsils. Diphtheria is suspected. His 3-year-old brother has received his last DPT booster 16 months ago. What is the recommended prophylaxis for his brother? (PG Entrance program)
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Since the brother received his last booster 16 months ago, he should receive a booster of diphtheria toxoid for prophylaxis. Close contacts of diphtheria cases should be given a booster dose of diphtheria toxoid if they have been vaccinated in the past, or a full course of vaccination if not.

Can transmit either as X-linked or autosomal recessive defect
Person susceptible to recurrent and severe infections

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All are true about severe combined immunodeficiency except:
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation:
(a,b,d,e) (B & T cell.., Adenosine deaminase..,Can transmit.., Person susceptible..) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials
of Medical Microbiology 1/e p190
In Severe Combined Immunodeficiencies (SCID), both CMI are AMI are affected. It runs as:
• X linked: Mutation in cytokine receptor
• Autosomal recessive: It occurs as: (i) Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency, (ii) Jak3 mutation, (iii) RAG mutation
and (iv) Class II MHC deficiency
• The affected infants are susceptible to severe recurrent infections by a wide array of pathogens, including Candida,
Pneumocystis, cytomegalovirus and Pseudomonas.
• Prognosis of SCID is poor. Bone marrow transplantation is the mainstay of treatment.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Chronic granulomatous disorder is due to defect in:
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation:
(b) (NADPH oxidase) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p191, Ananthanarayan 9/e p172
Chronic granulomatous disease:
• Due to defect in phagocytosis (results from absence of NADPH oxidase)
• ↑Recurrent catalase +ve pyogenic infection (catalase –ve organisms are handled normally)
• Screening test used- Nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) reduction test is negative.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The phenomenon of Satellitism is exhibited by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Haemophilus influenzae exhibits satellitism around colonies of Staphylococcus aureus. S. aureus provides X and V factors, allowing H. influenzae to grow in its vicinity.

chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation:
(b) (Kidney) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p194, Ananthanarayan 9/e p184, 166
• Hyperacute graft rejection is seen in kidney and skin grafting and is preformed antibody mediated (Type III
Hypersensitivity reaction)

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Skin transplant was done from sister to brother. After few years, brother to sister skin transplant was done, but rejection occurred. What is this phenomena called?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation:
(c) (Eichwald Silms....) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p194, Ananthanarayan 9/e p185
• While transplants between members of a highly inbred strain of animals are successful, an exception is seen when the
donor is a male and the recipient a female.
• Such grafts are rejected as the grafted male tissue (XY) will have antigens determined by the Y chromosome which will
be absent in the female (XX) recipient.
• Grafts from the female to the male will succeed.
• This unilateral sex linked histoincompatibility is known as the Eichwald-Silmser effect.
Systemic Bacteriology

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Satellitism is a characteristic growth pattern of Haemophilus influenzae around Staphylococcus aureus. This phenomenon is used in the laboratory identification of H. influenzae.

mcqs.explanation: Chlamydiae are obligate intracellular parasites and cannot be isolated on cell-free media. They require host cells for replication and are cultured in cell lines or embryonated eggs.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: According to national immunisation schedule, which of the following is recommended for a child of 5-year of age?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation:
(d) (DPT booster and vitamin A) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p205, Park 22/e p115
According to national immunization schedule in India:
• DPT schedule: 1st/2nd/3rd dose at 6/10/14 weeks and two boosters at 16–24 months and 5–6 yr
• Vitamin A: 1st dose at 9 month (along with measles), 2nd dose at 16–24 months (along with DPT booster) and the 3rd
to 9th dose given every 6 month till 5 yrs.
• OPV schedule: Zero dose at birth, then 1st/2nd/3rd dose at 6/10/14 weeks and booster at 16–24 months.
[UPDATE 2026] India's UIP has expanded considerably since this book: IPV (2015), rotavirus vaccine (2016, scaled nationwide by 2019-20), measles-rubella vaccine (2017, replacing measles-only), and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (2017) have all been added. HPV vaccination for 14-year-old girls was introduced in February 2026, and an indigenously manufactured Td vaccine was launched the same month. Pentavalent vaccine (DTwP + HepB + Hib) has replaced standalone DPT for the primary series.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
