chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
62. Bacterial Atypical Interstitial Pneumonia: Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella
mcqs.explanation: The cold agglutination test is used in the diagnosis of primary atypical pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Cold agglutinins are IgM antibodies that agglutinate red blood cells at low temperatures.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following organisms is an obligate intracellular parasite?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
62. Bacterial Atypical Interstitial Pneumonia: Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella
mcqs.explanation: Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular parasite. It requires host cells for replication and cannot survive outside the host cell.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Primary atypical pneumonia is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
62. Bacterial Atypical Interstitial Pneumonia: Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella
mcqs.explanation: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a common cause of primary atypical pneumonia. It is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia, particularly in young adults.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Psittacosis is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
62. Bacterial Atypical Interstitial Pneumonia: Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella
mcqs.explanation: Psittacosis is caused by Chlamydia psittaci. It is transmitted from birds to humans and causes respiratory infection.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Ziehl-Neelsen staining is used for the demonstration of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Ziehl-Neelsen staining is used to demonstrate acid-fast bacilli, such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis. This staining method uses carbolfuchsin as the primary stain, followed by acid-alcohol decolorization, and then a counterstain.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: BCG vaccine is a
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guerin) is a live attenuated vaccine used for tuberculosis. It is derived from Mycobacterium bovis and is used to prevent severe forms of tuberculosis in children.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The Mantoux test is a
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: The Mantoux test is a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction (Type IV) used to detect tuberculosis infection. It involves the intradermal injection of tuberculin (PPD) and measuring the induration 48-72 hours later.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Atypical mycobacteria are also called
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Atypical mycobacteria are also known as non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM). These mycobacteria are not part of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex and are usually opportunistic pathogens.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Reynolds-Braude phenomenon is seen in one of the following
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: The Reynolds-Braude phenomenon is associated with the encapsulation and mucoid colony formation of Cryptococcus neoformans. This phenomenon describes the formation of mucoid colonies due to the production of the polysaccharide capsule, which can be visualized using India ink preparation or seen as mucoid colonies on culture media.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Candida albicans is differentiated from other candida species by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Candida albicans can be differentiated from other Candida species by the germ tube test, chlamydospore formation, and sugar assimilation tests. The germ tube test is a rapid method where C. albicans forms germ tubes when incubated in serum at 37°C for 2-3 hours. Chlamydospore formation on corn meal agar is also characteristic of C. albicans. Sugar assimilation patterns further differentiate C. albicans from other Candida species (e.g., C. tropicalis, C. krusei, C. glabrata).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a rapid grower among mycobacteria?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: M. fortuitum is a rapidly growing mycobacterium. It is part of the Runyon group IV (rapid growers), which also includes M. chelonae and M. abscessus.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: In DPT vaccine, the component which act as an adjuvant is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: The killed Bordetella pertussis bacilli in the DPT vaccine serve as an adjuvant, enhancing the immune response to the diphtheria and tetanus toxoids. This is why whole-cell pertussis vaccine is more immunogenic than the acellular vaccine.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following organisms is Gram negative?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Bordetella is a Gram-negative bacterium, whereas Clostridium, Bacillus, and Actinomyces are Gram-positive. Bordetella pertussis, the causative agent of whooping cough, is a Gram-negative coccobacillus.

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
65. Nonfermenting Gram-Negative Bacilli: Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Burkholderia
mcqs.explanation: Pyocyanin is a distinctive blue-green pigment produced by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. This pigment is responsible for the characteristic blue-green color of the organism's colonies and is a key feature in its identification.

tags: Infections due to Non-fermenting Gram-negative Bacilli
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is most commonly associated with infection in "Burns" cases?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
65. Nonfermenting Gram-Negative Bacilli: Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Burkholderia
mcqs.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is frequently associated with infections in burn patients due to its opportunistic nature and resistance to many antibiotics. It can cause severe wound infections and sepsis in burn patients.

tags: Infections due to Non-fermenting Gram-negative Bacilli
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A hospital disinfectant solution containing chlorhexidine and cetrimide found to be heavily contaminated with a bacterium. This bacterium is most likely to be
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
65. Nonfermenting Gram-Negative Bacilli: Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Burkholderia
mcqs.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa can survive and thrive in solutions containing disinfectants like chlorhexidine and cetrimide, making it a common contaminant in hospital settings. It is a significant cause of healthcare-associated infections.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Pandemic of influenza results due to
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
66. Myxovirus Infections: Influenza, Parainfluenza, Mumps, RSV
mcqs.explanation: Pandemics of influenza occur due to antigenic shift, which involves major changes in the viral genome leading to new subtypes. This occurs when two different influenza viruses infect the same cell and reassort their genes.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following are used for sterilization of surgical instrument:
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation:
(c) (d) (e) (Autoclaving, Glutaraldehyde, Hot air oven) Ref: Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization in Healthcare
Facilities, CDC, 2008
• For the sterilization of surgical instruments: Most medical and surgical devices are made of materials that are heat
stable and therefore can be sterilized best by autoclave (moist heat)
• Heat labile instruments (e.g. plastics) can be sterilized by Ethylene oxide gas or other new, low-temperature sterilization
systems (e.g. hydrogen peroxide gas plasma, peracetic acid immersion, ozone)
• Dry-heat sterilizers such as hot air oven should be used only for materials that might be damaged by moist heat or that
are impenetrable to moist heat (e.g., powders, petroleum products, sharp instruments)
• Ionizing radiation: There are no FDA-approved ionizing radiation sterilization processes for use in healthcare facilities.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which strain of influenza was declared a pandemic (PG Entrance 2020)
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
66. Myxovirus Infections: Influenza, Parainfluenza, Mumps, RSV
mcqs.explanation: The H1N1 strain of influenza was declared a pandemic in 2009 by the World Health Organization. This strain was a novel influenza A virus that emerged from swine.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The virus causing the disease SARS is a
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) is caused by a coronavirus, specifically SARS-CoV. The virus emerged in 2002-2003 and caused a global outbreak.

tags: Miscellaneous Viral Infections of Respiratory Tract

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
68. Miscellaneous Viral Respiratory: Rhinovirus, Adenovirus, Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV)
mcqs.explanation: Adenovirus is a common cause of "swimming-pool conjunctivitis." It is transmitted through contaminated water and causes acute follicular conjunctivitis.

tags: Parasitic and Fungal Infections of Respiratory Tract
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is characteristic of Aspergillus?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
69. Parasitic and Fungal Infections Respiratory: Paragonimiasis, Zygomycosis, Aspergillosis, Pneumocystosis
mcqs.explanation: Aspergillus is characterized by the presence of septate hyphae. These hyphae are branching and have cross walls (septa), distinguishing Aspergillus from zygomycetes which have aseptate hyphae.

tags: Parasitic and Fungal Infections of Respiratory Tract
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Paragonimus westermani primarily infects
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
69. Parasitic and Fungal Infections Respiratory: Paragonimiasis, Zygomycosis, Aspergillosis, Pneumocystosis
mcqs.explanation: Paragonimus westermani, the lung fluke, primarily infects the lungs. It causes paragonimiasis, a parasitic infection of the lungs.

tags: Parasitic and Fungal Infections of Respiratory Tract

mcqs.question: Fungal ball is seen in
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
69. Parasitic and Fungal Infections Respiratory: Paragonimiasis, Zygomycosis, Aspergillosis, Pneumocystosis
mcqs.explanation: Fungal balls, or aspergillomas, are commonly caused by Aspergillus species, particularly in the lungs. They are found in pre-existing cavities in the lungs and are an important complication of chronic lung disease.

tags: Infective Syndromes of Central Nervous System
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in adults?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in adults. It accounts for approximately 60% of cases in adults and is associated with high morbidity and mortality, particularly in the elderly. The organism is a Gram-positive, encapsulated diplococcus that colonizes the nasopharynx and can spread to the meninges through bacteremia.

tags: Infective Syndromes of Central Nervous System
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The organism most commonly associated with meningitis in neonates is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus) is the most common cause of meningitis in neonates. It is transmitted from the mother during childbirth. Other common causes in neonates include Escherichia coli and Listeria monocytogenes.

tags: Infective Syndromes of Central Nervous System
mcqs.subject: Microbiology

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Neisseria meningitidis is a Gram-negative diplococcus known to cause meningitis and can lead to septic shock with a characteristic petechial rash. The petechial rash is due to endothelial damage and meningococcal septicemia.

Infectious causes of pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO)- refer chapter review

mcqs.question: Which Corynebacterium carries toxin similar to that causing diphtheria toxin?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: (c) (C. ulcerans) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p244

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following sites is to be sampled for detecting the carrier state of Neisseria meningitidis?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
71. Bacterial Meningitis: Acute Pyogenic and Chronic
mcqs.explanation: The nasopharynx is the primary site for detecting the carrier state of Neisseria meningitidis. Carriage is common in the nasopharynx, and asymptomatic carriers are an important reservoir for transmission.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All of the following are true about Neisseria meningitidis EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
71. Bacterial Meningitis: Acute Pyogenic and Chronic
mcqs.explanation: Neisseria meningitidis ferments glucose and maltose but does not ferment sucrose. This sugar fermentation pattern is used to differentiate N. meningitidis from other Neisseria species, such as N. gonorrhoeae (which ferments glucose only) and N. lactamica (which ferments lactose).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Incubation period of salmonella Typhi:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
30. Enteric Fever: Salmonella Typhi and Paratyphi
mcqs.explanation:
(b) (3-21 days) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p320, Harrison 19e/1049-53, 18/e p1275,
17/e p957
• ‘The incubation period for S. Typhi averages 10–14 days but ranges from 3 to 21 days, with the duration likely reflecting the
inoculum size and the host’s health and immune status.’

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The most common cause of bacterial meningitis in neonates is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
71. Bacterial Meningitis: Acute Pyogenic and Chronic
mcqs.explanation: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus) is the most common cause of meningitis in neonates. It is transmitted from the mother during childbirth.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: CSF findings in pyogenic meningitis include all of the following EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
71. Bacterial Meningitis: Acute Pyogenic and Chronic
mcqs.explanation: In pyogenic meningitis, CSF shows increased polymorphs (neutrophils), decreased glucose, and increased protein. Increased lymphocytes are characteristic of viral or tuberculous meningitis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The capsular polysaccharide of Neisseria meningitidis is used for
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
71. Bacterial Meningitis: Acute Pyogenic and Chronic
mcqs.explanation: The capsular polysaccharide of Neisseria meningitidis is used for serogrouping, which classifies meningococci into different groups (A, B, C, Y, W-135). Serogrouping is important for epidemiological purposes and vaccine development.

options.text: Increased lymphocytes, decreased glucose, increased protein
Increased neutrophils, decreased glucose, increased protein
Increased lymphocytes, normal glucose, increased protein
Increased neutrophils, normal glucose, normal protein

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: CSF examination in tuberculous meningitis shows
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
71. Bacterial Meningitis: Acute Pyogenic and Chronic
mcqs.explanation: Tuberculous meningitis is characterized by CSF findings of increased lymphocytes (lymphocytic pleocytosis), decreased glucose, and increased protein. A cobweb-like clot may also be seen.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The most common cause of meningitis in HIV-positive patients is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
71. Bacterial Meningitis: Acute Pyogenic and Chronic
mcqs.explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans is the most common cause of meningitis in HIV-positive patients. It is an opportunistic infection seen in immunocompromised patients, particularly those with CD4 counts below 100 cells/µL.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Pneumatoceles in chest X-ray are characteristically seen in pneumonia due to:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation:
(b) (S. aureus) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p215
Pneumatocele is shaggy, thin-walled cavities in lungs of neonates (commonly) and S. aureus is the MC cause.

options.text: Increased neutrophils, decreased glucose, increased protein
Increased lymphocytes, normal glucose, increased protein
Increased neutrophils, normal glucose, increased protein
Increased lymphocytes, decreased glucose, increased protein

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The CSF picture in viral meningitis typically shows
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
71. Bacterial Meningitis: Acute Pyogenic and Chronic
mcqs.explanation: Viral meningitis is characterized by CSF findings of increased lymphocytes (lymphocytic pleocytosis), normal glucose (or slightly decreased), and increased protein. Glucose is typically normal in viral meningitis, which helps differentiate it from bacterial meningitis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The following are features of tuberculous meningitis EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
71. Bacterial Meningitis: Acute Pyogenic and Chronic
mcqs.explanation: Tuberculous meningitis is characterized by basal exudate, cobweb clot formation in CSF, and hydrocephalus. Subdural empyema is not a typical feature of tuberculous meningitis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The most common cause of bacterial meningitis in adults is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
71. Bacterial Meningitis: Acute Pyogenic and Chronic
mcqs.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in adults. It accounts for approximately 60% of cases in adults.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A man with very high fever shows strongly positive agglutination test with OXK antigen. The most likely diagnosis is:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation:
(a) (Tsutsugamushi fever) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p 392, Harrison 18/e p1413
• For details refer chapter review.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of meningitis in neonates?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
71. Bacterial Meningitis: Acute Pyogenic and Chronic
mcqs.explanation: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus) is the most common cause of meningitis in neonates. It is transmitted from the mother during childbirth.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Fixed rabies virus grown in sheep brain inactivated by phenol or Beta propiolactone is called
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
74. Viral Encephalitis and Encephalopathy: Rabies, HSV, Arboviral, Nipah, Prion
mcqs.explanation: Semple vaccine is prepared from fixed rabies virus inactivated by phenol or Beta propiolactone. It is a nerve tissue vaccine, which is less commonly used today due to the risk of neurological complications.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which one of the following viruses is bullet shaped?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
74. Viral Encephalitis and Encephalopathy: Rabies, HSV, Arboviral, Nipah, Prion
mcqs.explanation: Rabies virus is bullet shaped. This distinctive morphology is characteristic of the Rhabdoviridae family, to which rabies virus belongs. The bullet shape is visible under electron microscopy.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Negri bodies are seen in
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
74. Viral Encephalitis and Encephalopathy: Rabies, HSV, Arboviral, Nipah, Prion
mcqs.explanation: Negri bodies are diagnostic of rabies infection. These are eosinophilic, cytoplasmic inclusions found in neurons of patients infected with rabies virus. They are most commonly seen in the Purkinje cells of the cerebellum and hippocampal neurons.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Following are the characteristics of fixed virus EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
74. Viral Encephalitis and Encephalopathy: Rabies, HSV, Arboviral, Nipah, Prion
mcqs.explanation: Fixed virus is not isolated from natural cases; it is derived from laboratory strains with a fixed incubation period. Fixed virus has been adapted to laboratory animals and has a shortened, predictable incubation period.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Rabies virus in human multiplies in
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
74. Viral Encephalitis and Encephalopathy: Rabies, HSV, Arboviral, Nipah, Prion
mcqs.explanation: Rabies virus can multiply in muscle, nerve endings, and connective tissue. The virus enters through a bite wound, replicates in muscle cells, then enters peripheral nerves and travels to the central nervous system.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Rabies vaccine was first developed by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
74. Viral Encephalitis and Encephalopathy: Rabies, HSV, Arboviral, Nipah, Prion
mcqs.explanation: Louis Pasteur developed the first rabies vaccine in 1885. He created the vaccine by attenuating the virus in rabbit spinal cords, which was a significant milestone in medical history.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The following rabies vaccine will not cause neurological complications?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
74. Viral Encephalitis and Encephalopathy: Rabies, HSV, Arboviral, Nipah, Prion
mcqs.explanation: Tissue culture vaccines are safer and less likely to cause neurological complications. They are prepared from rabies virus grown in cell cultures, unlike nerve tissue vaccines (Semple vaccine) which can cause neuroparalytic reactions.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Negri bodies are found in cells infected with
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
74. Viral Encephalitis and Encephalopathy: Rabies, HSV, Arboviral, Nipah, Prion
mcqs.explanation: Negri bodies are neurotropic inclusions found in neurons infected with rabies virus. They are characteristic of rabies infection and are used for postmortem diagnosis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Inclusion body produced by the Rabies virus is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
74. Viral Encephalitis and Encephalopathy: Rabies, HSV, Arboviral, Nipah, Prion
mcqs.explanation: Negri bodies are characteristic inclusion bodies found in rabies virus-infected cells. They are eosinophilic, cytoplasmic inclusions located in the neurons of infected animals.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The causative agent of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
74. Viral Encephalitis and Encephalopathy: Rabies, HSV, Arboviral, Nipah, Prion
mcqs.explanation: JC virus is the causative agent of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). PML is a demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that occurs in immunocompromised patients, particularly those with HIV/AIDS.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT true about Japanese Encephalitis? (PG Entrance 2020)
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
74. Viral Encephalitis and Encephalopathy: Rabies, HSV, Arboviral, Nipah, Prion
mcqs.explanation: Humans are not the reservoir for Japanese Encephalitis; they are incidental hosts (dead-end hosts). Pigs and birds are the main reservoir hosts. The virus is transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, particularly Culex tritaeniorhynchus.

tags: Parasitic and Fungal Infections of Central Nervous System
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of fungal meningitis?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
75. Parasitic and Fungal Infections CNS: Neurocysticercosis, Amoeba, Toxoplasma, Cryptococcus
mcqs.explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans is the most common cause of fungal meningitis, particularly in immunocompromised patients. It is a yeast-like fungus with a polysaccharide capsule, which is a major virulence factor.

tags: Parasitic and Fungal Infections of Central Nervous System
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Cryptococcus neoformans can be demonstrated in CSF by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
75. Parasitic and Fungal Infections CNS: Neurocysticercosis, Amoeba, Toxoplasma, Cryptococcus
mcqs.explanation: India ink preparation is used to demonstrate the encapsulated yeast cells of Cryptococcus neoformans in CSF. The capsule appears as a clear halo around the yeast cells against a dark background.

tags: Parasitic and Fungal Infections of Central Nervous System
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a free-living amoeba that can cause primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM)?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
75. Parasitic and Fungal Infections CNS: Neurocysticercosis, Amoeba, Toxoplasma, Cryptococcus
mcqs.explanation: Naegleria fowleri is a free-living amoeba that causes primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM). This rare but rapidly fatal infection is acquired through the inhalation of contaminated water during swimming.

tags: Parasitic and Fungal Infections of Central Nervous System
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The most common parasitic infection of the CNS is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
75. Parasitic and Fungal Infections CNS: Neurocysticercosis, Amoeba, Toxoplasma, Cryptococcus
mcqs.explanation: Neurocysticercosis, caused by the larval stage of Taenia solium, is the most common parasitic infection of the CNS. It is a major cause of epilepsy in endemic areas.

tags: Parasitic and Fungal Infections of Central Nervous System
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Toxoplasmosis in immunocompetent individuals is usually
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
75. Parasitic and Fungal Infections CNS: Neurocysticercosis, Amoeba, Toxoplasma, Cryptococcus
mcqs.explanation: Toxoplasmosis in immunocompetent individuals is usually asymptomatic or may present with mild flu-like symptoms. Severe disease occurs primarily in immunocompromised individuals and in congenital infections.

tags: Parasitic and Fungal Infections of Central Nervous System
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is used for the diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
75. Parasitic and Fungal Infections CNS: Neurocysticercosis, Amoeba, Toxoplasma, Cryptococcus
mcqs.explanation: India ink preparation is used for the diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis by demonstrating the encapsulated yeast cells. The capsule appears as a clear halo around the cells.

tags: Parasitic and Fungal Infections of Central Nervous System
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The most common cause of meningitis in HIV patients is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
75. Parasitic and Fungal Infections CNS: Neurocysticercosis, Amoeba, Toxoplasma, Cryptococcus
mcqs.explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans is the most common cause of meningitis in HIV patients. It is an opportunistic infection seen in immunocompromised patients, particularly those with CD4 counts below 100 cells/µL.

tags: Infective Syndromes of Urinary Tract and Sexually Transmitte
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Bacterium is considered significant when the bacterial count per ml of urine is more than
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
76. Urinary Tract Infections and STIs: Enterobacteriaceae, Enterococcus, BK, Schistosoma
mcqs.explanation: Significant bacteriuria is typically defined as the presence of more than 100,000 (10⁵) organisms per milliliter of urine. This is the standard criterion for diagnosing a urinary tract infection.

tags: Infective Syndromes of Urinary Tract and Sexually Transmitte
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following organisms demonstrates Swarming growth when grown on solid media?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
76. Urinary Tract Infections and STIs: Enterobacteriaceae, Enterococcus, BK, Schistosoma
mcqs.explanation: Proteus species are known for their characteristic swarming motility on solid media. This occurs due to their ability to produce flagella and move across the surface of agar plates.

tags: Infective Syndromes of Urinary Tract and Sexually Transmitte
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Virulence factor of proteus for urinary tract infection
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
76. Urinary Tract Infections and STIs: Enterobacteriaceae, Enterococcus, BK, Schistosoma
mcqs.explanation: The production of urease by Proteus increases the pH of urine, which can lead to the formation of kidney stones and is a significant virulence factor for urinary tract infections. Urease hydrolyzes urea to ammonia, raising the pH.

tags: Infective Syndromes of Urinary Tract and Sexually Transmitte
mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Urethritis in males is not caused by (PG Entrance 2020)
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
76. Urinary Tract Infections and STIs: Enterobacteriaceae, Enterococcus, BK, Schistosoma
mcqs.explanation: Haemophilus ducreyi is the causative agent of chancroid, not urethritis. Urethritis in males is commonly caused by organisms like Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Trichomonas vaginalis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Pathogenicity of Neisseria gonorrhoeae is due to
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
77. Infective Syndromes Genital Tract: Syphilis, LGV, Donovanosis, Chancroid, Herpes, Gonorrhea, NGU, Vulvovaginitis
mcqs.explanation: Pili (fimbriae) allow Neisseria gonorrhoeae to attach to mucosal surfaces and evade the host immune response, contributing significantly to pathogenicity. They mediate adhesion and resistance to phagocytosis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: VDRL test is a
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
77. Infective Syndromes Genital Tract: Syphilis, LGV, Donovanosis, Chancroid, Herpes, Gonorrhea, NGU, Vulvovaginitis
mcqs.explanation: The VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) test is a flocculation (precipitation) test used for the serological diagnosis of syphilis. It detects antibodies against cardiolipin.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the causative agent of donovanosis? (PG Entrance 2020)
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
77. Infective Syndromes Genital Tract: Syphilis, LGV, Donovanosis, Chancroid, Herpes, Gonorrhea, NGU, Vulvovaginitis
mcqs.explanation: Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly Calymmatobacterium granulomatis). It is a chronic, granulomatous infection of the genital region.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Treponema pallidum can be cultivated in
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
77. Infective Syndromes Genital Tract: Syphilis, LGV, Donovanosis, Chancroid, Herpes, Gonorrhea, NGU, Vulvovaginitis
mcqs.explanation: Treponema pallidum is cultivated in rabbit testes as it does not grow in standard culture media. This method is used for research and for maintaining the organism for diagnostic purposes.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which test for Syphilis is most suitable for treatment follow up?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
77. Infective Syndromes Genital Tract: Syphilis, LGV, Donovanosis, Chancroid, Herpes, Gonorrhea, NGU, Vulvovaginitis
mcqs.explanation: The VDRL test is used to monitor the effectiveness of syphilis treatment because it measures antibody levels that decline with successful therapy. It is a non-treponemal test that detects antibodies against cardiolipin.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: In patient of syphilis, which of the following test turns positive to negative on treatment?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
77. Infective Syndromes Genital Tract: Syphilis, LGV, Donovanosis, Chancroid, Herpes, Gonorrhea, NGU, Vulvovaginitis
mcqs.explanation: The VDRL test can turn negative after successful treatment of syphilis. This is because it measures non-treponemal antibodies that decline after treatment.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Dark ground illumination is useful for demonstration of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
77. Infective Syndromes Genital Tract: Syphilis, LGV, Donovanosis, Chancroid, Herpes, Gonorrhea, NGU, Vulvovaginitis
mcqs.explanation: Dark ground illumination is used to visualize spirochetes such as Treponema pallidum. This technique allows observation of the organism's characteristic corkscrew morphology.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Lymphogranuloma venereum is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
77. Infective Syndromes Genital Tract: Syphilis, LGV, Donovanosis, Chancroid, Herpes, Gonorrhea, NGU, Vulvovaginitis
mcqs.explanation: Lymphogranuloma venereum is an infection caused by certain serotypes (L1, L2, L3) of Chlamydia trachomatis. It causes inguinal lymphadenopathy and genital ulceration.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Frei's test is used for the diagnosis of
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
77. Infective Syndromes Genital Tract: Syphilis, LGV, Donovanosis, Chancroid, Herpes, Gonorrhea, NGU, Vulvovaginitis
mcqs.explanation: Frei's test is a skin test used for the diagnosis of Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV). It detects delayed-type hypersensitivity to chlamydial antigens.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is caused by L1, L2, L3 serotypes of Chlamydia trachomatis?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
77. Infective Syndromes Genital Tract: Syphilis, LGV, Donovanosis, Chancroid, Herpes, Gonorrhea, NGU, Vulvovaginitis
mcqs.explanation: Lymphogranuloma venereum is caused by the L1, L2, and L3 serotypes of Chlamydia trachomatis. These serotypes are more invasive than those that cause trachoma or inclusion conjunctivitis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Swimming pool conjunctivitis is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Adenovirus is a common cause of "swimming-pool conjunctivitis." It is transmitted through contaminated water and causes acute follicular conjunctivitis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Ophthalmia neonatorum is most commonly caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common cause of ophthalmia neonatorum (neonatal conjunctivitis). It is transmitted to the newborn during delivery through the birth canal.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Keratoconjunctivitis caused by adenovirus is also known as
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Adenoviral keratoconjunctivitis is also known as swimming pool conjunctivitis. It is transmitted through contaminated water and causes acute follicular conjunctivitis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The most common cause of otitis externa is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most common cause of otitis externa (swimmer's ear). It is an opportunistic pathogen that thrives in moist environments.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Inclusion conjunctivitis is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
mcqs.explanation: Inclusion conjunctivitis is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis (serotypes D-K). It is a sexually transmitted infection that can cause conjunctivitis in newborns and adults.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common congenital infection?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
79. Congenital Infections: CMV, Varicella, Neonatal Herpes, Rubella, Toxoplasmosis, Syphilis, Zika
mcqs.explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the most common congenital infection. It is transmitted from mother to fetus during pregnancy and can cause a wide range of congenital anomalies.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Congenital toxoplasmosis is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
79. Congenital Infections: CMV, Varicella, Neonatal Herpes, Rubella, Toxoplasmosis, Syphilis, Zika
mcqs.explanation: Congenital toxoplasmosis is caused by Toxoplasma gondii, a protozoan parasite. It is transmitted from mother to fetus during pregnancy.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Congenital rubella syndrome is characterized by all of the following EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
79. Congenital Infections: CMV, Varicella, Neonatal Herpes, Rubella, Toxoplasmosis, Syphilis, Zika
mcqs.explanation: Congenital rubella syndrome is characterized by the classic triad of cataract, deafness, and heart defects. Hepatomegaly is not a typical feature.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The most common cause of congenital syphilis is
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
79. Congenital Infections: CMV, Varicella, Neonatal Herpes, Rubella, Toxoplasmosis, Syphilis, Zika
mcqs.explanation: Congenital syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum transmitted from mother to fetus. It can cause stillbirth, neonatal death, and a range of congenital anomalies.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Congenital rubella syndrome is caused by infection with rubella virus during
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
79. Congenital Infections: CMV, Varicella, Neonatal Herpes, Rubella, Toxoplasmosis, Syphilis, Zika
mcqs.explanation: Congenital rubella syndrome occurs when rubella virus infection occurs during the first trimester of pregnancy. This is the period of maximal risk for fetal damage.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of congenital CMV infection?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
79. Congenital Infections: CMV, Varicella, Neonatal Herpes, Rubella, Toxoplasmosis, Syphilis, Zika
mcqs.explanation: Congenital CMV infection is characterized by hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, and microcephaly. Macrocephaly is not a feature.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an oncogenic RNA virus?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
80. Organisms with Oncogenic Potential: HPV, KSHV, HTLV, HIV, EBV, HBV, HCV
mcqs.explanation: HTLV-1 is an oncogenic RNA virus (retrovirus) associated with adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. It is transmitted through blood transfusion, sexual contact, and breast milk.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
80. Organisms with Oncogenic Potential: HPV, KSHV, HTLV, HIV, EBV, HBV, HCV
mcqs.explanation: Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV). It is commonly seen in immunocompromised patients, particularly those with AIDS.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All of the following are oncogenic viruses EXCEPT
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
80. Organisms with Oncogenic Potential: HPV, KSHV, HTLV, HIV, EBV, HBV, HCV
mcqs.explanation: Influenza virus is not an oncogenic virus. HPV, EBV, and HCV are well-known oncogenic viruses associated with various cancers.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is associated with
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
80. Organisms with Oncogenic Potential: HPV, KSHV, HTLV, HIV, EBV, HBV, HCV
mcqs.explanation: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer). It is a major cause of liver cancer worldwide.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Case history of pneumonia. Sputum staining reveled partially acid fast branching bacillus. Identify the pathogen?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
55. Miscellaneous Bacterial Skin: Anthrax, Actinomycosis, Nocardiosis, Nonvenereal Treponematoses
mcqs.explanation: (Nocardia) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1st/p295.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The association between HPV and cervical cancer is strongest with which HPV types?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
80. Organisms with Oncogenic Potential: HPV, KSHV, HTLV, HIV, EBV, HBV, HCV
mcqs.explanation: HPV types 16 and 18 are the high-risk types most strongly associated with cervical cancer. They are responsible for approximately 70% of cervical cancers.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following oncogenic viruses is a DNA virus?
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
80. Organisms with Oncogenic Potential: HPV, KSHV, HTLV, HIV, EBV, HBV, HCV
mcqs.explanation: HPV is a DNA virus. HTLV-1 and HIV are RNA viruses (retroviruses). HCV is an RNA virus.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology

options.text: Direct endothelial injury; immediate and sustained
Contraction of endothelial cells; immediate and transient (15–30 minutes)
Leukocyte-mediated injury; delayed by several days

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which mechanism of increased vascular permeability is the most common, and what is its typical time course?
mcqs.explanation:
- Contraction of endothelial cells, forming endothelial gaps, is the COMMONEST mechanism of increased vascular permeability. It occurs immediately after injury and is short-lived (15–30 minutes) — hence termed the "immediate transient response."
- Direct endothelial injury (A) does cause an immediate response, but it is SUSTAINED (e.g. in burns), not transient — this is the key distinguishing feature tested here.
- Leukocyte-mediated injury (C) is not primarily a delayed phenomenon over days in this context.
- Increased transcytosis (D) is a real but less common mechanism, not the most common one.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: In a postoperative ward, 4 out of 10 patients developed wound discharge, which on culture was found to be positive for coagulase positive gram positive cocci. Antimicrobial susceptibility showed that the strain was resistant to Methicillin. On surveillance cultures, a health care personnel attending to the patients was found to be a nasal carrier for the same agent. The following are true regarding the agent responsible for the outbreak:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 7: Skin, Soft Tissue and Musculoskeletal System Infections
mcqs.explanation:
(c) (The orga...) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p219, Ananthanarayan 9/e p205, 8/e p197
• Coagulase positive gram positive cocci: Indicates Staphylococcus aureus
• Resistant to Methicillin: Indicates MRSA (Methicillin resistant S taphylococcus aureus)
• Health care personnel of the hospital found to be nasal carrier for the same agent: Indicates that the infection has spread
to the patient from health care personnel of the hospital
• “The MC way of spread of infection in hospital: Through the hospital staff (not from other patient from the hospital)”
• Mechanism of Resistance of MRSA: Due to chromosomally mediated Mec A gene which codes for altered PBP 2a (Penicillin
Binding protein or receptor 2a) which has less affinity for β lactam drugs.
About Other Options
• The major route of spread causing the outbreak is through the hands of hospital staff
• The resistance to Methicillin is chromosomally mediated
• Since MRSA coded altered PBP 2a (Penicillin Binding protein 2a) has less affinity for β lactam drugs, so MRSA
strains are resistant to all β lactam drugs. Even combination of β lactam and β lactamase inhibitor will not work.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with a localized skin infection presents with warmth, redness, swelling, and pain over the site. The pain is mediated primarily by which class of chemical mediators?
mcqs.explanation:
- Dolor (pain), one of the four cardinal signs described by Celsus, is specifically mediated by prostaglandins and kinins (e.g. bradykinin).
- C3b and iC3b (A) are opsonins that promote phagocytosis, not pain mediators.
- Selectins and integrins (C) mediate leukocyte rolling and adhesion, not pain.
- Acute-phase proteins (D) are involved in the systemic response (e.g. CRP, fibrinogen), not local pain generation.

options.text: Direct endothelial injury; immediate and sustained
Contraction of endothelial cells; immediate and transient (15–30 minutes)
Leukocyte-mediated injury; delayed by several days

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which mechanism of increased vascular permeability is the most common, and what is its typical time course?
mcqs.explanation:
- Contraction of endothelial cells, forming endothelial gaps, is the COMMONEST mechanism of increased vascular permeability. It occurs immediately after injury and is short-lived (15–30 minutes) — hence termed the "immediate transient response."
- Direct endothelial injury (A) does cause an immediate response, but it is SUSTAINED (e.g. in burns), not transient — this is the key distinguishing feature tested here.
- Leukocyte-mediated injury (C) is not primarily a delayed phenomenon over days in this context.
- Increased transcytosis (D) is a real but less common mechanism, not the most common one.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Chemotaxis of leukocytes toward a site of bacterial infection occurs along a concentration gradient of chemoattractants. Which of the following is an ENDOGENOUS chemoattractant (as opposed to a bacterial product)?
mcqs.explanation:
- Leukotriene B4 is an endogenous chemoattractant, produced by the host via the lipoxygenase pathway of arachidonic acid metabolism, along with complement component C5a and chemokines like IL-8.
- N-formylmethionine (A), LPS (C), and peptidoglycan (D) are all exogenous, bacterial-derived chemoattractants/products, not host-derived signals.

options.text: Endogenous pyrogens (IL-1, TNF) → decreased cyclooxygenase activity → decreased prostaglandins → fever
Exogenous pyrogens (e.g. LPS) → stimulate leukocytes to release endogenous pyrogens (IL-1, TNF) → increased cyclooxygenase activity → prostaglandins act on hypothalamus → fever
Prostaglandins directly damage the hypothalamus, causing permanent thermoregulatory failure
Fever occurs independently of any cytokine or prostaglandin involvement

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: During a febrile response to a bacterial infection, which sequence correctly describes the mechanism of fever generation?
mcqs.explanation:
- The correct sequence is: bacterial products (exogenous pyrogens, e.g. LPS) stimulate leukocytes to release endogenous pyrogens (IL-1 and TNF), which increase cyclooxygenase activity, converting arachidonic acid into prostaglandins that act on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center to produce fever.
- A incorrectly states DECREASED cyclooxygenase activity/prostaglandins — the actual mechanism involves an INCREASE, which is also why NSAIDs (which inhibit this pathway) reduce fever.
- C mischaracterizes the mechanism as permanent structural damage rather than a reversible, receptor-mediated resetting of the thermoregulatory set point.
- D is incorrect, since cytokines and prostaglandins are central, well-established mediators of this pathway.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the "Six Rs" of the acute inflammatory response?
mcqs.explanation:
- "Rejection" is not one of the Six Rs; the actual six are: Recognition, Reaction of blood vessels, Reaction/recruitment of leukocytes, Removal of the causative agent, Regulation, and Resolution and repair.
- A, B, and D are all genuine components of the Six Rs framework.
- The distractor "rejection by antibody neutralization alone" also misrepresents how the injurious agent is actually removed (phagocytosis and multiple mechanisms, not antibody alone).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: ==Which infection is a notable exception to the usual 24–48 hour neutrophil-to-monocyte switch, with neutrophils instead predominating for 2 to 4 days?==
mcqs.explanation:
- Pseudomonas infection is specifically noted as an exception where neutrophils continue to predominate for 2 to 4 days, rather than being replaced by monocytes at the usual 24–48 hour mark.
- Staphylococcus aureus (A), Streptococcus pyogenes (C), and E. coli (D) infections follow the more typical neutrophil-to-monocyte transition timeline.

mcqs.question: A VDRL reactive mother gave birth to an infant. All of the following would help in determining the risk of transmission to the infant except:
chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
77. Infective Syndromes Genital Tract: Syphilis, LGV, Donovanosis, Chancroid, Herpes, Gonorrhea, NGU, Vulvovaginitis

Review article- Laboratory Diagnosis and Interpretation of Tests for Syphilis, CMR 1995/V8/no 1, Harrison 18/e p1384
TPHA test on the serum sample of the mother:
• Indicates mother has syphilis. But it doesn’t say about the congenital syphilis. Moreover, TPHA remains elevated even after
treatment. So, an adequately treated mother before 4th month of gestation has a very less risk of transmission but can still have an
elevated TPHA.
About Other Options:
• Since all the nontreponemal tests like VDRL mainly detects IgG, so they cannot be used to detect congenital syphilis as
maternally transferred IgG will be there till 12-18 months of birth. However, VDRL is used for screening in India, and the
interpretation should be done as follows…
• Simultaneous VDRL test of mother and baby:
○ If mother’s titer > baby’s titer → Indicates maternal transfer
○ If baby’s titer > mother’s titer → Indicates congenital infection
• TPHA test on the serum sample of the infant—suggestive of established congenital syphilis
• Adequate treatment of the mother before the 16th week of pregnancy should prevent fetal damage.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Major basic protein (MBP), a key microbicidal/cytotoxic substance released from leukocyte granules, is characteristically found in which cell type and is particularly toxic to which type of organism?
mcqs.explanation:
- Major basic protein (MBP) is present specifically in eosinophil granules and is cytotoxic to many parasites, explaining the important role of eosinophils in anti-parasitic immunity (and their contribution to tissue damage in allergic disease).
- A, C, and D all misattribute MBP to the wrong cell type — it is not a neutrophil, basophil, or macrophage granule constituent.

options.text: Arterioles, throughout the body without exception

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: ==Increased vascular permeability and leukocyte chemotaxis during inflammation occur predominantly in which type of vessel, with one organ-specific exception?==
mcqs.explanation:
- Venules are the most important vessel involved in inflammation, and increased permeability/chemotaxis occurs predominantly in venules — EXCEPT in the lungs, where this occurs in capillaries instead.
- Arterioles (A) and large elastic arteries (C) are not the primary site of these leaky/chemotactic events.
- Lymphatic vessels (D) drain the interstitial fluid produced by inflammation but are not themselves the primary site of the permeability/chemotaxis events described.

options.text: Spontaneous reversal to a pre-injury state with no scarring

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which outcome of acute inflammation occurs specifically when there is extensive fibrin exudation into a serous cavity (e.g. pleura or peritoneum) that cannot be adequately cleared, or when tissue destruction is too extensive for the native tissue to regenerate?
mcqs.explanation:
- Organization (healing by fibrosis) occurs specifically when there is extensive fibrin exudation into a serous cavity that cannot be removed/cleared, when there is significant tissue destruction, or when the affected tissue is incapable of regeneration — connective tissue grows into the damaged area and matures into a fibrous scar.
- Resolution (A) instead occurs when injury is limited, tissue damage is minimal, and the tissue IS capable of regeneration — the opposite scenario from the one described.
- C is a distinct possible outcome (driven by persistence of the injurious agent or abnormal healing), not specifically triggered by uncleared fibrin exudate or non-regenerative tissue as described here.
- D does not reflect any real outcome of acute inflammation — significant injury with non-regenerative tissue does not simply reverse without scarring.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Theory of web of causation was given by?
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation:
(a) (Mc Mohan and Pugh) Ref: Park 21/e p32
Concept of causation of disease:
• Spontaneous generation of life: Life can be created by chemical reactions. It was disproved by Louis Pasteur.
• Germ theory of life or single cause theory (Louis Pasteur) - one to one relationship between causative agent and
disease, i.e. [Agent→ Man→ Disease]. It suffered critics as Not everyone exposed to an agent develops disease.
• Multifactorial causation: Proposed by Pettenkofer and Munich.
• Theory of web of causation: Suggested by MacMahon, Pugh, and Ipsen (1960) in their book Epidemiologic principles
and methods’ that disease is due to the result of complex interrelationship between all the predisposing factors with
variable relative risk.

- B, C, and D are all forms/manifestations of tuberculosis, which characteristically produces CASEATING granulomas due to the combination of delayed-type hypersensitivity and the high lipid content of the mycobacterial cell wall.

• Among immunodeficiency diseases, primary immunodeficiency is relatively uncommon, when compared to secondary
immunodeficiency (common).
• The most common is isolated IgA deficiency, occurs in approximately 1 in 600 individuals (in Europe and North
America) and it is reported in about 0.2% of normal populations.
• Next most common disorder: Common variable immunodeficiency, characterized by pan hypogammaglobulinemia.
• Both of these immunodeficiency states often become clinically evident in young adults.
• The more severe forms of primary immunodeficiency are relatively rare, have their onset early in life, and frequently
result in death during childhood.

mcqs.explanation: Nosocomial infections are infections acquired in a hospital or healthcare facility. These infections develop 48 hours after hospital admission or within 3 days of discharge and are often associated with medical procedures, antibiotic use, or hospital-acquired pathogens.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology

chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Hand hygiene is the single most important measure to prevent hospital-acquired infections. mcqs.question: Which of the following best denotes classical complement pathway activation in immuno inflammatory condition:

(a) (C2, C4, C3...) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p142-3, Ananthanarayan 9/e p121
C2, C3, and C4 all are utilized in Classical pathway, hence their serum level will be low.
Classical pathway:
• Starts by Activation of C1 by antigen antibody complex
• Activated C1 in turn activates C4 to C4a (anaphylotoxin) and C4b
• C1 4b in turn activates C2 (in presence of Mg ion) to form C2a and C2b (kinin like, increases vascular permeability)
• C14b2a is known as C3 convertase which activates C3 to C3a (chemotactic and anaphylotoxin) and C3b
• C14b2a3b is known as C5 convertase which activates C5 to C5a (chemotactic and anaphylotoxin) and C5b
• Late components add to C5b – to form C56789 (membrane attack complex) which forms pores on cell membrane
causing cell lysis and also activates bystander cells to make them susceptible to lysis.

mcqs.question: A patient with recurrent episodes of non-pitting, non-pruritic swelling involving the face and, on occasion, the larynx (posing an airway risk) is found to have low levels of a specific complement regulatory protein. Which deficiency is most likely responsible?
mcqs.explanation:
- Recurrent angioedema, including potentially life-threatening laryngeal involvement, is the classic presentation of inherited C1 inhibitor deficiency, which normally restrains uncontrolled classical complement pathway activation.
- C2 deficiency (A) is the most COMMON complement deficiency overall, but it presents with recurrent Streptococcal septicemia and a lupus-like syndrome in children, not angioedema.
- Factor B deficiency (C) would affect the alternative pathway, not the clinical picture described.
- DAF deficiency (D) is associated with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (complement-mediated red cell lysis), a completely different clinical entity from angioedema.

mcqs.question: Which outcome of acute inflammation occurs specifically when there is extensive fibrin exudation into a serous cavity (e.g. pleura or peritoneum) that cannot be adequately cleared, or when tissue destruction is too extensive for the native tissue to regenerate?
mcqs.explanation:
- Organization (healing by fibrosis) occurs specifically when there is extensive fibrin exudation into a serous cavity that cannot be removed/cleared, when there is significant tissue destruction, or when the affected tissue is incapable of regeneration — connective tissue grows into the damaged area and matures into a fibrous scar.
- Resolution (A) instead occurs when injury is limited, tissue damage is minimal, and the tissue IS capable of regeneration — the opposite scenario from the one described.
- C is a distinct possible outcome (driven by persistence of the injurious agent or abnormal healing), not specifically triggered by uncleared fibrin exudate or non-regenerative tissue as described here.
- D does not reflect any real outcome of acute inflammation — significant injury with non-regenerative tissue does not simply reverse without scarring.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which mechanism of increased vascular permeability is the most common, and what is its typical time course?
mcqs.explanation:
- Contraction of endothelial cells, forming endothelial gaps, is the COMMONEST mechanism of increased vascular permeability. It occurs immediately after injury and is short-lived (15–30 minutes) — hence termed the "immediate transient response."
- Direct endothelial injury (A) does cause an immediate response, but it is SUSTAINED (e.g. in burns), not transient — this is the key distinguishing feature tested here.
- Leukocyte-mediated injury (C) is not primarily a delayed phenomenon over days in this context.
- Increased transcytosis (D) is a real but less common mechanism, not the most common one.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which family of adhesion molecules is primarily responsible for the FIRM adhesion of leukocytes to endothelium, as opposed to the initial rolling phase?
mcqs.explanation:
- Integrins (e.g. LFA-1 and Mac-1 binding ICAM-1; VLA-4 binding VCAM-1) mediate the firm adhesion of leukocytes to activated endothelium, following the initial weak, rolling interaction.
- Selectins (A) mediate the earlier, weaker rolling phase, not firm adhesion — this is the classic point of confusion being tested.
- Cadherins (C) are not the adhesion molecules described in leukocyte-endothelial interactions in this pathway.
- Collagenases (D) are enzymes leukocytes use to penetrate the basement membrane, not adhesion molecules.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Phagocytosis of a bacterium is markedly enhanced when the organism is coated with IgG antibody and complement fragment C3b. This enhancement process is called:
mcqs.explanation:
- Opsonization is specifically the process of coating a particle (e.g. a microbe) with opsonins — such as IgG and C3b — to increase its recognition and phagocytosis by leukocyte receptors (Fc receptor, CR1/CR3).
- Chemotaxis (A) is the directed migration of leukocytes toward a stimulus, not a coating/recognition process.
- Degranulation (C) refers to release of granule contents, unrelated to opsonin coating.
- Transcytosis (D) refers to transport of fluid/protein across endothelial cells, unrelated to phagocytosis enhancement.

mcqs.explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is acid-fast due to the presence of mycolic acid in its cell wall. mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A child with recurrent severe bacterial and fungal infections is found to have a negative nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test. What is the most likely underlying defect?
mcqs.explanation:
- The NBT test depends on direct reduction of NBT by superoxide anion, which requires functional NADPH oxidase (phagocyte oxidase); it is positive in normal individuals but NEGATIVE in chronic granulomatous disease (CGD), which is caused by defects in this enzyme complex — matching the clinical picture of recurrent infections.
- Chédiak-Higashi syndrome (B) involves defective phagolysosome fusion, which is not what the NBT test evaluates, and instead shows giant granules on peripheral smear.
- LAD1 (C) is a leukocyte adhesion defect, unrelated to the oxidative burst measured by NBT.
- Bruton disease (D) is a humoral immunodeficiency (defective opsonization from absent antibody), not a phagocyte oxidative burst defect — NBT would be expected to be normal.

options.text: They directly form the membrane attack complex that lyses bacteria

They are structurally identical to IgE antibodies

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: C3a and C5a are referred to as "anaphylatoxins." What is the basis for this terminology?
mcqs.explanation:
- C3a and C5a are termed anaphylatoxins because they stimulate histamine release from mast cells, causing increased vascular permeability and vasodilation — vascular effects that resemble those seen in anaphylactic reactions, even though the mechanism (complement-driven) differs from classic IgE-mediated anaphylaxis.
- A describes a different complement function (C5b-C9/MAC forming pores for lysis), unrelated to why C3a/C5a specifically are called anaphylatoxins.
- C is factually incorrect — C3a/C5a are complement fragments, structurally unrelated to IgE.
- D is the opposite of their actual action — they PROMOTE, not inhibit, mast cell degranulation.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which endothelial selectin and its complementary leukocyte ligand are correctly matched?
mcqs.explanation:
- P-selectin (CD62E) on endothelium binds Sialyl-Lewis X–modified proteins on the leukocyte — a correct pairing involved in rolling.
- B incorrectly pairs GlyCam-1/CD34 (which actually bind L-selectin/CD62L on the leukocyte) with Sialyl-Lewis X.
- C incorrectly pairs E-selectin (which also binds Sialyl-Lewis X, not L-selectin) with L-selectin.
- D incorrectly pairs L-selectin (a selectin involved in rolling) with ICAM-1 (an integrin ligand involved in the later adhesion step, not rolling).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which vasoactive amine is stored preformed mainly in platelets (along with some neurons and GI enterochromaffin cells), as opposed to the mediator whose richest source is mast cells?
mcqs.explanation:
- Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) is a preformed vasoactive mediator stored mainly in platelets, with additional sources in some neurons and enterochromaffin cells of the GI tract.
- Histamine (A) is instead richest in mast cells (also present in basophils and platelets) — the mediator being contrasted against in this question.
- Bradykinin (C) is a plasma-derived kinin, not a preformed cell-derived vasoactive amine.
- Substance P (D) is a neuropeptide, not a vasoactive amine.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: ==Which enzyme is described as an exception to the general rule that it is inducible rather than constitutive, since it is constitutively expressed in the endothelium and CNS?==
mcqs.explanation:
- COX-2 is generally inducible (in contrast to the mostly constitutive/housekeeping COX-1), but a notable exception is that COX-2 is constitutively present in the endothelium and CNS.
- COX-1 (A) is the one that is mostly constitutive throughout, not the exception being described.
- 5-lipoxygenase (C) and phospholipase A2 (D) are enzymes in the arachidonic acid pathway, but the specific constitutive/inducible exception described applies to COX-2.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which pairing of an endothelial ligand with its corresponding leukocyte integrin, both involved in firm adhesion, is correct?
mcqs.explanation:
- ICAM-1 (an endothelial immunoglobulin-family ligand) binds CD11b/CD18 integrins (LFA-1, Mac-1) on the leukocyte — the correct pairing for firm adhesion; ICAM-1 is also involved in the subsequent transmigration step.
- B incorrectly pairs ICAM-1 with L-selectin, which is instead involved in the earlier rolling step, not firm adhesion via ICAM-1.
- C incorrectly swaps the integrin pairing — VCAM-1 actually binds VLA-4, not CD11b/CD18.
- D incorrectly pairs VCAM-1 with Sialyl-Lewis X, which is instead the selectin ligand involved in rolling, not the VCAM-1/VLA-4 adhesion pairing.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Excess reactive oxygen species released by leukocytes can inactivate antiproteases such as α1-antitrypsin, contributing to tissue destruction in which classic clinical example?
mcqs.explanation:
- ROS-mediated inactivation of α1-antitrypsin (a key antiprotease that normally restrains neutrophil elastase) allows unchecked elastase activity to destroy lung elastic tissue — the classic mechanistic link to emphysema (and the basis for why α1-antitrypsin-deficient patients are especially prone to early emphysema).
- B, C, and D each substitute a plausible-sounding but incorrect disease/enzyme pairing not linked to this specific ROS-antiprotease mechanism.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which outcome of acute inflammation occurs specifically when there is extensive fibrin exudation into a serous cavity (e.g. pleura or peritoneum) that cannot be adequately cleared, or when tissue destruction is too extensive for the native tissue to regenerate?
mcqs.explanation:
- Organization (healing by fibrosis) occurs specifically when there is extensive fibrin exudation into a serous cavity that cannot be removed/cleared, when there is significant tissue destruction, or when the affected tissue is incapable of regeneration — connective tissue grows into the damaged area and matures into a fibrous scar.
- Resolution (A) instead occurs when injury is limited, tissue damage is minimal, and the tissue IS capable of regeneration — the opposite scenario from the one described.
- C is a distinct possible outcome (driven by persistence of the injurious agent or abnormal healing), not specifically triggered by uncleared fibrin exudate or non-regenerative tissue as described here.
- D does not reflect any real outcome of acute inflammation — significant injury with non-regenerative tissue does not simply reverse without scarring.

• The Acute HIV Syndrome presents as acute infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever) like syndrome and characterized
by:
○ General: Fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, headache, arthralgia/myalgia, weight loss and vomiting/diarrhea
○ Neurologic: Meningitis, encephalitis, peripheral neuropathy and myelopathy
○ Dermatologic: Rash and mucocutaneous ulceration
• Lyme disease is not associated with HIV
• Diarrhea in HIV patient is associated with fungal infection such as Histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, and penicilliosis
but not Oropharyngeal candidiasis
• Diarrhea in HIV patient is associated with MAC infection; but not Pulmonary MTB
• Also remember, Causes of Diarrhea in HIV infected patients-
• Bacterial: Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter, Clostridium difficile and MAC
• Parasitic: Cryptosporidium, microsporidia, and Isospora belli
• Fungal: Histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, and penicilliosis
• Viral: CMV colitis
• AIDS enteropathy (chronic diarrheal syndrome for which no etiologic agent)
[UPDATE 2026] This organism was reclassified in 2016 and is now named Clostridioides difficile (the abbreviation C. difficile is unchanged).

mcqs.explanation:
(d) (Microscopy + ELISA) Ref: Harrison 18/e p1685, Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Parasitology 1/e p34
• ‘Microscopy, often combined with serologic testing, remains the standard diagnostic approach in many hospitals and clinics
worldwide for the diagnosis of amebiasis.’
• Stool Microscopy— done to demonstrate:
○ Trophozoites: Indicates active infection
○ Quadrinucleated cysts: Indicates carrier state
• Microscopy is poorly sensitive (25–60% with single sample) but the sensitivity increases to 85–95% when three stool
samples are examined. It cannot differentiate between E. histolytica and other Entamoeba histolytica subspecies such as
E. dispar and E. moshkovskii.
• ELISA detecting 170 kDa of lectin antigen in stool shows > 95% sensitivity and specificity. It can also differentiate
pathogenic E. histolytica (lectin antigen positive) and nonpathogenic E.dispar ((lectin antigen negative).
• Polyxenic culture: 50–70% sensitivity and 100% specificity (gold standard). Serves as a research tool but not available
for clinical use.
• PCR assay for DNA in stool samples is currently the most sensitive and specific method for identifying E. histolytica
infection and has become a valuable epidemiologic and research tool.

mcqs.question: CMV retinitis in HIV occurs when the CD4 counts falls below:

Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation:
(a) (50) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p508, Harrison 18/e p1563
• The majority of cases of CMV retinitis occur in patients with a CD4+ T-cell count < 50/μl.
• CD4+ T-cell count < 50/μl is more prone for infections with MAC, T.gondii & CMV
• CD4+ T-cell count < 200/μl is more prone for infections with Pneumocystis jirovecii.
• Patients with HIV infection should have CD4+ T-cell measurements performed at the time of diagnosis and every 3–6
months thereafter.
• CD4 T-cell count < 350/μl is an indication for consideration of initiating ARV therapy.
• Decline in CD4+ T-cell count of > 25% is an indication for considering a change in therapy.
• Once the CD4+ T-cell count is < 200/μl, patients should be placed on a regimen for P. jiroveci prophylaxis,
• Once the count is < 50/μl, primary prophylaxis for MAC infection is indicated.

Anaero bic bacteria do not have cytochrome system for oxygen metabolism and hence are
unable to neutralize toxic oxygen metabolites. They can be classified as:
• Obligate anaerobes: They cannot grow in presence of oxygen as they completely lack
superoxide dismutase and catalase and are susceptible to the lethal effects of oxygen. For
example, Clostridium and non-sporing anaerobes
• Aerotolerant anaerobes: They do not utilize oxygen for growth, but tolerate its presence.
This is because they possess small amounts of superoxide dismutase and peroxidase
(but lack catalase) which may neutralize the toxic oxygen radicals. Examples include
Clostridium histolyticum and Bacteroides.

chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Anaphylaxis is a severe, immediate allergic reaction classified as type I hypersensitivity. It is mediated by IgE antibodies that trigger mast cells and basophils to release histamine and other mediators, causing vasodilation, bronchoconstriction, and cardiovascular collapse.

chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A lung biopsy from a severely immunocompromised patient (advanced HIV/AIDS) with disseminated tuberculosis shows sheets of macrophages packed with numerous acid-fast bacilli, but no organized epithelioid cell aggregates, giant cells, or caseous necrosis. What best explains this appearance?
mcqs.explanation:
- Because granuloma formation fundamentally depends on an intact CD4+ T-cell response (antigen presentation, Th1 differentiation, IFN-γ-mediated macrophage activation), severely immunocompromised patients — classically advanced HIV/AIDS — often cannot mount an organized granulomatous response. Instead, tissue shows poorly organized sheets of macrophages heavily laden with mycobacteria, reflecting uncontrolled bacterial proliferation without effective immune containment.
- A is incorrect — the findings described (heavy bacterial load, no organization) indicate active, uncontrolled infection, not latent/controlled disease.
- C is incorrect — this description does not match sarcoidosis, which shows well-formed non-caseating granulomas, not sheets of bacteria-laden macrophages.
- D is incorrect — healed disease would show fibrosis and calcification, not active macrophage sheets packed with organisms.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Eosinophils are recruited to sites of parasitic infection or allergic inflammation predominantly under the influence of which chemokine?
mcqs.explanation:
- Eotaxin is the chemokine specifically responsible for recruiting eosinophils to sites of parasitic infection and allergic (IgE-mediated) inflammation.
- IL-8 (A) is a chemokine more classically associated with neutrophil recruitment, not eosinophils specifically.
- LTB4 (C) and C5a (D) are general chemoattractants for multiple leukocyte types (including neutrophils), not eosinophil-selective recruiting factors like eotaxin.

options.text: Mast cells do not express any antibody receptors

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Mast cells participate in inflammatory reactions through receptors that bind which portion of an antibody, triggering degranulation upon antigen exposure?
mcqs.explanation:
- Mast cells express receptors that bind the Fc portion of IgE; when antigen cross-links IgE bound to these receptors, the mast cell degranulates, releasing histamine — the basis of allergic/anaphylactic reactions.
- B, C, and D all misdescribe the actual receptor-antibody relationship responsible for mast cell activation, which specifically involves IgE Fc receptors (FcεRI).

[UPDATE 2026] WHO revised these definitions in January 2021. XDR-TB now means MDR/RR-TB plus resistance to any fluoroquinolone plus resistance to at least one other Group A drug (bedaquiline or linezolid). A new category, pre-XDR-TB, covers MDR/RR-TB with fluoroquinolone resistance alone. The older definition, based on resistance to a fluoroquinolone plus a second-line injectable (amikacin, kanamycin or capreomycin), is no longer used, since injectables have been dropped from recommended regimens.

genital tract.

in countries where Hib vaccines are used widely.

Concept of causation of disease:
• Spontaneous generation of life: Life can be created by chemical reactions. It was disproved by Louis Pasteur.
• Germ theory of life or single cause theory (Louis Pasteur) - one to one relationship between causative agent and
disease, i.e. [Agent→ Man→ Disease]. It suffered critics as Not everyone exposed to an agent develops disease.
• Multifactorial causation: Proposed by Pettenkofer and Munich.
• Theory of web of causation: Suggested by MacMahon, Pugh, and Ipsen (1960) in their book Epidemiologic principles
and methods’ that disease is due to the result of complex interrelationship between all the predisposing factors with
variable relative risk.

mcqs.question: Which of the following correctly describes the opposing local vascular actions of thromboxane A2 (TXA2) and prostacyclin (PGI2), both products of the cyclooxygenase pathway?

- C and D both incorrectly claim identical or absent effects, ignoring the well-established opposing roles of these two eicosanoids.

- Lipoxins (C) are anti-inflammatory and would not cause bronchospasm.
- 5-HETE (D) is chemotactic for neutrophils and a leukotriene precursor, not itself the primary bronchospasm mediator.

options.text: Predominance of mononuclear cells (macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells) rather than neutrophils, along with evidence of tissue destruction and repair occurring together
