mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which feature most reliably distinguishes chronic inflammation from acute inflammation on histology?
mcqs.explanation:
- The histologic hallmark distinguishing chronic from acute inflammation is the predominance of mononuclear cells (macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells) instead of neutrophils, together with simultaneous evidence of ongoing tissue destruction and attempted repair (angiogenesis, fibrosis).
- B is meaningless as a distinguishing feature — blood vessels are present in essentially all vascularized inflamed tissue, acute or chronic.
- C is incorrect — both acute and chronic inflammation are defined by the PRESENCE, not absence, of immune cells.
- D is incorrect — fibrinous exudate is a pattern seen in ACUTE inflammation (e.g. fibrinous pericarditis), not something exclusive to chronic inflammation.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with a serous effusion in a joint (synovitis) following a mild viral illness is found to have thin, straw-colored fluid with few cells on aspiration. This is an example of which morphologic pattern of acute inflammation?
mcqs.explanation:
- Serous inflammation is characterized by a marked outpouring of thin, straw-yellow, cell-poor fluid — classic examples include skin blisters from burns/viral infection, synovitis, and pleural effusions complicating pneumonia, matching this scenario.
- Suppurative inflammation (B) would show thick, purulent, neutrophil-rich pus, not thin serous fluid.
- Fibrinous inflammation (C) would show a fibrin-rich exudate, not a clear, cell-poor fluid.
- Necrotizing inflammation (D) refers to a pattern combining necrosis with bacterial putrefaction (gangrene), unrelated to this presentation.

mcqs.explanation:
- Pseudomembranous colitis is classically caused by Clostridium difficile colonization of the bowel, typically following disruption of normal flora by broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment.
- Corynebacterium diphtheriae (A) causes membranous inflammation of the pharynx/larynx (diphtheria), a different anatomic site and a distinct (though related-sounding) morphologic pattern.
- Staphylococcus aureus (C) is a classic cause of suppurative/abscess-forming infections (e.g. boils), not pseudomembranous colitis.
- Mycobacterium tuberculosis (D) causes caseating granulomatous disease, unrelated to this pattern.

options.text: Tuberculosis granulomas lack any lymphocytic component
The combination of the delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction and the high lipid content of the mycobacterial cell wall produces caseation
Caseous necrosis occurs in all granulomas equally, regardless of cause
Caseation results purely from bacterial exotoxin release

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the primary explanation for why tuberculosis granulomas characteristically undergo central caseous necrosis, unlike most other granulomas (e.g. sarcoidosis)?
mcqs.explanation:
- The characteristic caseous necrosis of TB granulomas results from the combined effect of the host's own delayed-type hypersensitivity response and the high lipid content of the mycobacterial cell wall — this combination is relatively distinctive to mycobacterial (and some fungal) infections.
- A is factually incorrect — TB granulomas DO have a peripheral lymphocytic cuff, like other immune granulomas.
- C is incorrect — caseation is specifically a feature of certain granulomas (TB, some fungal infections), not a universal feature (sarcoidosis and foreign body granulomas are non-caseating).
- D is incorrect — Mycobacterium tuberculosis does not act primarily through a classical secreted exotoxin; the necrosis is host-immune-mediated rather than direct toxin-mediated.

options.text: Lymphocytic cuff → epithelioid cells → caseous necrosis → fibroblasts
Caseous necrosis → epithelioid cells (with Langhans giant cells) → lymphocytic cuff → peripheral fibroblasts
Fibroblasts → caseous necrosis → lymphocytic cuff → epithelioid cells
Epithelioid cells → caseous necrosis → fibroblasts → lymphocytic cuff

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: On microscopy of a tuberculous granuloma, going from the center outward, which is the correct order of zones?
mcqs.explanation:
- The classic tuberculous granuloma is organized with central eosinophilic caseous necrosis, surrounded by a rim of epithelioid cells (often palisading, with scattered Langhans giant cells), then an outer cuff of lymphocytes, with fibroblasts and early fibrosis at the very periphery.
- The other options scramble this center-to-periphery order and do not reflect the actual zonal architecture.

• Emerging infectious diseases are defined by WHO
• Those infections, the incidence of which in humans has either increased during the last 2 decades or threatens to
increase in near future
• These are newly appearing infectious diseases or those spreading to new geographical areas.
[UPDATE 2026] Two further highly pathogenic coronaviruses have emerged since SARS-CoV (2002-03): MERS-CoV (Saudi Arabia, 2012, with dromedary camels as the reservoir) and SARS-CoV-2, which emerged in Wuhan in December 2019 and caused the COVID-19 pandemic (declared a PHEIC in January 2020; PHEIC status ended in May 2023). SARS-CoV-2 is now an endemic seasonal respiratory pathogen.
[UPDATE 2026] Nipah virus has caused repeated outbreaks in Kerala since 2018, with further episodes in subsequent years, alongside near-annual outbreaks in Bangladesh. Fruit bats of the genus Pteropus are the reservoir; transmission occurs via contaminated date palm sap, intermediate hosts and person-to-person spread. There is still no licensed vaccine or specific antiviral.

○ For rapid diagnosis along with rapid drug sensitivity detection.

chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control

The region spans approximately 4 megabases and is one of the most polymorphic regions of the human genome.

mcqs.question: Which family of adhesion molecules is primarily responsible for the FIRM adhesion of leukocytes to endothelium, as opposed to the initial rolling phase?
mcqs.explanation:
- Integrins (e.g. LFA-1 and Mac-1 binding ICAM-1; VLA-4 binding VCAM-1) mediate the firm adhesion of leukocytes to activated endothelium, following the initial weak, rolling interaction.
- Selectins (A) mediate the earlier, weaker rolling phase, not firm adhesion — this is the classic point of confusion being tested.
- Cadherins (C) are not the adhesion molecules described in leukocyte-endothelial interactions in this pathway.
- Collagenases (D) are enzymes leukocytes use to penetrate the basement membrane, not adhesion molecules.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: C1 inhibitor deficiency can cause
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Deficiency of C1 inhibitor leads to hereditary angioneurotic oedema (HAE). This condition is characterized by recurrent episodes of edema in the skin, gastrointestinal tract, and airways due to uncontrolled activation of the complement and contact systems. C1 inhibitor normally prevents excessive complement activation.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Hereditary angioneurotic oedema is caused by
chapterPath: PART I: General Microbiology, Immunology and Hospital Infection Control
mcqs.explanation: Hereditary angioneurotic oedema is caused by a deficiency of C1 inhibitor, which normally regulates the complement and contact systems. Without C1 inhibitor, excessive C1 activation leads to increased vascular permeability and edema. This condition is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.

mcqs.explanation: Toxoids are modified toxins that are antigenic but no longer toxic. They are produced by treating toxins with heat or formaldehyde to inactivate their toxic properties while retaining immunogenicity. Toxoids are used in vaccines to induce immunity against diphtheria and tetanus.

Ebola virus:

• Ebola then spreads among people via DIRECT CLOSE CONTACT (through broken skin or mucous membranes of
eyes, nose, or mouth)
• There is no specific drug available, only symptomatic treatment can be given.
• The largest outbreak occurred in 2014; mainly in three West African countries: Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
[UPDATE 2026] Since the 2014-16 West African epidemic, an rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine (Ervebo) was licensed in 2019 and two monoclonal antibody treatments (Inmazeb and Ebanga) were approved in 2020 for Zaire ebolavirus. Further outbreaks have occurred in DR Congo and Uganda, including Sudan virus outbreaks for which the Ervebo vaccine does not protect.

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Humans are not the reservoir for Japanese Encephalitis; they are incidental hosts (dead-end hosts). Pigs and birds (especially water birds like herons) are the main reservoir hosts. The virus is transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, particularly Culex tritaeniorhynchus and Culex vishnui. Vaccination of pigs has been shown to reduce transmission in endemic areas by breaking the transmission cycle.

chapterPath: PART II: Systemic Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
Section 4: Bloodstream and Cardiovascular System Infections
mcqs.explanation: Plasmodium falciparum typically presents with multiple ring forms within the same red blood cell and is known for its high parasitemia levels. The rings appear delicate and thin, and the red blood cells are not enlarged, which are typical features of P. falciparum infection. Also, P. falciparum has appliqué (accolé) forms with rings at the edge of RBCs, and Maurer's dots may be present.

15. Immune Responses: Cell Mediated and Antibody Mediated
mcqs.explanation:
(b) (Thymocytes whose..) Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology 1/e p150
CD 4 and CD 8 double positive (DP) T-cells are not eliminated completely. They have three fates:
• Positive selection: The 5% of DP T-cells, whose αβ receptors are capable of recognizing their MHC molecules are
positively selected. This results in MHC restriction.
• Death by neglect: Majority of DP cells (95%) fail positive selection because they do not specifically recognize their MHC
molecules.
• Negative selection: The survived cells that undergo positive selection (5%) are MHC restricted. However, some of these
surviving cells (2–5%) react to the self antigens and therefore, they are selected to be killed by apoptosis and removed
(negatively selection).
• The remaining DP T-cells (2–5%) having αβ type TCR selectively loose either CD4 or CD8 and become single positive
mature T-cells
About Other options:
• Mature thymocytes are single positive; i.e. they express either CD 4 or CD 8; but never both.
• Mature B cells (not thymocytes) express surface IgM and IgD.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the "Six Rs" of the acute inflammatory response?
mcqs.explanation:
- "Rejection" is not one of the Six Rs; the actual six are: Recognition, Reaction of blood vessels, Reaction/recruitment of leukocytes, Removal of the causative agent, Regulation, and Resolution and repair.
- A, B, and D are all genuine components of the Six Rs framework.
- The distractor "rejection by antibody neutralization alone" also misrepresents how the injurious agent is actually removed (phagocytosis and multiple mechanisms, not antibody alone).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: C3a and C5a are referred to as "anaphylatoxins." What is the basis for this terminology?
mcqs.explanation:
- C3a and C5a are termed anaphylatoxins because they stimulate histamine release from mast cells, causing increased vascular permeability and vasodilation — vascular effects that resemble those seen in anaphylactic reactions, even though the mechanism (complement-driven) differs from classic IgE-mediated anaphylaxis.
- A describes a different complement function (C5b-C9/MAC forming pores for lysis), unrelated to why C3a/C5a specifically are called anaphylatoxins.
- C is factually incorrect — C3a/C5a are complement fragments, structurally unrelated to IgE.
- D is the opposite of their actual action — they PROMOTE, not inhibit, mast cell degranulation.

options.text: Arterioles, throughout the body without exception
Venules, except in the lungs, where it occurs in capillaries
Large elastic arteries, in all organs

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: ==Increased vascular permeability and leukocyte chemotaxis during inflammation occur predominantly in which type of vessel, with one organ-specific exception?==
mcqs.explanation:
- Venules are the most important vessel involved in inflammation, and increased permeability/chemotaxis occurs predominantly in venules — EXCEPT in the lungs, where this occurs in capillaries instead.
- Arterioles (A) and large elastic arteries (C) are not the primary site of these leaky/chemotactic events.
- Lymphatic vessels (D) drain the interstitial fluid produced by inflammation but are not themselves the primary site of the permeability/chemotaxis events described.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 16-year-old boy sustained blunt trauma to the abdomen when the vehicle he was driving struck a bridge abutment at high speed. Peritoneal lavage shows a hemoperitoneum, and at laparotomy, a small portion of the left lobe of the liver is removed because of the injury. Several weeks later, a CT scan of the abdomen shows that the liver has nearly regained its size before the injury. Which of the following processes best explains this CT scan finding?
mcqs.explanation:
(E) The liver is one of the few organs in the human body that can partially regenerate. This is a form of compensatory hyperplasia. The stimuli to hepatocyte mitotic activity cease when the liver has attained its normal size.
Apoptosis is single cell death and frequently occurs with viral hepatitis.
Dysplasia is disordered epithelial cell growth that can be premalignant.
Fatty change can lead to hepatomegaly; this is not a regenerative process but is the result of toxic hepatocyte injury.
Hydropic change, or cell swelling, does not produce regeneration.
Hepatocytes can reenter the cell cycle and proliferate to regenerate the liver; they do not just increase in size (hypertrophy).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
